nodes.title: Definition of Convergence
nodes.content:
**Definition 177**  
A sequence $\{x_n\}$ of points of a metric space $X$ converges to $x \in X$ if for each neighborhood $B_\varepsilon(x)$ of $x$ there exists $n_\varepsilon \ge 1$ such that $x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x)$ for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$. In this case, we write
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \quad \text{or} \quad x_n \to x.
$$ The point $x$ is called the limit of the sequence $\{x_n\}$; a sequence that has a limit point is called **convergent**.


Your definition says:

- $\{x_n\}$ is a sequence of points of the metric space $X$.
- Convergence is defined as $x_n \to x$ with $x \in X$.
- Neighborhoods $B_\varepsilon(x)$ are neighborhoods in $X$.

There is no requirement in the definition that $x \in C$.  
So even if every $x_n$ lies in $C$, the definition only checks proximity in $X$.


Key consequence (very important).  
A subset $C \subset X$ is closed if and only if every sequence $\{x_n\} \subset C$ that converges in $X$ has its limit in $C$.

So:
- limits outside $C$ can happen;
- closed sets are exactly the ones where this never happens.


Concrete example.  
Let

$$
X = \mathbb{R}, \quad C = (0,1)
$$

Define

$$
x_n = \frac{1}{n}
$$

Then:
- $x_n \in C$ for all $n \ge 2$;

but

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = 0
$$

and

$$
0 \in X \quad \text{but} \quad 0 \notin C
$$

So the sequence converges in $X$, but not in $C$.

nodes.title: Limit characterization of convergence
nodes.content:
**Lemma 178**  
A sequence $\{x_n\}$ of points of a metric space $X$ converges to $x \in X$ if and only if
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} d(x_n, x) = 0.
$$

**Proof**  
*“Only if.”* Let $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x$. We want to show that the sequence of scalars $\{d(x_n, x)\}$ converges to $0$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ (any!). By definition, there is $n_\varepsilon \ge 1$ such that $x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x)$ for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$, that is, such that $d(x_n, x) < \varepsilon$ for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$. Since $|d(x_n, x) - 0| = d(x_n, x)$, this in turn implies $|d(x_n, x) - 0| < \varepsilon$ for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$, and so $\lim_{n \to \infty} d(x_n, x) = 0.$

*“If.”* Suppose that $\lim_{n \to \infty} d(x_n, x) = 0$. We want to show that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ converges to $x$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\lim_{n \to \infty} d(x_n, x) = 0$, **by definition** (learn this) there exists $n_\varepsilon \ge 1$ such that $|d(x_n, x) - 0| < \varepsilon$ for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$. Since $d(x_n, x) = |d(x_n, x) - 0|$, this in turn implies $d(x_n, x) < \varepsilon$, and so $x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x)$ for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$, as desired.

nodes.title: Example of convergence in R. Always use the characterization
nodes.content:
Example 179.  
Let $X = \mathbb{R}^2$, endowed with the Euclidean metric, and consider the sequence (6.10). We have

$$
d_2\left((0,0), \left(\frac{1}{n}, \frac{1}{n^2}\right)\right)
= \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right)^2}
= \frac{\sqrt{n^2 + 1}}{n^2} \to 0
$$

and therefore the sequence converges to $x = (0,0)$. The sequence (6.11), instead, does not converge to any vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

nodes.title: Examples of convergence in seuquences
nodes.content:
Example 180.  
Let $X = C([0,1])$, endowed with the metric $d_\infty$, and let $0$ be the identically null function. For the sequence $\{f_n\}$ given by (6.13), that is $f_n(t) = \frac{t^n}{n}$, we have

$$
0 \le d_\infty(f_n,0)
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)|
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} \frac{t^n}{n}
\le \frac{1}{n} \to 0
$$

which implies $d_\infty(f_n,0) \to 0$. The sequence thus converges to the function $0 \in C([0,1])$.


Example 181.  
As to the sequence (6.12), we have

$$
d_1(f_n,0)
= \int_0^1 |f_n(t)|
= \int_0^1 t^n \, dt
= \frac{1}{n+1} \to 0
$$

and so also this sequence converges to $0$. It is important to note that this is an example of a sequence that is convergent according to a metric (the $d_1$), but divergent according to another metric (the $d_\infty$). In fact, suppose by contradiction that this is the case, and let $f \in C([0,1])$ be such that $t^n \to f$ with respect to $d_\infty$. Therefore,

$$
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |t^n - f(t)| \to 0
$$

so that $|t^n - f(t)| \to 0$ for each $t \in [0,1]$, that is $t^n \to f(t)$ for each $t \in [0,1]$. Since $t^n \to 0$ for each $t \in [0,1)$, while $t^n \to 1$ if $t = 1$, it follows that

$$
f(t) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } t = 1\\
0 & \text{if } t \in [0,1)
\end{cases}
$$

Since $f$ has a jump at $t = 1$ and so it is not continuous, this contradicts $f \in C([0,1])$. We conclude that the sequence (6.12) is not convergent in $C([0,1])$.

nodes.title: Point wise characterization of convergence
nodes.content:
**Proposition 182**  
Let $\{x_n\}_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of vectors $x_n = (x_{n1}, \ldots, x_{nm})$ of $\mathbb{R}^m$. We have $x_n \xrightarrow{d_1} x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ if and only if $x_{ni} \to x_i \in \mathbb{R}$ for each $i = 1, \ldots, m$.

**Proof**  
- Suppose that $x_n \xrightarrow{d_1} x \in \mathbb{R}^m$. By [[6.2.4 Lemma 178 Limit Characterization of convergence]],$$
d_1(x_n, x) = \sum_{i=1}^m |x_{ni} - x_i|  \to 0.
$$Therefore,$$
0 \le |x_{ni} - x_i| \le \sum_{i=1}^m |x_{ni} - x_i| \to 0,
$$for each $i = 1, \ldots, m$, and consequently $x_{ni} \to x_i \in \mathbb{R}$ for each $i = 1, \ldots, m$.

- Vice-versa, suppose that $x_{ni} \to x_i \in \mathbb{R}$ for each $i = 1, \ldots, m$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ (any!!). For each $i = 1, \ldots, m$ there exists $n_i^\varepsilon \ge 1$ such that $|x_{ni} - x_i| < \varepsilon / m$ for each $n \ge n_i^\varepsilon$. Therefore, we have $|x_{ni} - x_i| < \varepsilon / m$ for each $n \ge \max_{i = 1, \ldots, m} n_i^\varepsilon$ and each $i = 1, \ldots, m$. It follows that for each $n \ge \max_{i=1,\ldots,m} n_i^\varepsilon$ we have
$$
d_1(x_n, x) = \sum_{i=1}^m |x_{ni} - x_i| < \frac{\varepsilon}{m} + \cdots + \frac{\varepsilon}{m} = \varepsilon,
$$
	and therefore $x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x)$. In conclusion, $x_n \xrightarrow{d_1} x$. Proposition 182 is easily seen to hold also for the metrics $d_2$ and $d_\infty$.

nodes.title: Uniqueness of the limit
nodes.content:
**Proposition 183 — A convergent sequence in a metric space has a unique limit.**

**Proof.**  
Let $\{x_n\}$ be a convergent sequence of a metric space $X$.  

Suppose there exist $x, y \in X$ such that $x_n \to x$ and $x_n \to y$.  We want to prove that $x = y$.

Suppose by contradiction that $x \ne y$.  
For $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small, we have two neighborhoods $B_\varepsilon(x)$ and $B_\varepsilon(y)$ such that
$$
B_\varepsilon(x) \cap B_\varepsilon(y) = \varnothing.
$$
By [[6.2.3 Definition 177 Convergence in X]], there exist $n_\varepsilon^1, n_\varepsilon^2 \ge 1$ such that
$$
x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x) \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_\varepsilon^1
$$
and
$$
x_n \in B_\varepsilon(y) \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_\varepsilon^2.
$$
Therefore,
$$
x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x) \cap B_\varepsilon(y)
\quad \text{for all } n \ge \max\{ n_\varepsilon^1, n_\varepsilon^2 \},
$$
which contradicts
$$
B_\varepsilon(x) \cap B_\varepsilon(y) = \varnothing.
$$
It follows that $x = y$, and the limit is therefore unique. ■

nodes.title: A point is a limit point iff each of its neigh contains all the poitns of the sequence except a finite number
nodes.content:
**Proposition 184 — A sequence of points of a metric space $X$ converges to $x \in X$ if and only if each neighborhood of $x$ contains all points of the sequence, except at most a finite number of them.**

**Proof.**  
Suppose that $x_n \to x$. For each $\varepsilon > 0$, there  $\exists n_\varepsilon \ge 1$ s.t.
$$
x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x) \quad \text{for each } n \ge n_\varepsilon.
$$
Therefore, except for the points $x_n$ with $1 \le n < n_\varepsilon$, all other points of the sequence belong to $B_\varepsilon(x)$.
Vice-versa, given a neighborhood $B_\varepsilon(x)$, suppose that all points of the sequence belong to it, except at most a finite number of them.  
Denote by $\{x_{n_k}\}_{k=1}^m$ the set of points of the sequence that do **not** belong to $B_\varepsilon(x)$.

Setting $n_\varepsilon = n_m + 1$, we therefore have
$$
x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x) \quad \text{for each } n \ge n_\varepsilon.
$$
Since this is true for each neighborhood $B_\varepsilon(x)$ of $x$, it follows that $x_n \to x$. ■

nodes.title: A convergent sequence in a metric space is bounded
nodes.content:
**Proposition 185 — A convergent sequence in a metric space is bounded.**

**Proof.**  
Suppose that $x_n \to x$. Setting $\varepsilon = 1$, there exists $n_1 \ge 1$ such that
$$
x_n \in B_1(x) \quad \text{for each } n \ge n_1.
$$
Let $M > 0$ be such that
$$
M > \max \{ 1,\ d(x_1,x),\ \dots,\ d(x_{n_1-1},x) \}.
$$
We have $d(x_n,x) < M$ for each $n \ge 1$ and, therefore, the image of the sequence is contained in the neighborhood $B_M(x)$.  The sequence is therefore bounded. ■

Proposition 185 gives us a simple sufficient condition for a sequence to diverge: if the image of the sequence is not bounded, then the sequence diverges. For example, the sequence $x_n = 2n$ diverges because it has as image the unbounded set $\{1,2,3,\dots,n,\dots\}$.


**Definition**
A sequence $\{x_n\}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is increasing if $x_n \le x_{n+1}$ for each $n \ge 1$, while it is decreasing if $x_n \ge x_{n+1}$ for each $n \ge 1$.  
In general, a sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ is monotonic if it is increasing or decreasing (it is both increasing and decreasing if and only if it is constant).  
For this class of sequences, boundedness is a necessary and sufficient condition for convergence.

nodes.title: A monotonic sequence in R is convergent if and only if it is bounded.
nodes.content:
idea: perchè non può oscillare!

**Proposition 186 — A monotonic sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ is convergent if and only if it is bounded.**

**Proof.**  
Let $\{x_n\}$ be an increasing sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ (the proof of the decreasing case is similar).  
If it is convergent, Proposition 185 guarantees that it is bounded.

Viceversa, suppose that this sequence is bounded. We want to prove that it is convergent.  
Let $E$ be the image of the sequence. By hypothesis, it is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$.  
By the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, $\sup E$ exists. Set $x = \sup E$.

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ (any!). Since $x$ is the supremum of $E$, we have:  
(i) $x \ge x_n$ for each $n \ge 1$,  
(ii) there $\exists$ an element of $E$, denoted $x_{n_\varepsilon}$, such that
$$
x_{n_\varepsilon} > x - \varepsilon.
$$
Since $\{x_n\}$ is an increasing sequence, it follows that
$$
x \ge x_n \ge x_{n_\varepsilon} > x - \varepsilon,
\qquad \forall n \ge n_\varepsilon,
$$
and therefore
$$
x_n \in B_\varepsilon(x) \quad \text{for each } n \ge n_\varepsilon, \forall \varepsilon
$$
and this proves convergence, as desired. ■

nodes.title: Definition of bounded
nodes.content:
Given a sequence $f : \mathbb{N} - \{0\} \to X$ of points of a metric space, $f(\mathbb{N} - \{0\})$ is called the image of the sequence. Naturally, the image does not take into account the repetitions that may occur in the sequence. For example, the constant sequence $\{2,2,2,\ldots\}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ has as image the singleton $\{2\}$, while the sequence $\{-1,1,-1,1,\ldots\}$ has as image the set of the two elements $\{-1,1\}$.

A sequence $\{x_n\}$ is said to be **bounded** if its image is a bounded set of $X$.

nodes.title: Sequential definition of closure
nodes.content:
**Theorem 188**  
Let $A$ be a set of a metric space $X$. We have $x \in \overline{A}$ $\iff$ there $\exists$ a sequence $\{x_n\} \subseteq A$ such that $x_n \to x$.

**Proof**  
“Only if.” Let $x \in \overline{A}$. If $x$ is an isolated point of $A$, set $x_n = x$ for each $n \ge 1$. This constant sequence trivially converges to $x$. If $x \in A'$, consider the neighborhoods $B_{1/n}(x)$ of $x$. Each of these neighborhoods contains a point $x_n$ of $A$ distinct from $x$. Pick any such point and construct the sequence $\{x_n\}$. Since $d(x_n, x) < 1/n$, this sequence converges to $x$, as desired.

“If.” Let $x \in X$ be st there $\exists$ a sequence $\{x_n\} \subseteq A$ with $x_n \to x$. Each neighborhood $B_\varepsilon(x)$ of $x$ (the limit points) contains points of the sequence (by definition of convergence), that is, $B_\varepsilon(x) \cap A \neq \varnothing$. The point $x$ therefore is not an interior point of $A^c$, that is, $x \notin \operatorname{int} A^c$. It follows that $x \in \overline{A}$ since in the first part of the proof of point (i) of Proposition 171 we proved that $\operatorname{int} A^c = \overline{A}^c$.

nodes.title: Sequential definition of closed sets
nodes.content:
The only point in 189 is that the limit point has to belong to the set! 
**Corollary 189**  
A set $A$ is closed if and only if $x \in A$ whenever there exists a sequence $\{x_n\} \subseteq A$ such that $x_n \to x$.

**Proof**  
“Only if.” Let $A$ be closed. Since $A = \overline{A}$, by Theorem 188 it holds $x \in A$ if and only if there exists a sequence $\{x_n\} \subseteq A$ such that $x_n \to x$.

“If.” Let $x \in \overline{A}$. By Theorem 188 there exists $\{x_n\} \subseteq A$ such that $x_n \to x$. By hypothesis, this implies $x \in A$, and so $\overline{A} \subseteq A$. Therefore, $\overline{A} = A$, which implies that $A$ is closed.


Thanks to this corollary, to establish whether a set $A$ is closed it is sufficient to consider a generic sequence $\{x_n\} \subseteq A$ such that $x_n \to x$. If we prove that also the limit point $x$ belongs to $A$, we can conclude that $A$ is closed.

nodes.title: Cauchy Criterion
nodes.content:
**Definition 192**  
A sequence $\{x_n\}$ of a metric space $(X,d)$ satisfies the Cauchy criterion if, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, there $\exists n_\varepsilon \ge 1$ st $d(x_n, x_m) < \varepsilon$ for each $n, m \ge n_\varepsilon$.

nodes.title: Convergent Sequences are cauchy
nodes.content:
**Proposition 193**  
Each convergent sequence in a metric space is a Cauchy sequence.

**Proof**  
Let $x_n \to x$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $n_\varepsilon \ge 1$ such that $d(x_n, x) < \varepsilon/2$ for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$. Hence, for each $n, m \ge n_\varepsilon$, we have
$$
d(x_n, x_m) \le d(x_n, x) + d(x, x_m) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon,
$$
and so the sequence $\{x_n\}$ is Cauchy.

As this proof shows, if a sequence converges to a limit point, the points of the sequence become closer and closer to this point and, consequently, they also become closer and closer among them. On the other hand, there are metric spaces in which there exist Cauchy sequences that are not convergent.

nodes.title: Cauchy sequences may not converge
nodes.content:
Example 194.  
Let $X = (0,1)$, endowed with the standard metric of the real line. The sequence $\{1/n\}$ converges to the point $0$, which does not belong to $X$. This sequence is easily seen to be Cauchy in $X$, but it is not convergent in such space.

The problem is that the sequence is converging to a “hole” in the space.

nodes.title: Completeness
nodes.content:
**Definition 195**  
A metric space in which Cauchy sequences are convergent is called complete.

The space $X = (0,1)$ of the last example, as well as the space of rational points $\mathbb{Q}$ endowed with the usual distance $\lvert q' - q'' \rvert$, are not complete.

**Now, to know whether a sequence converges it is enough to know whether it is cauchy**

nodes.title: Example: Rn with d1, d2, dinf is complete!
nodes.content:
**Theorem 196**  
The space $\mathbb{R}^n$, endowed with any of the metrics $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$, is complete.

**Proof**  
We only consider the case $n = 1$, as the general case easily follows from [[6.2.7 Proposition 182 Point-Wise characterization of convergence in d1]]. Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ that satisfies the Cauchy criterion. We want to prove that this sequence is convergent.

We start by proving that it is bounded. Setting $\varepsilon = 1$, there exists $n_1 \ge 1$ such that $\color{purple}{\lvert x_n - x_m \rvert < 1}$ for each $n, m \ge n_1$. Hence, for each $n \ge n_1$ we have:
$$
\lvert x_n \rvert = \lvert x_n - x_{n_1} + x_{n_1} \rvert 
\le \textcolor{purple}{\lvert x_n - x_{n_1} \rvert} 
+ \lvert x_{n_1} \rvert 
< 1 + \lvert x_{n_1} \rvert ,
$$
which implies that for the image $E$ of the sequence $\{x_n\}$ we have $E \subset (-1 - \lvert x_{n_1} \rvert , 1 + \lvert x_{n_1} \rvert )$. The sequence is therefore bounded.

Define two scalar sequences $\{z_n\}$ and $\{y_n\}$ by $z_n = \inf_{k \ge n} x_k$ and $y_n = \sup_{k \ge n} x_k$, so that $\limsup x_n = \lim_n y_n$ and $\liminf x_n = \lim_n z_n$. Since $\{x_n\}$ is bounded, both limits $y = \lim_n y_n$ (note that y is the limit of a sequence of suprema!) and $z = \lim_n z_n$ exist because the two scalar sequences are monotone [[6.2.10 Proposition 185-186 A convergence sequence is bounded]]. Note this says that the limit of the supremum exists, not that the supremum is attained! 

Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\{x_n\}$ is Cauchy, there exist $n_1, n_2, n_3 \ge 1$ such that $\lvert y - y_{n_1} \rvert < \varepsilon/5$ for all $n \ge n_1$, $\lvert z_n - z \rvert < \varepsilon/5$ for all $n \ge n_2$, and $\lvert x_n - x_m \rvert < \varepsilon/5$ for all $n, m \ge n_3$.

Define $\bar{n} = \max\{n_1, n_2, n_3\}$. By definition of $y_n$ and $z_n$ (by definition of supremum and infimum), there $\exists$ $\tilde{n}_1, \tilde{n}_2 \ge \bar{n}$ such that $y_{\bar{n}} - x_{\tilde{n}_1} < \varepsilon/5$ and $x_{\tilde{n}_2} - z_{\bar{n}} < \varepsilon/5$. Since $\tilde{n}_1, \tilde{n}_2 \ge \bar{n} \ge n_3$, we have that $\lvert x_{\tilde{n}_1} - x_{\tilde{n}_2} \rvert < \varepsilon/5$. Being $\bar{n} \ge n_1, n_2$, we conclude that
$$
\lvert y - z \rvert \le \lvert y - y_{\bar{n}} \rvert + \lvert y_{\bar{n}} - x_{\tilde{n}_1} \rvert + \lvert x_{\tilde{n}_1} - x_{\tilde{n}_2} \rvert + \lvert x_{\tilde{n}_2} - z_{\bar{n}} \rvert + \lvert z_{\bar{n}} - z \rvert \le \frac{\varepsilon}{5} + \frac{\varepsilon}{5} + \frac{\varepsilon}{5} + \frac{\varepsilon}{5} + \frac{\varepsilon}{5} = \varepsilon .
$$
Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrarily chosen, this yields that $y = z$. That is, $\limsup x_n = \liminf x_n$. In turn, this implies that $\lim x_n$ exists (and equals $z$).

nodes.title: Example: C with d_inf is complete
nodes.content:
## Theorem 197
The metric space $(C([0,1]),d_\infty)$ is complete, where
$$
d_\infty(f,g)=\|f-g\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|f(x)-g(x)|.
$$
Proof
Let $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq C([0,1])$ be a Cauchy sequence with respect to $d_\infty$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $N\in\mathbb N$ such that for all $n,m\ge N$,
$$
|f_n(x)-f_m(x)| \le \sup_{x\in[0,1]}|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|<\varepsilon.
$$
Now fix a point $x\in[0,1]$. At this single point, each function produces a real number. So from the sequence of functions $(f_n)$ we obtain a sequence of real numbers $(f_n(x))\subset\mathbb R.$ Hence $(f_n(x))$ is a **Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb R$**.  Since $\mathbb R$ is complete, there exists a (unique) real number $f(x)$ such that $f_n(x)\to f(x)$. Fix $n\ge N$ and any $x\in[0,1]$. Letting $m\to\infty$ and using $f_m(x)\to f(x)$ gives
$$
|f_n(x)-f(x)|
=
\lim_{m\to\infty}|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|
\le
\varepsilon.
$$
Taking the supremum over $x\in[0,1]$ yields
$$
\|f_n-f\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le\varepsilon
\quad
\forall n\ge N,
$$
so indeed $\|f_n-f\|_\infty\to0$.

We now want to prove that $f\in C([0,1])$, i.e. that $f$ is continuous at every $x_0\in[0,1]$. Fix $x_0\in[0,1]$ and $\varepsilon>0$.

Step 1: Uniform approximation by a continuous function
Since $f_n\to f$ uniformly, there exists $N$ such that
$$
\|f-f_N\|_\infty<\frac{\varepsilon}{3}.
$$
By definition of the sup norm, this means
$$
|f(x)-f_N(x)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{3}
\quad
\text{for all }x\in[0,1],
$$
in particular at $x$ and at $x_0$.

Step 2: Use continuity of $f_N$
The function $f_N$ is continuous at $x_0$, so there exists $\delta>0$ such that
$$
|x-x_0|<\delta \implies |f_N(x)-f_N(x_0)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{3}.
$$
Step 3: For $|x-x_0|<\delta$, add and subtract: 
$$
|f(x)-f(x_0)|
\le
|f(x)-f_N(x)|
+
|f_N(x)-f_N(x_0)|
+
|f_N(x_0)-f(x_0)|.
$$
Each term is smaller than $\varepsilon/3$, so
$$
|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon.
$$
Conclusion: Thus $f$ is continuous at $x_0$. Since $x_0$ was arbitrary,
$$
f\in C([0,1]).
$$
**Key point:** uniform convergence lets us control $f$ everywhere using a single continuous function $f_N$.

nodes.title: Example: C with d_2 is not complete
nodes.content:
## Theorem
The metric space $(C([0,1]),d_2)$ is not complete
## Proof (simple counterexample)

### Step 0: A function that is not continuous
Define
$$
s:[0,1]\to\mathbb R
$$
by
$$
s(x)=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x<\frac12,\\
1 & \text{if } x\ge\frac12.
\end{cases}
$$
Then
$$
s\notin C([0,1]),
$$
### Step 1: A sequence of continuous functions approximating the jump

For each $n\in\mathbb N$ define
$$
f_n:[0,1]\to\mathbb R
$$
by
$$
f_n(x)=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x\le \frac12-\frac1n,\\
n\left(x-\left(\frac12-\frac1n\right)\right) & \text{if } \frac12-\frac1n < x < \frac12,\\
1 & \text{if } x\ge \frac12.
\end{cases}
$$
Each $f_n$ is continuous on $[0,1],$ hence $$ f_n\in C([0,1])\quad\forall n. $$

### Step 2: Compute the $d_2$-distance from $f_n$ to $s$
Outside the interval
$$
\left(\frac12-\frac1n,\frac12\right)
$$
we have
$$
f_n(x)=s(x),
$$
so
$$
d_2(f_n,s)^2
=
\int_0^1 |f_n(x)-s(x)|^2\,dx
=
\int_{\frac12-\frac1n}^{\frac12} |f_n(x)-s(x)|^2\,dx.
$$
On this interval we have $s(x)=0$ and $f_n(x)=n\left(x-\left(\frac12-\frac1n\right)\right)$.

Set
$$
t=x-\left(\frac12-\frac1n\right).
$$
Then by using the intergal endpoints :
$$
t\in\left(0,\frac1n\right)
$$
and
$$
f_n(x)=nt.
$$
Hence
$$
d_2(f_n,s)^2
=
\int_0^{\frac1n} (nt)^2\,dt
=
n^2\int_0^{\frac1n} t^2\,dt
=
n^2\left[\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^{\frac1n}
=
\frac{1}{3n}.
$$
Therefore
$$
d_2(f_n,s)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3n}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.
$$
Thus $f_n\to s$ in the metric $d_2.$


### Step 3: Convergent implies Cauchy
Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $d_2(f_n,s)\to 0$, there exists $N\in\mathbb N$ such that for all $n\ge N$,
$$
d_2(f_n,s)<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
$$
Then for all $n,m\ge N$, by the triangle inequality,
$$
d_2(f_n,f_m)
\le
d_2(f_n,s)+d_2(s,f_m)
<
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
=
\varepsilon.
$$
Hence $(f_n)$ is a $d_2$-Cauchy sequence in $C([0,1])$.

### Step 4: The Cauchy sequence does not converge in $C([0,1])$
Assume by contradiction that there exists $g\in C([0,1])$ such that $d_2(f_n,g)\to 0$. Since also $d_2(f_n,s)\to 0$, the triangle inequality gives
$$
d_2(g,s)
\le
d_2(g,f_n)+d_2(f_n,s)
\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.
$$
Thus $d_2(g,s)=0$. This means
$$
\int_0^1 |g(x)-s(x)|^2\,dx=0,
$$
hence $g(x)=s(x)$ for almost every $x\in[0,1]$.

Since $g(x)=0$ for almost every $x\in\left[0,\frac12\right)$, there exists a sequence $x_k<\frac12$ such that $x_k\to\frac12$ and $g(x_k)=0$. By continuity of $g$ at $\frac12$,
$$
g\left(\frac12\right)=\lim_{k\to\infty} g(x_k)=0.
$$
Similarly, since $g(x)=1$ for almost every $x\in\left(\frac12,1\right]$, there exists a sequence $y_k>\frac12$ such that $y_k\to\frac12$ and $g(y_k)=1$. Continuity gives
$$
g\left(\frac12\right)=\lim_{k\to\infty} g(y_k)=1,
$$
a contradiction. Therefore no continuous $g$ can satisfy $d_2(g,s)=0$.

## Conclusion
There exists a $d_2$-Cauchy sequence $(f_n)\subset C([0,1])$ that does not converge in $C([0,1])$. Hence
$$
(C([0,1]),d_2)
$$
is not complete.

nodes.title: Example: C with d_1 is not complete!
nodes.content:
## Simplest example: $(C([0,1]),d_1)$ is not complete

Let
$$
d_1(f,g)=\int_0^1 |f(x)-g(x)|\,dx.
$$
Define
$$
f_n(x)=x^n
\qquad\text{for }x\in[0,1].
$$
Each $f_n$ belongs to $C([0,1])$.

---
#### Step 1: $(f_n)$ is Cauchy in $d_1$

For $m>n$ we have $0\le x^m\le x^n\le 1$ on $[0,1]$, hence
$$
|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|=x^n-x^m\le x^n.
$$
Therefore
$$
d_1(f_n,f_m)
\le
\int_0^1 x^n\,dx
=
\frac1{n+1}
\to 0.
$$
So $(f_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $(C([0,1]),d_1)$.


#### Step 2: The $d_1$-limit is not continuous

Point-wise, we have$$
x^n \to
\begin{cases}
0 & x\in[0,1),\\
1 & x=1.
\end{cases}
$$Define$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
0 & x\in[0,1),\\
1 & x=1.
\end{cases}
$$Then$$
d_1(f_n,f)=\int_0^1 |x^n-f(x)|\,dx=\int_0^1 x^n\,dx=\frac1{n+1}\to0,
$$
so $f_n\to f$ in $d_1$.

But $f$ is discontinuous at $x=1$, hence
$$
f\notin C([0,1]).
$$

---

nodes.title: Compact Set
nodes.content:
**Definition 201**  
A subset $A$ of a metric space is compact if each open cover of $A$ has a finite subcover.
(By Proposition 199, the closed and bounded intervals $[a,b]$ are compact sets of $\mathbb{R}$)

nodes.title: Intro: compactness in R
nodes.content: In Calculus, compact sets of $\mathbb R$ are defined as the closed and bounded sets, the most important example being the closed and bounded intervals $[a,b]$.

nodes.title: Terminology; Open covers and finite subcovers
nodes.content:
We now extend the notion of compactness to general metric spaces. To this end, we start by considering the compactness in $\mathbb R$ from a different perspective. We first need a piece of terminology: given a set $A$ of a metric space, an open cover of $A$ is any collection of open sets $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ such that
$$
A \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} G_i.
$$
In turn, a finite subcover of the open cover $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ is a finite collection of sets, say $\{G_1,\ldots,G_n\}$, taken from the open cover $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ that still are able to cover the set $A$, that is, such that
$$
A \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^n G_i.
$$

nodes.title: only in Euclidean spaces: for closed and bounded sets Each open cover has a finite subcover ()
nodes.content:
**Proposition 199**  
Each open cover of a closed and bounded interval $[a,b]$ of $\mathbb R$ has a finite subcover (this will become our new characterization of compactness!!!). 

In other words, each open cover $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ of a closed and bounded interval $[a,b]$ of the real line has a finite subcover, that is, a family $\{G_1,\ldots,G_n\}\subseteq\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ such that $[a,b] \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^n G_i.$

Lemma 200  
Let $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\ge1}$ be a collection of closed and bounded intervals of $\mathbb R$ with $[a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq[a_n,b_n]$ for each $n\ge1$. We have$$
\bigcap_{n\ge1}[a_n,b_n]\ne\varnothing.
$$Proof  
- Given the collection $\{[a_n,b_n]\}_{n\ge1}$
- Let $A=\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n,\ldots\}$.  We have $A\subseteq[a_1,b_1]$ and therefore $A$ is a bounded set. By the completeness of $\mathbb R$, we can set $x=\sup A$. Since each $b_n$ is an upper bound for $A$, we have $b_n\ge x$ for each $n\ge1$. Hence, $a_n\le x\le b_n$ for each $n\ge1$, and therefore
$$
x\in\bigcap_{n\ge1}[a_n,b_n].
$$
This implies
$$
\bigcap_{n\ge1}[a_n,b_n]\ne\varnothing,
$$
as desired.


**Proof of Proposition 199.** Suppose per contra that there exists an open cover $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ of $[a,b]$ that does not contain any finite sub-cover of $[a,b]$. Let $\delta=b-a$ and $c_1=(a+b)/2$. 
- The collection $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ is an open cover also of the intervals $[a,c_1]$ and $[c_1,b]$. Therefore, at least one of these two intervals has no finite sub-cover of $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$. Otherwise, from $[a,b]=[a,c_1]\cup[c_1,b]$ it would follow that $[a,b]$ itself would have such a sub-cover. 
- Wlog, suppose therefore that $[a,c_1]$ has no finite sub-cover of $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$. Set $c_2=(a+c_1)/2$. 
- By repeating the argument just seen, we can assume that also $[a,c_2]$ does not have such a finite sub-cover.
- By proceeding in this way we can construct a collection of intervals $\{[a,c_n]\}_{n\ge1}$ such that $[a,c_{n+1}]\subseteq[a,c_n]$ and $c_n-a=\delta/2^n$ for each $n\ge1$. Moreover, none of these closed intervals has a finite sub-cover of $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$. By Lemma 178,
$$
\bigcap_{n\ge1}[a,c_n]\ne\varnothing.
$$

Let $x\in\bigcap_{n\ge1}[a,c_n]$. Since $[a,b]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I} G_i$, there exists $i\in I$ such that $x\in G_i$.  As $x$ is an interior point of $G_i$, there exists a neighborhood $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ such that
$$
(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq G_i.
$$
For $n$ sufficiently large, we have $\delta/2^n<\varepsilon$, and therefore
$$
[a,c_n]\subseteq\left(x-\frac{\delta}{2^n},x+\frac{\delta}{2^n}\right)\subseteq(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq G_i.
$$
Consequently $\{G_i\}$ is a finite sub-cover of $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ that covers $[a,c_n]$, which contradicts the fact that all the intervals $[a,c_n]$ do not have such sub-covers. From this contradiction it follows that $[a,b]$ has a finite subcover of $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$.

Proposition 199 motivates the next definition.

nodes.title: Example: compact set
nodes.content:
## Example 204

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, let $(x_n)$ be a convergent sequence in $X$ with limit $x$, and let
$$
E=\{x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}.
$$
Then the set
$$
E\cup\{x\}
$$
is compact.

---

### Proof

Let $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $E\cup\{x\}$.

#### Step 1: isolate the limit point
Since $x\in E\cup\{x\}$, there exists an index $i_x\in I$ such that
$$
x\in G_{i_x}.
$$
Because $G_{i_x}$ is open and $x_n\to x$, there exists $\bar n\in\mathbb N$ such that
$$
x_n\in G_{i_x}
\quad
\text{for all }n\ge \bar n.
$$

#### Step 2: control the remaining points
Hence the set
$$
E\cap G_{i_x}^c=\{x_1,\dots,x_{\bar n-1}\}
$$
is finite. Note here $G_{i_x}^c$ is the set of all points **not** contained in the open set $G_{i_x}$.

For each $y\in E\cap G_{i_x}^c$, choose an index $i_y\in I$ such that
$$
y\in G_{i_y}.
$$
This is possible since $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ covers $E\cup\{x\}$.

#### Step 3: construct a finite subcover
We then have
$$
E=(E\cap G_{i_x})\cup(E\cap G_{i_x}^c)
\subseteq
G_{i_x}\cup\bigcup_{y\in E\cap G_{i_x}^c} G_{i_y}.
$$
The right-hand side is a finite union of open sets. Therefore,
$$
\{G_{i_x}\}\cup\{G_{i_y}:y\in E\cap G_{i_x}^c\}
$$
is a finite subcover of $E\cup\{x\}$.

Since the open cover was arbitrary, $E\cup\{x\}$ is compact. $\square$

nodes.title: Example: a non compact set
nodes.content:
## A basic non-compact example

Consider
$$
A=(0,1)\subseteq\mathbb R,
$$
and define, for each $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$
G_n=\left(0,1-\frac1n\right).
$$
Each $G_n$ is open and
$$
\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}G_n=(0,1),
$$
so $\{G_n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is an open cover of $A$.

Let $\{G_{n_1},\dots,G_{n_k}\}$ be any finite subcollection with
$$
n_1<n_2<\dots<n_k.
$$
Since
$$
G_{n_1}\subseteq G_{n_2}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq G_{n_k},
$$
we have
$$
\bigcup_{i=1}^k G_{n_i}=G_{n_k}=\left(0,1-\frac1{n_k}\right),
$$
which does not cover $A$.

Thus $(0,1)$ admits an open cover with no finite subcover and is therefore **not compact**.

nodes.title: Compact subsets  of a metric space are closed and bounded
nodes.content:
**Theorem 205** *Compact subsets of a metric space are closed and bounded.*

**Proof** Let $K$ be a compact set of a metric space $X$.

A. We prove that $K^c$ is open. Let $x \in K^c$. For each $y \in K$, let $G_y$ and $V_y$ be, respectively, neighborhoods of $y$ and $x$ with radius lower than $d(x,y)/2$. This implies that
$$
G_y \cap V_y = \varnothing
$$
for each $y \in K$. Since the collection $\{G_y\}_{y \in K}$ is an open cover of $K$ (We used the open cover to inglobate K! ), there $\exists$ a finite sub-cover $\{G_{y_j}\}_{j=1}^n$ of $K$ . Setting
$$
G = \bigcup_{j=1}^n G_{y_j},
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
V = \bigcap_{j=1}^n V_{y_j}
$$
we have $K \subseteq G$ and $V \cap G = \varnothing$. Hence, $V$ is a neighborhood of $x$ such that $V \subseteq K^c$, which implies that $x$ is an interior point of $K^c$ (we needed a finite cover otherwise V would have been an infinite intersection, potentially not an open set). Thus, $K^c$ is open.

B. It remains to show that $K$ is bounded. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, for each $x \in K$ let $B_\varepsilon(x)$ be a neighborhood of radius $\varepsilon$. Since the collection $\{B_\varepsilon(x)\}_{x \in K}$ is an open cover of $K$, there $\exists$ a finite set $E \subset K$ such that $\{B_\varepsilon(x)\}_{x \in E}$ is a finite sub-cover of $K$, that is,
$$
K \subset \bigcup_{x \in E} B_\varepsilon(x).
$$Set
$$
M = \max_{x',x'' \in E} d(x',x'').
$$
Let $y',y'' \in K$. There exist $x',x'' \in E$ such that $y' \in B_\varepsilon(x')$ and $y'' \in B_\varepsilon(x'')$. Therefore,
$$
d(y',y'') \le d(y',x') + d(x',x'') + d(x'',y'') < 2\varepsilon + M.
$$
It follows that, taking any $y \in K$, we have
$$
K \subset B_{2\varepsilon+M}(y),
$$
which implies that $K$ is a bounded set. ■

nodes.title: Note!
nodes.content: The two proofs prove the same phenomenon (Heine–Borel), but they use two different characterizations of compactness and two different foundational tools. Note how using sequences make it so easier

nodes.title: Closed and bounded sets in Euclidean spaces are compact
nodes.content:
## Theorem 206 (Heine-Borel)
Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, endowed with any of the metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, and $d_\infty$. A subset $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is compact $\iff$ it is closed and bounded.

## Proof
By Proposition 205, if $K$ is compact then $K$ is closed and bounded. It remains to prove the converse: if $K$ is closed and bounded, then $K$ is compact. We will show that every sequence in $K$ admits a convergent subsequence whose limit belongs to $K$.

#### Step 1: boundedness gives a convergent subsequence
Let $(x_m)_{m\in\mathbb N}$ be any sequence in $K$. Since $K$ is bounded, the sequence $(x_m)$ is bounded in $\mathbb R^n$. By the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem in $\mathbb R^n$ (with the Euclidean metric $d_2$), there exist a subsequence $(x_{m_k})_{k\in\mathbb N}$ and a point $x\in\mathbb R^n$ such that 
$$
x_{m_k}\xrightarrow[d_2]{} x.
$$
This would not work outside Rn! *see note!*
#### Step 2: closedness keeps the limit inside $K$
Because $K$ is closed and $x_{m_k}\in K$ for all $k$, we have
$$
x\in K.
$$

Thus every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence converging (for $d_1$, $d_2$, or $d_\infty$) to a point of $K$, so $K$ is sequentially compact. In metric spaces, sequential compactness implies compactness. Hence $K$ is compact. $\square$



*Note* convergence is the same for $d_1,d_2,d_\infty$
In $\mathbb R^n$ the norms $\|\cdot\|_1$, $\|\cdot\|_2$, and $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ are equivalent, hence the induced metrics $d_1,d_2,d_\infty$ generate the same convergent sequences. Therefore,
$$
x_{m_k}\xrightarrow[d]{} x
$$
also holds for $d=d_1$ and for $d=d_\infty$.

nodes.title: Closed and bounded but not compact
nodes.content:
At this point it is important to see an example of a space where there is a closed and bounded set that is not compact, thus showing that Theorem 206 is in general false in non-Euclidean spaces.

## Example 207
Let $X=\mathbb Q$ be the space of rational numbers, endowed with the usual metric
$$
d(q_1,q_2)=|q_1-q_2|
\quad
\text{for each }q_1,q_2\in\mathbb Q.
$$
Consider the set
$$
A=\{\,q\in\mathbb Q:\sqrt2<q<\sqrt3\,\}.
$$

Clearly, $A$ is bounded. It is also closed. Indeed, let $\{q_n\}\subseteq A$ be such that $q_n\to q\in\mathbb Q$. Since for each $n\ge1$ we have $\sqrt2<q_n<\sqrt3$, it follows that
$$
\sqrt2\le q\le\sqrt3.
$$
Being $q$ a rational number, this implies
$$
\sqrt2<q<\sqrt3,
$$
that is, $q\in A$. By Corollary 189, we conclude that $A$ is closed (**THIS IS WHAT MAKES THE EXAMPLE WORK WITH THE USE OF Q!!!**, OTHERWISE WOULD HAVE BEEN ANOTHER EXAMPLE OF AN OPEN SET!).

The set $A$ is not compact. Consider the family of open sets $\{G_n\}$ defined by
$$
G_n=\{\,q\in\mathbb Q:\sqrt2<q<\sqrt3-\tfrac1n\,\}.
$$
One can easily check that it is an open cover of $A$, that is,
$$
A\subseteq\bigcup_n G_n,
$$
and that it does not admit any finite sub-cover. Therefore, $A$ is an example of a closed and bounded set that is not compact.


SUPER INTERESTING AS A MODALITY: We close by showing that $A$ is also open. Take any $q\in A$. By the density of $\mathbb Q$ in $\mathbb R$, there exist $q_1,q_2\in\mathbb Q$ such that
$$
\sqrt2<q_1<q<q_2<\sqrt3.
$$
Since $(q_1,q_2)$ is an open neighborhood of $q$ entirely contained in $A$, the point $q$ is an interior point of $A$. We conclude that $A$ is both closed and open.

nodes.title: Closed and bounded but not compact for a set S, the discrete metric
nodes.content:
Let $X$ be any infinite set endowed with the discrete metric $d$. All subsets of $X$ are both open and closed under this metric (Example 154). They are also all bounded: given any $x\in X$ and any $\varepsilon>1$ it trivially holds
$$
B_\varepsilon(x)=X,
$$
and so
$$
A\subseteq B_\varepsilon(x)
\quad
\text{for all }A\subseteq X.
$$
In sum, all subsets of $X$ are closed and bounded.

However, a subset of $X$ is compact if and only if it is finite. Indeed, consider any infinite subset $A\subseteq X$. The collection of singletons
$$
\{\{x\}\}_{x\in A}
$$
is an open cover of $A$, since
$$
A=\bigcup_{x\in A}\{x\},
$$
and singletons are open sets under the discrete metric. Clearly, this open cover does not admit any finite subcover.

We conclude that, under the discrete metric, infinite subsets of $X$ are closed and bounded, but not compact. For instance, if $X=\mathbb R$ and $A=\mathbb N$, the infinite set $\mathbb N$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R$ under the discrete metric, but it is not compact.

nodes.title: Closed subsets of a compact set are compact
nodes.content:
The next result shows that compactness is inherited by closed subsets of compact sets.

## Proposition 209
In a metric space the closed subsets of a compact set are themselves compact.

### Proof
Let $F$ be a closed subset of a compact set $K$. Let $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $F$. We want to prove that there exists a finite subcover of $F$.

Since $F$ is closed, the complement $F^c$ is open. Therefore, the collection
$$
\{G_i\}_{i\in I}\cup\{F^c\}
$$
is an open cover of $K$.

Since $K$ is compact, there exists a finite subcover
$$
\{G_i\}_{i=1}^n \cup \{F^c\}
$$
of $K$, that is,
$$
K \subseteq F^c \cup \bigcup_{i=1}^n G_i.
$$
This implies
$$
F \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^n G_i,
$$
and therefore $\{G_i\}_{i=1}^n$ is a finite subcover of $F$. $\square$

By Theorem 212, a metric space is compact if and only if every sequence has at least a convergent subsequence. This leads to the following important result.

nodes.title: Compact metric spaces are complete
nodes.content:
## Theorem 216: Compact metric spaces are complete.

### Proof
Let $\{x_n\}\subseteq X$ be a Cauchy sequence in a compact space $X$. We want to prove that $\{x_n\}$ is convergent. Since $X$ is compact, there exists a subsequence $\{x_{n_k}\}$ of $\{x_n\}$ such that
$$
x_{n_k}\to x\in X
$$
(Theorem 212). Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $\{x_n\}$ is Cauchy, there exists $n_\varepsilon$ such that
$$
d(x_n,x_m)<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\quad
\forall n,m\ge n_\varepsilon.
\tag{6.17}
$$
At the same time, since $\{x_{n_k}\}$ converges to $x$, there exists $k_\varepsilon$ such that
$$
d(x,x_{n_k})<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\quad
\forall k\ge k_\varepsilon.
\tag{6.18}
$$
Set
$$
\bar n_\varepsilon=\max\{n_\varepsilon,n_{k_\varepsilon}\}.
$$
By (6.18),
$$
d(x,x_{\bar n_\varepsilon})<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
$$
By (6.17),
$$
d(x_n,x_{\bar n_\varepsilon})<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\quad
\text{for each }n\ge \bar n_\varepsilon,
$$
since $n\ge \bar n_\varepsilon\ge n_\varepsilon$. It thus holds
$$
d(x,x_n)
\le
d(x,x_{\bar n_\varepsilon})+d(x_n,x_{\bar n_\varepsilon})
<
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
=
\varepsilon
\quad
\forall n\ge \bar n_\varepsilon,
$$
and so $x_n\to x$, as desired. $\square$

The converse of Theorem 216 is false: the real line is a simple example of a complete metric space that is not compact. There exists, however, a condition that combined with completeness makes a metric space compact.

nodes.title: Characterization with total boundedness
nodes.content:
## Definition 217
A metric space $X$ is totally bounded if, for each $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a finite collection of points $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n$ of $X$ such that
$$
X=\bigcup_{i=1}^n B_\varepsilon(x_i).
$$
In other words, for each $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a finite “net” of points from which each point of the space has distance lower than $\varepsilon$. Naturally, what gives bite to the property is that such net is finite. For example, the real line does not have this property. This is not by chance: the next result completes Theorem 216 by showing that total boundedness is actually the property that, combined with completeness, leads to compactness (we omit the proof).

## Theorem 218
A metric space is compact $\iff$ it is both complete and totally bounded.


We conclude with an important topological characterization of compactness. In order to state it, we need a piece of terminology: a collection $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$ of sets in a metric space has the finite intersection property if each finite subcollection has nonempty intersection, that is, it holds
$$
\bigcap_{i\in J} C_i \ne \varnothing
$$
where $J$ is any finite subset of $I$.

nodes.title: Characterization with finite intersection proerty
nodes.content:
## Theorem 219
A metric space $X$ is compact if and only if each collection of closed sets $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$ with the finite intersection property has nonempty overall intersection, that is,
$$
\bigcap_{i\in I} C_i \ne \varnothing.
$$
### Proof
**“If.”** Suppose that each collection of closed sets $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$ with the finite intersection property is such that
$$
\bigcap_{i\in I} C_i \ne \varnothing.
$$
We want to show that $X$ is compact. Let $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $X$. If we set
$$
C_i = G_i^c
\quad
\text{for all } i\in I,
$$
we have that $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$ is a collection of closed sets of $X$. Since $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ is an open cover of $X$, it also holds
$$
\bigcap_{i\in I} C_i
=
\bigcap_{i\in I} G_i^c
=
\left(\bigcup_{i\in I} G_i\right)^c
=
X^c
=
\varnothing.
$$
Since, by assumption, each collection of closed sets $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$ with the finite intersection property is such that $\bigcap_{i\in I} C_i \ne \varnothing$, it follows that $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$ cannot have the finite intersection property, that is, there exists a finite subset $J$ of $I$ such that
$$
\varnothing \ne \bigcap_{i\in J} C_i
=
\bigcap_{i\in J} G_i^c
=
\left(\bigcup_{i\in J} G_i\right)^c.
$$
In turn this implies
$$
\bigcup_{i\in J} G_i = X,
$$
that is, the open cover $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ admits a finite subcover, thus proving the compactness of $X$.

**“Only if.”** Suppose that $X$ is compact. Let $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$ be a collection of closed sets with the finite intersection property. We want to show that
$$
\bigcap_{i\in I} C_i \ne \varnothing.
$$
Suppose, per contra, that
$$
\bigcap_{i\in I} C_i = \varnothing.
$$
If we set
$$
G_i = C_i^c
\quad
\text{for all } i\in I,
$$
we have that $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ is a collection of open sets of $X$. Since $\bigcap_{i\in I} C_i = \varnothing$, it also holds
$$
\bigcup_{i\in I} G_i
=
\bigcup_{i\in I} C_i^c
=
\left(\bigcap_{i\in I} C_i\right)^c
=
\varnothing^c
=
X,
$$
that is, $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$ is an open cover of $X$. Since $X$ is compact, there exists a finite subset $J$ of $I$ such that
$$
X
=
\bigcup_{i\in J} G_i
=
\bigcup_{i\in J} C_i^c
=
\left(\bigcap_{i\in J} C_i\right)^c,
$$
that is,
$$
\bigcap_{i\in J} C_i = \varnothing.
$$
This contradicts the hypothesis that $\{C_i\}_{i\in I}$ is a collection with the finite intersection property.

nodes.title: Linking vecor spaces and metric spaces
nodes.content:
Vector spaces: bases dimentions.. no distances etc <- DNA = basis

Metric spaces: topology, no dimensions etc <- DNA = unit ball (if closed and bounded...)


Those are totally separate concepts... up to now! 

Theorem.
Let $(V,\|\cdot\|)$ be a normed vector space.
The following are equivalent.

1) $V$ is finite dimensional.
2) The unit ball $B=\{x\in V:\|x\|\le 1\}$ is compact.
3) $V$ has the Heine–Borel property, that is,
every closed and bounded subset of $V$ is compact.
Idea: In infinite-dimensional normed vector spaces, closed and bounded sets need not be compact.



(1) $\Rightarrow$ (3).
Assume $\dim V = n < \infty$.   Prove: if $K \subseteq V$ is **closed and bounded**, then $K$ is **compact**.

Reduce the problem to $\mathbb R^n$, where Heine–Borel is known, by identifying vectors in $V$ with their coordinates.

---

## Step 1 — Identify $V$ with $\mathbb R^n$

Fix a basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ and define
$$
T:\mathbb R^n \to V,
\qquad
T(a_1,\dots,a_n)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i.
$$

Facts:
- $T$ is **linear**
- $T$ is **bijective**
- Every $x\in V$ has a unique coordinate vector $a\in\mathbb R^n$ such that $x=T(a)$

So $V$ and $\mathbb R^n$ are the same space written in different coordinates.

---

## Step 2 — Pull the norm back to $\mathbb R^n$

Define a norm on $\mathbb R^n$ by
$$
\|a\|_* := \|T(a)\|
\qquad
(a\in\mathbb R^n).
$$

Interpretation:
- Measure a coordinate vector by first turning it into a vector of $V$
- Then measure its size using the norm of $V$

With this norm, $T$ becomes an **isometry**:
$$
\|T(a)\| = \|a\|_*.
$$

---

## Step 3 — Use finite dimensionality (key step)

Since $\mathbb R^n$ is finite dimensional, **all norms are equivalent**.

Therefore, there exist constants $c,C>0$ such that
$$
c\|a\|_2 \le \|a\|_* \le C\|a\|_2
\qquad
\forall a\in\mathbb R^n.
$$

Consequences:
- $T:(\mathbb R^n,\|\cdot\|_2)\to(V,\|\cdot\|)$ is **continuous**
- $T^{-1}:(V,\|\cdot\|)\to(\mathbb R^n,\|\cdot\|_2)$ is **continuous**

This is exactly where finite dimensionality is used.

---

## Step 4 — Transfer compactness

Let $K\subset V$ be **closed and bounded**.

### Preimage in $\mathbb R^n$
$$
T^{-1}(K)\subset\mathbb R^n
$$

- Closed: preimage of a closed set under continuous $T^{-1}$
- Bounded: image of a bounded set under continuous $T^{-1}$

### Apply Heine–Borel in $\mathbb R^n$
Since $\mathbb R^n$ satisfies Heine–Borel,
$$
T^{-1}(K)\ \text{is compact}.
$$

### Push compactness back to $V$
Because $T$ is continuous,
$$
K = T(T^{-1}(K)) \ \text{is compact}.
$$


Finite dimensional normed spaces behave exactly like $\mathbb R^n$ because all norms are equivalent, so compactness transfers through coordinates.



(3) $\Rightarrow$ (2).
$B$ is closed and bounded, so by (3) it is compact.

(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1).
We prove the contrapositive: if $V$ is infinite dimensional, then $B$ is not compact.

Lemma (Riesz lemma, convenient form).
If $W\subset V$ is a proper closed subspace and $0<\alpha<1$, then there exists $x\in V$ with
$$
\|x\|=1
\quad\text{and}\quad
\inf_{w\in W}\|x-w\|\ge\alpha.
$$
Assume $\dim V=\infty$.
Let $0<\alpha=\frac12$.
Choose $x_1$ with $\|x_1\|=1$.
Let $W_1=\mathrm{span}\{x_1\}$ and let $\overline{W_1}$ be its closure (still proper).
By Riesz lemma, choose $x_2$ with $\|x_2\|=1$ and
$$
\mathrm{dist}(x_2,\overline{W_1})\ge\frac12.
$$
Inductively, having chosen $x_1,\dots,x_n$, let
$$
W_n=\mathrm{span}\{x_1,\dots,x_n\},
\quad
\text{and choose }x_{n+1}\text{ with }\|x_{n+1}\|=1\text{ and }\mathrm{dist}(x_{n+1},\overline{W_n})\ge\frac12.
$$
Then for $m>n$, since $x_n\in W_{m-1}\subseteq\overline{W_{m-1}}$, we get
$$
\|x_m-x_n\|\ge\frac12.
$$
So $(x_n)$ is a sequence in the unit sphere (hence in $B$) with no Cauchy subsequence, hence no convergent subsequence.
Therefore $B$ is not sequentially compact, hence not compact.
Contradiction with (2).
Thus $V$ must be finite dimensional.

This proves (1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (2) $\Leftrightarrow$ (3).
