nodes.title: Limits def
nodes.content:
We start with the notion of limit of a function. In Calculus, given a function $f : A \subseteq \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and an accumulation point $x_0$ of $A$, we write $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = L \in \mathbb{R}$ if, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that

$$
0 < |x - x_0| < \delta_\varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon \qquad \forall x \in A
$$

The point $x_0$ is not required to belong to $A$, but it is enough that it is an accumulation point of $A$. This notion can be naturally extended to general metric spaces.


Definition 220.  
Given a function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ and an accumulation point $x_0$ of $A$, we write $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = y \in Y$ if, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that

$$
0 < d_X(x,x_0) < \delta_\varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; d_Y(f(x),y) < \varepsilon \qquad \forall x \in A
$$

The special case seen in Calculus corresponds to $(X,d_X) = (\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ and $(Y,d_Y) = (\mathbb{R},d)$, where $d$ is the standard metric of the real line.

The limit value $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x)$ is, therefore, the value to which the function tends as $x$ becomes closer and closer to $x_0$. Note that we do not require any relation between such limit value and the value $f(x_0)$ that the function actually takes at the point $x_0$. Indeed, the point $x_0$ may even not belong to the domain $A$ of the function (in which case $f(x_0)$ does not exist); it is only required to be an accumulation point of $A$. A standard example is the function $f : \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $f(x) = (\sin x)/x$. In this case $A = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$, and the point $x_0 = 0$ is an accumulation point of $A$ that does not belong to $A$. As well known, $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 1$.

As in Calculus, the previous $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition can be easily stated in terms of neighborhoods by saying that we write $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = y \in Y$ if, for every neighborhood $B_\varepsilon(y)$ of $y$, there exists a neighborhood $B_{\delta_\varepsilon}(x_0)$ of $x_0$ such that

$$
x \in B_{\delta_\varepsilon}(x_0) \cap A \text{ and } x \ne x_0 \;\Rightarrow\; f(x) \in B_\varepsilon(y)
$$

Before showing some examples, we characterize limits through sequences.

nodes.title: Limits characterization
nodes.content:
Proposition 221.  
Given a function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ and an accumulation point $x_0$ of $A$, we have $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = y \in Y$ if and only if

$$
x_n \to x_0 \;\Rightarrow\; f(x_n) \to y
$$

for each sequence $\{x_n\}$ of points of $A$, with $x_n \ne x_0$ for each $n$.

To be precise, we should have written $x_n \xrightarrow[d_X]{} x_0$ and $f(x_n) \xrightarrow[d_Y]{} y$, but for simplicity we only write $x_n \to x_0$ and $f(x_n) \to y$.


Proof (“if”).  
Suppose $f(x_n) \to y$ for each sequence $\{x_n\}$ of points of $A$, with $x_n \ne x_0$ for each $n$, such that $x_n \to x_0$. Suppose it is false that $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = y$. Then there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that, for each $\delta > 0$, there exists $x_\delta \in A$ with

$$
0 < d_X(x_\delta,x_0) < \delta
$$

and

$$
d_Y(f(x_\delta),y) \ge \varepsilon.
$$

For each $n$, set $\delta = 1/n$ and let $x_n$ be the corresponding point of $A$, just denoted by $x_\delta$. For the sequence $\{x_n\}$ of points of $A$ constructed in this way we have

$$
d_X(x_0,x_n) < \frac{1}{n}
$$

for each $n$. Therefore,

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} d_X(x_0,x_n) = 0.
$$

By Lemma 178, $x_n \to x_0$. But, by construction, we have

$$
d_Y(f(x_n),y) \ge \varepsilon
$$

for each $n$, and therefore the sequence $\{f(x_n)\}$ does not converge to $y$. This contradicts the hypothesis, and so we conclude that

$$
\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = y.
$$


Proof (“only if”).  
Suppose $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = y \in Y$. Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence of points of $A$, with $x_n \ne x_0$ for each $n$, such that $x_n \to x_0$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. There exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that for each $x \in A$ with

$$
0 < d_X(x,x_0) < \delta_\varepsilon
$$

we have

$$
d_Y(f(x),y) < \varepsilon.
$$

Since $x_n \to x_0$ and $x_n \ne x_0$, there exists $n_\varepsilon \ge 1$ such that

$$
0 < d_X(x_n,x_0) < \delta_\varepsilon
$$

for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$. Therefore, for each $n \ge n_\varepsilon$ we have

$$
d_Y(f(x_n),y) < \varepsilon,
$$

which implies $f(x_n) \to y$.

Since each sequence $\{f(x_n)\}$ converges to a unique limit (Proposition 183), Proposition 221 also ensures the uniqueness of the limit value $y$ in Definition 220.

nodes.title: Example limit is a point
nodes.content:
Example 222.  
Let $(X,d_X) = (\mathbb{R},d)$ and $(Y,d_Y) = (\mathbb{R}^2,d_2)$, and let $F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by

$$
F(x) = (\sin x, \cos x)
$$

for each $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Using Proposition 221 it is easy to verify that

$$
\lim_{x \to 0} F(x) = (0,1) \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$


Example 223.  
Let $(X,d_X) = (Y,d_Y) = (\mathbb{R}^2,d_2)$, and let $F = (F_1,F_2) : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by

$$
F_1(x) =
\begin{cases}
x_1 + x_2 + 1 & x \ne (0,0)\\
0 & x = (0,0)
\end{cases}
$$

and

$$
F_2(x) = 1 + x_1^2 x_2
\qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

For example, for $x = (2,1)$ we have $F(x) = (F_1(x),F_2(x)) = (4,5)$, while for $x = (0,0)$ we have $F(x) = (F_1(x),F_2(x)) = (0,1)$. Using Proposition 221, it is easy to verify that

$$
\lim_{x \to (2,1)} F(x) = (4,5)
$$

and

$$
\lim_{x \to (0,0)} F(x) = (1,1).
$$

Note that $\lim_{x \to (2,1)} F(x) = F(2,1)$, while $\lim_{x \to (0,0)} F(x) \ne F(0,0)$.


Behind the scenes:  
How Proposition 221 is used in Example 222.

Example 222.  
We want to compute

$$
\lim_{x \to 0} F(x).
$$

Using Proposition 221, take any sequence $x_n \to 0$. Then

$$
F(x_n) = (\sin x_n, \cos x_n).
$$

Since we know from elementary Calculus that

$$
\sin x_n \to 0
$$

and

$$
\cos x_n \to 1,
$$

we get

$$
F(x_n) \to (0,1).
$$

Since this is true for every sequence approaching $0$, Proposition 221 implies

$$
\lim_{x \to 0} F(x) = (0,1).
$$

That is the role of Proposition 221 in Example 222.


Fundamental rule.

To compute $ \lim_{x \to x_0} F(x) $:

1. Ignore the value of $F(x_0)$.  
   It plays no role in the limit.

2. Use the formula valid for $x \ne x_0$.  
   That is the function that governs the behaviour near the point.

3. Take the limit of that formula.

4. If the limit exists, it gives the value of $ \lim_{x \to x_0} F(x) $, even if

$$
F(x_0) \ne \lim_{x \to x_0} F(x).
$$

nodes.title: Example limit is a function
nodes.content:
It is the limit of the map $F$ when the input function gets close to the zero function in $d_\infty$.


Example 224.  
Let $(X,d_X) = (C([0,1]), d_\infty)$ and $(Y,d_Y) = (\mathbb{R}, d)$, and let $F : C([0,1]) \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by

$$
F(f) = \int_0^1 f(t)\,dt
$$

for each $f \in C([0,1])$. Let $0 \in C([0,1])$ be the identically null function. We have $\lim_{f \to 0} F(f) = 0$, that is, $\lim_{f \to 0} F(f) = F(0)$.

In fact, let $\{f_n\}$ be a sequence in $C([0,1])$, with $f_n \ne 0$, such that $f_n \to 0$. By Proposition 221, in order to prove that $\lim_{f \to 0} F(f) = 0$ we have to prove that $F(f_n) \to 0$. We have

$$
f_n \to 0 \iff d_\infty(f_n,0)
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t) - 0(t)|
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)| \to 0
$$

Let $g_n \in C([0,1])$ be the constant function such that

$$
g_n(t) = \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)|
\qquad \text{for each } t \in [0,1].
$$

The previous expression implies

$$
0 \le d(F(f_n),0)
= |F(f_n) - 0|
= \left|\int_0^1 f_n(t)\,dt\right|
\le \int_0^1 |f_n(t)|\,dt
\le \int_0^1 g_n(t)\,dt
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)| \to 0
$$

Therefore, by Lemma 178 we have $F(f_n) \to 0$, as desired.


Example 225.  
Let $(X,d_X) = (Y,d_Y) = (C([0,1]), d_\infty)$, and let $F : C([0,1]) \to C([0,1])$ be defined by

$$
F(f) = f^2
$$

for each $f \in C([0,1])$. For example, if $f(t) = \sin t$, we have $F(f)(t) = \sin^2 t$.

We prove that $\lim_{f \to 0} F(f) = 0$, that is, $\lim_{f \to 0} F(f) = F(0)$. Let $\{f_n\}$ be a sequence in $C([0,1])$, with $f_n \ne 0$, such that $f_n \to 0$. By Proposition 221, in order to prove that $\lim_{f \to 0} F(f) = 0$ we have to prove that $F(f_n) \to 0$. We have

$$
f_n \to 0 \iff d_\infty(f_n,0)
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t) - 0(t)|
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)| \to 0
$$

which implies

$$
0 \le d_\infty(F(f_n),0)
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |F(f_n)(t) - 0(t)|
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |F(f_n)(t)|
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n^2(t)|
$$

and hence

$$
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n^2(t)|
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} \bigl(|f_n(t)|\,|f_n(t)|\bigr)
\le \left(\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)|\right)
\left(\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)|\right)
\to 0.
$$

By Lemma 178, we have $F(f_n) \to 0$, as desired.

Note how this is continuous but nonlinear.

We need here Lemma 178 (Limit characterization of convergence) because we are proving the limit using distances. This is because such functions have two layers: the superficial one, where you treat them as in Examples 222 and 223, and the deeper one, where you use distances and Lemma 178.

nodes.title: Continuity definition
nodes.content:
Definition 227.  
A function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ is said to be continuous at the point $x_0 \in A$ if, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that

$$
d_X(x,x_0) < \delta_\varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; d_Y(f(x),f(x_0)) < \varepsilon
\qquad \forall x \in A.
$$

In other words, $f$ is continuous at $x_0 \in A$ if, for each neighborhood $B_\varepsilon(f(x_0))$ of $f(x_0)$, there exists a neighborhood $B_{\delta_\varepsilon}(x_0)$ of $x_0$ such that $f(x) \in B_\varepsilon(f(x_0))$ for each $x \in B_{\delta_\varepsilon}(x_0)$. Equivalently, for each open set $V$ containing $f(x_0)$, there exists an open set $G$ containing $x_0$ such that $f(x) \in V$ for each $x \in G$.

Observe that the point $x_0$ must belong to the domain of the function. A function continuous at each point of a set $E \subseteq A$ is called continuous on $E$. The function is called continuous if it is continuous at all the points of its domain.


Connecting to Definition 220 (limit of a function).  
For accumulation points of $A$, this is exactly the same as saying:
(i) the limit exists, and
(ii) the limit equals the value of the function.


Note that we are saying that for each $\varepsilon$ there exists a $\delta$: however close we want the images to be, we can find a small enough neighborhood in the domain. It is not required that a small neighborhood in the domain is translated into a small neighborhood in the codomain.

Here we are saying: small changes in the input imply small changes in the output. This is continuity.

The inverse condition,

$$
d_Y(f(x),f(x_0)) < \varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; d_X(x,x_0) < \delta_\varepsilon,
$$

is much stronger: if the outputs are close, then the inputs must be close.


## What the reverse implication says

The reverse implication would be
$$
d_Y(f(x),f(x_0))<\varepsilon \Rightarrow d_X(x,x_0)<\delta.
$$

This means:
- from the fact that the outputs are close
- we try to conclude that the inputs must have been close

 
 This is 1) not what we define as continuity, and actually  2) **It is much stronger than continuity** 3) resembles a local injecitivty condition (if the image is equal then the oitns must be very close)

The reverse implication forbids far points from having similar images.  
This forces a form of local injectivity, which continuity does not require.

3. **Continuous functions typically fail it**

For example, consider $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ defined by $f(x)=x^2$ at $x_0=0$.

The function is continuous at $0$, but
$$
f(1)=f(-1),
$$
so closeness of outputs does not imply closeness of inputs.

nodes.title: Characterization of continity with limits
nodes.content:
Corollary 230.  
A function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ is continuous at a point $x_0 \in A$ if and only if

$$
x_n \to x_0 \;\Rightarrow\; f(x_n) \to f(x_0)
$$

for each sequence $\{x_n\}$ of points of $A$.


Proof.  
The result follows immediately by Proposition 229, once we observe that when $x_0$ is an isolated point of $A$ we can consider the constant sequence

$$
\{x_0, x_0, \ldots\}.
$$

nodes.title: Continuity characterization for accumualtinn poitns of A
nodes.content:
Obvious 

Proposition 229.  
A function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ is continuous at a point $x_0 \in A \cap A'$ if and only if

$$
\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = f(x_0).
$$

This result follows immediately from Definitions 220 and 227. The notion of continuity seen in Calculus, usually presented as $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = f(x_0)$, can therefore be recovered by setting $(X,d_X) = (\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ and $(Y,d_Y) = (\mathbb{R},d)$.


Proof.  

Definition 227.  
A function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ is said to be continuous at the point $x_0 \in A$ if, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that

$$
d_X(x,x_0) < \delta_\varepsilon
\;\Rightarrow\;
d_Y(f(x),f(x_0)) < \varepsilon
\qquad \forall x \in A.
$$


Definition 220.  
Given a function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ and an accumulation point $x_0$ of $A$, we write $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = y \in Y$ if, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that

$$
0 < d_X(x,x_0) < \delta_\varepsilon
\;\Rightarrow\;
d_Y(f(x),y) < \varepsilon
\qquad \forall x \in A.
$$

As you can clearly see, we cannot apply the definition of limit to an isolated point.


Thanks to the characterization given by Proposition 229, we can fully understand the meaning of continuity: a function is continuous at an accumulation point $x_0 \in A \cap A'$ when the value that the function takes at $x_0$, that is $f(x_0)$, is consistent with the value to which the function tends when $x$ gets closer and closer to $x_0$, that is $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x)$.

nodes.title: Anu funciton is continuous at each isolated point
nodes.content:
Lemma 228.  
Any function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ is continuous at each isolated point of $A$.


Proof.  
Let $x_0$ be an isolated point of $A$. There exists a neighborhood $B_\delta(x_0)$ of radius $\delta > 0$ such that

$$
B_\delta(x_0) \cap A = \{x_0\}.
$$

Therefore, it holds that $x \in A$ and $d_X(x,x_0) < \delta$ if and only if $x = x_0$. It follows that, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $x \in A$ and $d_X(x,x_0) < \delta$ implies $x = x_0$, so that

$$
d_Y(f(x),f(x_0)) = 0 < \varepsilon.
$$


As you can clearly see, we cannot apply the definition of limit to an isolated point.


Definition 220.  
Given a function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ and an accumulation point $x_0$ of $A$, we write $\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = y \in Y$ if, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that

$$
0 < d_X(x,x_0) < \delta_\varepsilon
\;\Rightarrow\;
d_Y(f(x),y) < \varepsilon
\qquad \forall x \in A.
$$

nodes.title: Images and preimages
nodes.content:
In the sequel we will need some properties of images and preimages. Recall that, given a function $f : X \to Y$, the preimage of $E \subseteq Y$ is given by

$$
f^{-1}(E) = \{x \in X : f(x) \in E\},
$$

while the image of $A \subseteq X$ is

$$
f(A) = \{y \in Y : f(x) = y \text{ for some } x \in A\}.
$$

Recall also that $f$ is surjective if $f(X) = Y$ and is injective if $f(x_1) \ne f(x_2)$ for each $x_1, x_2 \in X$ with $x_1 \ne x_2$. A function that is both injective and surjective is called bijective.

It is immediate to see that

$$
f(A_1) \subseteq f(A_2) \text{ if } A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq X
\quad \text{and} \quad
f^{-1}(E_1) \subseteq f^{-1}(E_2) \text{ if } E_1 \subseteq E_2 \subseteq Y.
$$

The next result, whose proof is left to the reader, collects other important properties of images and preimages. Properties (i) and (v) are especially important as they show that preimages are well behaved with respect to the set operations, that is, unions, intersections, and complements.


Lemma 236.  
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a function between two sets $X$ and $Y$. We have:

(i)

$$
f^{-1}\!\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} E_i\right) = \bigcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}(E_i)
\quad \text{and} \quad
f^{-1}\!\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} E_i\right) = \bigcap_{i \in I} f^{-1}(E_i),
$$

where $E_i \subseteq Y$ for each $i \in I$.

(ii)

$$
f\!\left(\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\right) \subseteq \bigcap_{i \in I} f(A_i)
\quad \text{and} \quad
f\!\left(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\right) = \bigcup_{i \in I} f(A_i),
$$

where $A_i \subseteq X$ for each $i \in I$.

(iii)

$$
f\!\left(f^{-1}(E)\right) \subseteq E \quad \text{for each } E \subseteq Y;
$$

the equality holds if $f$ is surjective.

(iv)

$$
f^{-1}\!\left(f(A)\right) \supseteq A \quad \text{for each } A \subseteq X;
$$

the equality holds if $f$ is injective.

(v)

$$
f^{-1}(E^c) = \left(f^{-1}(E)\right)^c \quad \text{for each } E \subseteq Y.
$$

nodes.title: Topologycal characterization
nodes.content:
Theorem 237 (Topological characterization of continuity).  
A function $f : X \to Y$ is continuous if and only if the preimage $f^{-1}(G)$ of each open set $G$ of $Y$ is itself an open set of $X$.


Proof.

($\Rightarrow$)  
Suppose that $f$ is continuous. Let $G$ be an open set of $Y$, and let $x_0 \in f^{-1}(G)$. We prove that $x_0$ is an interior point of $f^{-1}(G)$. Since $f(x_0) \in G$ and $G$ is open, there exists a neighborhood $B_\varepsilon(f(x_0))$ such that

$$
B_\varepsilon(f(x_0)) \subseteq G.
$$

Since $f$ is continuous at $x_0$, there exists $\delta_\varepsilon > 0$ such that

$$
f(x) \in B_\varepsilon(f(x_0))
$$

for each $x \in B_{\delta_\varepsilon}(x_0)$. Hence $f(x) \in G$ for each $x \in B_{\delta_\varepsilon}(x_0)$, which implies

$$
B_{\delta_\varepsilon}(x_0) \subseteq f^{-1}(G).
$$

Therefore $x_0$ is an interior point of $f^{-1}(G)$, and $f^{-1}(G)$ is open.

($\Leftarrow$)  
Suppose that, for each open set $G$ of $Y$, the set $f^{-1}(G)$ is open in $X$. Let $x_0 \in X$. Let $V$ be an open set containing $f(x_0)$. Since $V$ is open, $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$. Since $x_0 \in f^{-1}(V)$, there exists an open set $G$ containing $x_0$ such that

$$
G \subseteq f^{-1}(V).
$$

Therefore $f(x) \in V$ for each $x \in G$, and we conclude that $f$ is continuous at $x_0$.


Comment on the second implication.  
Here $V$ is an arbitrary open set of $Y$, not necessarily hit by the function. The argument is simply a rewriting of the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition in topological language.


Counterexample showing failure when continuity does not hold.

Define the function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by

$$
f(x) =
\begin{cases}
0 & x < 0,\\
1 & x \ge 0.
\end{cases}
$$

This is the step function.


1. $f$ is not continuous.

At $x_0 = 0$, for every $\delta > 0$ there exist points $x < 0$ and $x > 0$ such that $|x - 0| < \delta$, but

$$
f(x) \in \{0,1\}.
$$

Hence, for $\varepsilon < 1$, there exists no $\delta > 0$ such that

$$
|x - 0| < \delta \;\Rightarrow\; |f(x) - f(0)| < \varepsilon.
$$

Therefore $f$ is not continuous at $0$.


2. There exists an open set whose preimage is not open.

Let

$$
G = \left(\frac{1}{2}, 2\right) \subseteq \mathbb{R}.
$$

Then

$$
f^{-1}(G)
= \{x : f(x) \in (1/2,2)\}
= [0,\infty).
$$

But $[0,\infty)$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$. Hence the preimage of an open set need not be open when the function is not continuous.


Check using the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition.

Continuity at $x_0 = 0$ would require that, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that

$$
|x - 0| < \delta \;\Rightarrow\; |f(x) - f(0)| < \varepsilon.
$$

For $\varepsilon < 1$, this is impossible, so continuity fails.


Remark (constant functions).

If $f$ is a constant function, then for every open set $G \subseteq Y$ the preimage $f^{-1}(G)$ is either $\varnothing$ or $X$, and both are open. Hence every constant function is continuous.

nodes.title: Example
nodes.content:
Example 238.  
Consider a real-valued function $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ defined on a metric space $X$. Denote by $(f < t)$ the set

$$
(f < t) = \{x \in X : f(x) < t\} = f^{-1}((-\infty,t)).
$$

If $f$ is continuous, then by Theorem 237 the set $(f < t)$ is open in $X$, because it is the preimage of the open set $(-\infty,t)$ of $\mathbb{R}$. In a similar way, we prove that $(f > t)$ is also an open set in $X$, while $(f \le t)$ and $(f \ge t)$ are closed sets in $X$. Finally, $(f = t)$ is a closed set in $X$ because

$$
(f = t) = f^{-1}(\{t\}),
$$

and the singleton $\{t\}$ is a closed set of $\mathbb{R}$.


Images versus preimages.  
There is no counterpart of Theorem 237 for images: given a continuous function $f$, in general the image $f(G)$ of an open set is not open, and the image $f(F)$ of a closed set is not closed.


Example 239.  
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by

$$
f(x) = x^2.
$$

For $G = (-1,1)$ we have

$$
f(G) = [0,1),
$$

which is not open.


Example 240.  
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by

$$
f(x) = e^x.
$$

The real line $\mathbb{R}$ is a closed set (it is also an open set, but this is not relevant here), and we have

$$
f(\mathbb{R}) = (0,+\infty),
$$

which is not closed.

In the last example the closed set considered, namely $\mathbb{R}$, is not bounded and hence is not compact. This does not happen by chance: the next result shows that when a closed set is compact, its image is compact.


Theorem 241.  
If a function $f : A \subseteq X \to Y$ is continuous on a compact subset $K \subseteq A$ of $X$, then the image $f(K)$ of $K$ is a compact set of $Y$.


Proof.  
By Theorem 212, it is enough to show that the image $f(K)$ has the Bolzano–Weierstrass property. Let $\{y_n\} \subseteq f(K)$ be any sequence. By definition, there exists a sequence $\{x_n\} \subseteq K$ such that

$$
f(x_n) = y_n
$$

for each $n$. Since $K$ is compact, it has the Bolzano–Weierstrass property, and therefore there exists a subsequence $\{x_{n_k}\}$ that converges to some $x \in K$. Since $f$ is continuous at $x$, we have

$$
\lim_{k \to \infty} f(x_{n_k}) = f(x).
$$

Setting $y = f(x)$, it follows that

$$
\lim_{k \to \infty} y_{n_k} = y \in f(K),
$$

and therefore the subsequence $\{y_{n_k}\}$ converges to a point of $f(K)$. Hence $f(K)$ is compact.

nodes.title: Extra properties of continuous functions
nodes.content:
Proposition 242.  
Let $f : A \subseteq X \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g : A \subseteq X \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions defined on a subset $A$ of a metric space $X$. If both $f$ and $g$ are continuous at a point $x_0 \in A$, we have:

(i) $\alpha f + \beta g$ is continuous at $x_0$ for each $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$;

(ii) $fg$ is continuous at $x_0$;

(iii) $f/g$ is continuous at $x_0$, provided $g(x_0) \ne 0$.


This shows, *inter alia*, that the set of functions that are continuous at a point $x_0 \in X$ is a vector space. The same is true for the collection of functions that are continuous on a set, for example $C([a,b])$.


Consider now the functions $f : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$. These functions can be written as

$$
f = (f_1,\ldots,f_m) : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m,
$$

where each $f_i : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, for $i = 1,\ldots,m$, is a real-valued function on $A$.


Proposition 243.  
A function $f = (f_1,\ldots,f_m) : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is continuous at $x \in A$ if and only if each function $f_i : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, for $i = 1,\ldots,m$, is itself continuous at $x$.


Example 244.  
Let $F = (F_1,F_2) : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined as in Example 223, that is,

$$
F_1(x) =
\begin{cases}
x_1 + x_2 + 1 & x \ne (0,0),\\
0 & x = (0,0),
\end{cases}
$$

and

$$
F_2(x) = 1 + x_1^2 x_2,
\qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

The function $F_2 : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^2$, while the function $F_1 : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at all points of $\mathbb{R}^2$ except the origin. By Proposition 243, $F$ is therefore continuous at all points of $\mathbb{R}^2$ except the origin. This is not by chance: in Example 223 we verified that

$$
\lim_{x \to (0,0)} F(x) \ne F(0,0).
$$


Given two functions $f : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and $g : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$, the function $fg : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is given by

$$
(fg)(x) = f(x) \cdot g(x),
\qquad \forall x \in A,
$$

that is, it is given by the inner product of the two vectors $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ of $\mathbb{R}^m$. It is easy to see that if $f$ and $g$ are continuous at a point $x \in A$, then also the functions $fg$ and $f + g$ are continuous at $x$. In other words, *mutatis mutandis*, points (i) and (ii) of Proposition 242 hold also for functions with values in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

nodes.title: Example boh
nodes.content:
Example 231.  
The function of Example 222 is continuous at each point of its domain. The function of Example 223 is not continuous at the point $(0,0)$, but it is continuous at all the other points of its domain.


1. Continuity of Example 222 (the map $G$).

Let $G = (G_1,G_2) : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$, where

$$
G_1(x) = x_1 + x_2 + 1
\quad \text{and} \quad
G_2(x) = 1 + x_1^2 x_2.
$$

Both $G_1$ and $G_2$ are polynomials in $x_1,x_2$. Polynomials are continuous on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and sums and products of continuous functions are continuous. Therefore $G_1$ and $G_2$ are continuous at every $x \in \mathbb{R}^2$.

By Proposition 243, a vector-valued function is continuous at a point if and only if each component is continuous at that point. Hence $G$ is continuous at every point of its domain.

Thus, the function of Example 222 is continuous everywhere.


2. Continuity properties of Example 223 (the map $F$).

2.1. Discontinuity at $(0,0)$.

We must show that

$$
\lim_{x \to (0,0)} F(x) \ne F(0,0).
$$

From the definition, we have

$$
F(0,0) = (0,1).
$$

Consider the sequence

$$
x^{(n)} = \left(\frac{1}{n},0\right).
$$

Then $x^{(n)} \to (0,0)$ and $x^{(n)} \ne (0,0)$ for all $n$. For $x \ne (0,0)$, we have

$$
F(x) = (x_1 + x_2 + 1,\, 1 + x_1^2 x_2).
$$

Thus

$$
F(x^{(n)}) = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n},\, 1\right) \to (1,1).
$$

Hence

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} F(x^{(n)}) = (1,1) \ne (0,1) = F(0,0).
$$

By Corollary 230 (sequential characterization of continuity), the function $F$ is not continuous at $(0,0)$.


2.2. Continuity at every $x^0 \ne (0,0)$.

Let $x^0 \ne (0,0)$. We can choose a small ball centered at $x^0$ that does not contain the origin. On that ball, the function $F$ coincides with the polynomial function $G$. Since polynomials are continuous, $F$ is continuous at $x^0$.

Thus, $F$ is continuous at every point except $(0,0)$.


Sequential proof that $f(x)=x^2$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

We want to prove that

$$
f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, \quad f(x)=x^2,
$$

is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

By Corollary 230, $f$ is continuous at $x_0$ if and only if for every sequence $x_n \to x_0$ we have

$$
f(x_n) \to f(x_0).
$$

Fix an arbitrary $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $x_n \to x_0$. We must show

$$
x_n^2 \to x_0^2.
$$

Compute the difference:

$$
x_n^2 - x_0^2 = (x_n - x_0)(x_n + x_0).
$$

Since $x_n \to x_0$, we have

$$
x_n - x_0 \to 0
\quad \text{and} \quad
x_n + x_0 \to 2x_0.
$$

By the product rule for limits,

$$
(x_n - x_0)(x_n + x_0) \to 0.
$$

Thus

$$
x_n^2 - x_0^2 \to 0,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
x_n^2 \to x_0^2.
$$

Since $x_0$ was arbitrary, $f(x)=x^2$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.


General proof that all real polynomials are continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

Let

$$
p(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n,
\quad a_k \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

We prove that $p$ is continuous at every $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$.

Building blocks.

1. Constant functions are continuous.  
If $f(x)=c$, then

$$
|f(x)-f(x_0)| = 0 < \varepsilon
$$

for all $\varepsilon > 0$.

2. The identity function is continuous.  
If $g(x)=x$, then choosing $\delta=\varepsilon$ gives

$$
|x-x_0|<\delta \Rightarrow |g(x)-g(x_0)|<\varepsilon.
$$


Closure properties.

If $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $x_0$, then:
- $f+g$ is continuous at $x_0$,
- $cf$ is continuous at $x_0$ for any $c \in \mathbb{R}$,
- $fg$ is continuous at $x_0$.


Monomials are continuous.

Define $h_k(x)=x^k$.

- For $k=0$, $h_0(x)=1$ is constant.
- For $k=1$, $h_1(x)=x$ is the identity.

Assume $h_k$ is continuous. Then

$$
h_{k+1}(x) = x^{k+1} = x^k \cdot x = h_k(x) \cdot h_1(x).
$$

By closure under products, $h_{k+1}$ is continuous. By induction, $x^k$ is continuous for all integers $k \ge 0$.


Polynomials are finite sums of monomials.

Write

$$
p(x) = a_0 h_0(x) + a_1 h_1(x) + \cdots + a_n h_n(x).
$$

Each $h_k$ is continuous, multiplication by $a_k$ preserves continuity, and finite sums of continuous functions are continuous. Hence $p$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.


Multivariable polynomials.

Example:

$$
p(x,y) = 3x^2y - 5xy^3 + 7.
$$

Goal.  
Let

$$
p(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \sum_\alpha a_\alpha x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_n^{\alpha_n}.
$$

Show that $p$ is continuous everywhere.


Step 1. Projection functions.

Define

$$
\pi_i : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \quad \pi_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=x_i.
$$

Each projection is continuous.


Key inequality.

For $x,x^0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$
|x_i - x_i^0| \le \|x-x^0\|.
$$


$\varepsilon$–$\delta$ proof of continuity of projections.

Fix $x^0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $\delta=\varepsilon$. If

$$
\|x-x^0\|<\delta,
$$

then

$$
|\pi_i(x)-\pi_i(x^0)| = |x_i-x_i^0| \le \|x-x^0\| < \varepsilon.
$$

Thus $\pi_i$ is continuous at $x^0$. Since $x^0$ and $i$ were arbitrary, every projection is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^n$.


Step 2. Build monomials from projections.

Each coordinate $x_i$ is $\pi_i$. Powers $x_i^{\alpha_i}$ are finite products of $\pi_i$. Products of continuous functions are continuous, so every monomial

$$
x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_n^{\alpha_n}
$$

is continuous.


Step 3. Build polynomials.

A polynomial is a finite linear combination of monomials. Since continuity is preserved under scalar multiplication and finite sums, every multivariable polynomial is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

nodes.title: Example bohhhhh
nodes.content:
6.6.10 Examples 232–233–234: continuity for functions with function inputs

In the next three examples we consider the metric space $(C([0,1]), d_\infty)$.


Example 232.  
The function of Example 224 is continuous at each point of its domain.

Let $f \in C([0,1])$, and let $\{f_n\}$ be a sequence in $C([0,1])$, with $f_n \ne f$, such that $f_n \to f$. By Corollary 230, to prove that $F$ is continuous at $f$ it is enough to prove that $F(f_n) \to F(f)$.

Since $f_n \to f$, we have

$$
f_n \to f
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
d_\infty(f_n,f)
=
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t) - f(t)| \to 0.
$$

Let $g_n \in C([0,1])$ be the constant function defined by

$$
g_n(t) = \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t) - f(t)|.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
d(F(f_n),F(f))
&=
|F(f_n) - F(f)| \\
&=
\left|\int_0^1 f_n(t)\,dt - \int_0^1 f(t)\,dt\right| \\
&=
\left|\int_0^1 (f_n(t)-f(t))\,dt\right| \\
&\le
\int_0^1 |f_n(t)-f(t)|\,dt \\
&\le
\int_0^1 g_n(t)\,dt \\
&=
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)-f(t)| \to 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by Lemma 178, we have $F(f_n) \to F(f)$, and $F$ is continuous at $f$.


Example 233.  
The function of Example 225 is continuous at each point of its domain.

Let $f \in C([0,1])$ and let $\{f_n\}$ be a sequence in $C([0,1])$ such that $f_n \to f$. By Corollary 230, it suffices to show that $F(f_n) \to F(f)$.

We have

$$
f_n \to f
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
d_\infty(f_n,f)
=
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)-f(t)| \to 0.
$$

Moreover,

$$
\begin{aligned}
d_\infty(F(f_n),F(f))
&=
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n^2(t)-f^2(t)| \\
&=
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |(f_n(t)-f(t))(f_n(t)+f(t))| \\
&\le
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)-f(t)|
\;
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)+f(t)|.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let

$$
m = \min_{t \in [0,1]} f(t),
\qquad
M = \max_{t \in [0,1]} f(t).
$$

By the Weierstrass Theorem, $m$ and $M$ are well defined. Without loss of generality assume $|m| \le |M|$.

Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $f_n \to f$, there exists $n_\varepsilon$ such that

$$
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)-f(t)| < \varepsilon,
\qquad \forall n \ge n_\varepsilon.
$$

Hence, for all $t \in [0,1]$ and $n \ge n_\varepsilon$,

$$
|f_n(t)+f(t)| < 2|M|+\varepsilon.
$$

Therefore, for all $n \ge n_\varepsilon$,

$$
d_\infty(F(f_n),F(f))
\le
\varepsilon(2|M|+\varepsilon)
\to 0.
$$

Thus $F(f_n) \to F(f)$, and by Lemma 178 the function $F$ is continuous at $f$.


Example 234.  
Fix $t_0 \in (0,1)$, and define $F : A \subset C([0,1]) \to \mathbb{R}$ by

$$
F(f) = f'(t_0),
\qquad \forall f \in C([0,1]).
$$

The domain $A$ consists of all functions in $C([0,1])$ that are differentiable at $t_0$. We prove that $F$ is discontinuous at every point of its domain.

For each $n \ge 1$, let $f_n \in C([0,1])$ satisfy

$$
f_n'(t_0) = 1
\quad \text{and} \quad
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)| < \frac{1}{n}.
$$

For example, define

$$
f_n(t)
=
\begin{cases}
0, & 0 \le t \le t_0 - \frac{1}{4n},\\
t - t_0 + \frac{1}{4n}, & t_0 - \frac{1}{4n} < t \le t_0 + \frac{1}{4n},\\
\frac{1}{2n}, & t_0 + \frac{1}{4n} < t \le 1.
\end{cases}
$$

Given $f \in A$, define

$$
g_n = f + f_n.
$$

Then $g_n \in C([0,1])$ and

$$
d_\infty(g_n,f)
=
\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f_n(t)|
<
\frac{1}{n}
\to 0,
$$

so $g_n \to f$ in $(C([0,1]), d_\infty)$.

However,

$$
F(g_n)
=
(f+f_n)'(t_0)
=
f'(t_0)+f_n'(t_0)
=
F(f)+1,
\qquad \forall n \ge 1.
$$

Hence the sequence $\{F(g_n)\}$ does not converge to $F(f)$, even though $g_n \to f$.

By Corollary 230, $F$ is not continuous at $f$. Since $f$ was arbitrary, $F$ is discontinuous at every point of its domain.


Intuition behind Example 234.

In the sup norm, we measure only the height of a function. The derivative, however, measures slopes. One can build functions that are very small in height but extremely steep near a point. Adding such a “tiny spike” does not change the function much in the sup norm, but it drastically changes the derivative. This mismatch causes discontinuity.


Summary.

- Integration defines a continuous map on $(C([0,1]),d_\infty)$.
- Squaring defines a continuous map on $(C([0,1]),d_\infty)$.
- Differentiation at a fixed point does not define a continuous map on $(C([0,1]),d_\infty)$.

nodes.title: Algebraic propeorties of sequences
The Cauchy Schwarz inequality for vectors and for integrals
nodes.content:
The **Cauchy–Schwarz** inequality states:

$$
|\langle x , y \rangle| \le \|x\|_2\, \|y\|_2
$$
Equivalently:
$$
\left| \sum_{i} x_i y_i \right|
\le
\sqrt{ \sum_{i} x_i^2 }\,
\sqrt{ \sum_{i} y_i^2 }.
$$

Sort of a CS for integrals: 
$$
\left| \int_{0}^{1} f(x) g(x)\, dx \right|
\le
\left( \int_{0}^{1} f(x)^{2}\, dx \right)^{1/2}
\left( \int_{0}^{1} g(x)^{2}\, dx \right)^{1/2}.
$$

nodes.title: Proof CS for vectors
nodes.content:
**Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality (Discrete Version)**

Let x = (x₁,…,xₙ), y = (y₁,…,yₙ) ∈ ℝⁿ.
Define the inner product
$$
\langle x , y \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i
$$
and the induced norm
$$
\|x\| = \sqrt{ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 }.
$$
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality states:

$$
|\langle x , y \rangle| \le \|x\|\, \|y\|.
$$
Equivalently:
$$
\left| \sum_{i} x_i y_i \right|
\le
\sqrt{ \sum_{i} x_i^2 }\,
\sqrt{ \sum_{i} y_i^2 }.
$$

**Equality condition**

Equality holds **if and only if** x and y are linearly dependent, that is:

$$
x = \lambda y \quad \text{for some real } \lambda.
$$


---
**Proof** 

Consider the function of a real variable t

$$
\varphi(t) = \|x - t y\|^2.
$$

By definition of the norm,

$$
\varphi(t)
=
\langle x - t y, x - t y\rangle.
$$

Using Inner product of composite vectors (linked):

$$
\varphi(t)
=
\langle x,x\rangle
- 2 t \langle x,y\rangle
+ t^2 \langle y,y\rangle.
$$
Thus (equal to the squared norm, not the norm itself!)
$$
\varphi(t)
=
\|x\|^2
- 2 t \langle x,y\rangle
+ t^2 \|y\|^2.
$$

This is a quadratic polynomial in t with leading coefficient $\|y\|^2 > 0.$Since
$$
\varphi(t) = \|x - t y\|^2 \ge 0
\quad
\text{for all real } t,
$$
Recall  a quadratic function is ≥ 0 for all real t only if its discriminant is ≤ 0.
Hence: 
$$
(-2\langle x,y\rangle)^2
- 4 \|y\|^2 \|x\|^2
\le 0.
$$
Hence
$$
4 \langle x,y\rangle^2
\le
4 \|x\|^2 \|y\|^2.
$$
Dividing by 4 and taking square roots gives

$$
|\langle x,y\rangle|
\le
\|x\|\,\|y\|.
$$

This proves the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
**Equality condition**

From the quadratic argument, equality holds exactly when the discriminant is 0.
Determinant 0 means that there $\exists$ one and only one real $t_0$ such that (definition of root)
$$
\varphi(t) = \|x - t_0 y\|^2 = 0
$$
As in any normed space:

$$
\|v\|^2 = 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; v = 0.
$$
Hence the condition above is equivalent to: 
$$
x - t y = 0.
$$

Equivalently, x and y are linearly dependent:

$$
x = \lambda y \quad \text{for some real } \lambda.
$$

nodes.title: Inner product for composite vectors
nodes.content:
We expand
$$
\langle x - t y,\; x - t y\rangle.
$$
Thanks to bilinearity*
$$
\langle x , x\rangle
- t\,\langle x , y\rangle
- t\,\langle y , x\rangle
+ t^{2}\langle y , y\rangle.
$$
Then by symmetry and collecting the terms: 
$$
\langle x , x\rangle
-
2 t \langle x , y\rangle
+
t^{2}\langle y , y\rangle.
$$

**Remark 1: what is Bilinearity***

1.
Linearity in the first argument:
$$
\langle u + v , w\rangle
=
\langle u , w\rangle + \langle v , w\rangle,
$$$$
\langle \alpha u , w\rangle
=
\alpha\,\langle u , w\rangle.
$$
2.
Linearity in the second argument:
$$
\langle u , v + w\rangle
=
\langle u , v\rangle + \langle u , w\rangle,
$$
$$
\langle u , \alpha v\rangle
=
\alpha\,\langle u , v\rangle.
$$

**Remark 2: do we need to prove Bilinearity ?
No!** 

The inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is **defined** by three axioms:

**Positivity:**  
$$
\langle x , x \rangle \ge 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \langle x , x \rangle = 0 \iff x = 0
$$

**Symmetry:**  
$$
\langle x , y \rangle = \langle y , x \rangle
$$

**Linearity in the first argument:**  
$$
\langle a x + b y , z \rangle = a \langle x , z \rangle + b \langle y , z \rangle
$$


We only assume the properties above.
From these properties, we can later _derive_ many other facts (Cauchy–Schwarz, triangle inequality, norms, projections, etc.), but the linearity axiom itself is foundational.
Because the inner product is an abstract object: we do _not_ initially assume a formula like  
$$⟨x,y⟩=x1y1+⋯+xn*yn$$
There are many inner products besides the standard dot product!
but they all respect the 3 axioms!
**Example 1.** **Weighted inner product, in  $\mathbb{R}^n$,**
$$
\langle x , y \rangle_w = w_1 x_1 y_1 + \cdots + w_n x_n y_n
$$
where each $w_i > 0$.
**Example 2.** **Matrix-defined inner product**
$$
\langle x , y \rangle_A = x^\top A y.
$$
For any symmetric positive definite matrix $A$,

**Example 3.** **Integral inner product (function spaces)**
On the space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$,
$$
\langle f , g \rangle = \int_0^1 f(t)\, g(t)\, dt.
$$**Example 4.
Inner products on polynomial spaces**

If $p,q$ are polynomials, a valid inner product is
$$
\langle p , q \rangle = p(0) q(0) + p(1) q(1) + p(2) q(2).
$$

nodes.title: Proof CS for continuous functions
nodes.content:
**Claim (Cauchy–Schwarz on [0,1]).**

If f , g : [0,1] → \mathbb{R} are continuous, then

$$
\left| \int_{0}^{1} f(x) g(x)\, dx \right|
\le
\left( \int_{0}^{1} f(x)^{2}\, dx \right)^{1/2}
\left( \int_{0}^{1} g(x)^{2}\, dx \right)^{1/2}.
$$

Moreover, equality holds iff f and g are linearly dependent in the sense that

$$
f = \lambda g \quad \text{on } [0,1]
$$
for some constant $\lambda$.
Because f and g are continuous on a compact interval, all these integrals exist and are finite.
---

# Proof

## 1 Basic idea
Consider the nonnegative function
$$
h_{\lambda}(x) := f(x) + \lambda g(x)
$$
for a real parameter $\lambda$.
Then
$$
\int_{0}^{1} h_{\lambda}(x)^{2}\, dx \ge 0 \qquad \text{for all } \lambda \in \mathbb{R},
$$
because the integrand is $\ge$ 0.
## 2.Expand the square
Compute

$$
h_{\lambda}(x)^{2}
=
f(x)^{2}
+
2\lambda f(x) g(x)
+
\lambda^{2} g(x)^{2}.
$$

Integrate term by term (we can, by continuity):

$$
\int_{0}^{1} h_{\lambda}(x)^{2}\, dx
=
\int_{0}^{1} f(x)^{2}\, dx
+
2\lambda \int_{0}^{1} f(x) g(x)\, dx
+
\lambda^{2} \int_{0}^{1} g(x)^{2}\, dx.
$$

Define the constants

$$
A := \int_{0}^{1} f(x)^{2}\, dx,
\qquad
B := \int_{0}^{1} f(x) g(x)\, dx,
\qquad
C := \int_{0}^{1} g(x)^{2}\, dx.
$$

So for every $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, 

$$
A + 2\lambda B + \lambda^{2} C \ge 0.
$$
A quadratic polynomial is $\ge 0$ for all $\lambda$ iff its discriminant is $\le 0$.
The discriminant is
$$
\Delta = (2B)^{2} - 4 C A = 4 B^{2} - 4 A C.
$$
So
$$
4 B^{2} - 4 A C \le 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
B^{2} \le A C.
$$

Recall what A, B, C were.
This gives exactly

$$
\left( \int_{0}^{1} f(x) g(x)\, dx \right)^{2}
\le
\left( \int_{0}^{1} f(x)^{2}\, dx \right)
\left( \int_{0}^{1} g(x)^{2}\, dx \right).
$$

Taking square roots:

$$
\left| \int_{0}^{1} f(x) g(x)\, dx \right|
\le
\left( \int_{0}^{1} f(x)^{2}\, dx \right)^{1/2}
\left( \int_{0}^{1} g(x)^{2}\, dx \right)^{1/2}.
$$

This is the desired inequality.

nodes.title: DIfferent inner products shape different spaces
nodes.content:
Different inner products measure *lengths* and *angles* differently. So the **shape of space** changes.


Example ‖x‖ = √⟨x,x⟩

And each norm induces a unit ball:

Unit ball = { x : ‖x‖ ≤ 1 }

Different inner products → different shapes for the unit ball:
- Dot product → circle (in R²)
- Weighted inner product → ellipse
- Matrix inner product → tilted ellipse


Changing the inner product changes:
- norms  
- orthogonality  
- projections  
- geometry  

All while keeping the same vector-space structure.

nodes.title: Norms Rationale and definition
nodes.content:
# 0.Intro
We have a vector space and we want to give it in a natural way a nice topological structure.
- Recall that in V = R, $d(x,y) = | x - y |$ , with d1 d2 and d3 collapsing into this.
- We want to give to $\mathbb{R}^n$ a topological structure that is a generalization of the one of the absolute value in R.
To do so, we degine the norm.
# 1.Norms Def
**Definition 245**  
Given a vector space V, a positive functional $\|\cdot\| : V \to [ 0,+\infty)$ is said to be a norm if:

(i)   $\|v\| = 0 \quad \iff \quad v = 0;$

(ii)  $\|v + w\| \le \|v\| + \|w\| \qquad \text{for each } v,w \in V;$ This is called sub-additivity 

(iii)  $\|\alpha v\| = |\alpha|\,\|v\| \qquad \text{for each } \alpha \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and each } v \in V.$

The properties above mimic the properties of the absolute value.
The Euclidean norm is an example of a norm in the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
*NOTE: V is the domain because norm is intended to measure the lenght of a vector while distances are ment to measure the distance between two vectors (two inputs, two points $\in X$)

nodes.content:

**A- Norms for euclidean spaces are equivalent in terms of compactess, continuity etc**

vs

**B- Norm for continnous function spaces are not equivalent!**

nodes.title: Euclidean norms with abs val
nodes.content:
Easy: expand and use ppts of abs val

**Example 249 ** 
In the vector space $\mathbb{R}^n$, the function $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1 : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by:
$$
\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert x_i\rvert
$$
for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ ,    is a norm.
Proof 

Trick: write it explicitely and then use ppt of abs val!
a)  $\|x\|_1 = 0 \iff \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i| = 0 \iff |x_i| = 0\ \forall i = \iff x_i = 0\ \forall i \iff x = 0$

b)  $\|\lambda x\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n |\lambda x_i| \underbrace{=}_\text{leveraging | -  | hom. }  |\lambda| \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i| = |\lambda|\,\|x\|_1$

c) $\|x + y\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i + y_i| \le \sum_{i=1}^n (|x_i| + |y_i|) = \|x\|_1 + \|y\|_1$




**Example Bonus**
Define, for $x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ $$
\|x\|_\infty = \max_{1 \le i \le n} |x_i|.
$$We must check the three norm axioms.
Trick: write it explicitely and then use ppt of abs val!
**1.Non-negativity and definiteness**  
• For each $i$, $|x_i| \ge 0$, hence $\|x\|_\infty = \max_i |x_i| \ge 0$.
• If $\|x\|_\infty = 0$ $\iff$ $\max_i |x_i| = 0$ $\iff$ $|x_i| = 0$ $\forall$ $i$ $\iff$ $x_i = 0$ $\forall$ $i$ $\iff$ $x = 0$.
**2.Homogeneity**  
Let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then
$$
\|\lambda x\|_\infty
= \max_i |\lambda x_i|
\underbrace{=}_\text{hom abs val} \max_i (|\lambda|\,|x_i|)
= |\lambda| \max_i |x_i|
= |\lambda| \|x\|_\infty.
$$
**3.Triangle inequality**  

For each coordinate $i$ we have the usual triangle inequality in $\mathbb{R}$:
$$
|x_i + y_i| \le |x_i| + |y_i|.
$$
Since this holds for every $i$, we may take the maximum over all $i$:
$$
\|x + y\|_\infty
= \max_{1 \le i \le n} |x_i + y_i|
\le
\max_{1 \le i \le n} (|x_i| + |y_i|) \le
\max_{1 \le i \le n} |x_i|
+
\max_{1 \le i \le n} |y_i| = \|x\|_\infty + \|y\|_\infty
$$

Thus the triangle inequality holds for $\|\cdot\|_\infty$.

nodes.title: Ex Euclidean Norms needing integral + CS
nodes.content:
Difficult: expand, remember where you want to go, use ppts of integrals.
Here triangular inequality is done with cauchy 


$\text{Let }x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $$ \|x\|_2= \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}$$
Trick: write it explicitely and then have fun

$\text{(1) Nonnegativity: }x_i^2\ge0\Rightarrow\|x\|_2\ge0.$ Then: 
$$\|x\|_2=0\iff\sum x_i^2=0\iff x_i=0\ \forall i\iff x=0.$$
Notice how important is the $\forall i$ for proving things on vectors


(2) Homogeneity: $$\|\lambda x\|_2=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n (\lambda x_i)^2\right)^{1/2}=\left(\lambda^2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right)^{1/2}=|\lambda|\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\right)^{1/2}=|\lambda|\|x\|_2$$
(3) Subadditivity:

$$\begin{align*}
\|x+y\|_2^2
&= \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i+y_i)^2                                   \\
&\le \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 \;+\; 2\underbrace{\left|\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i\right|}_{\text{by Cauchy–Schwarz } \le\,\|x\|_2\|y\|_2} \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2
 \\
&\le \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 + 2\|x\|_2\|y\|_2 + \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2      \\
&= (\|x\|_2+\|y\|_2)^2                                            \\
\end{align*}$$

Hence taking the square root:$$\|x+y\|_2 \le \|x\|_2+\|y\|_2$$

nodes.title: Norm for continuous functions using absolute val
nodes.content:
Easy: expand and use ppts of abs val




Example 246  In the vector space C([0,1]), the function $\|\cdot\|_{\infty} : C([0,1]) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by
$$
\|f\|_{\infty} = \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f(t)| , \qquad \forall f \in C([0,1]) ,
$$
is a norm.
Trick: write it explicitely and then use ppt of abs val!
**Proof**
-- First, for every continuous $f : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$, the maximum in the definition exists and is finite by the Weierstrass theorem (continuous function on the compact interval $[0,1]$ attains a maximum).
So $\|f\|_\infty$ is well-defined.
1.
Non-negativity and definiteness.
For all $t \in [0,1]$, $|f(t)| \ge 0$, hence $\|f\|_\infty \ge 0$.  
$\|f\|_\infty = 0$ $\iff$ $\max_{t \in [0,1]} |f(t)| = 0$ $\iff$ $|f(t)| \le 0$ $\forall t$ $\iff$ $|f(t)| = 0$ $\forall t$ $\iff$ $f(t) = 0$ $\forall t$, $\iff$ $f$ = 0.
Conversely, if $f = 0$, then $|f(t)| = 0$ for all $t$, so $\|f\|_\infty = 0$.
2.
Homogeneity.
Let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f \in C([0,1])$.
For all $t$ we have $(\lambda f)(t) = \lambda f(t)$, so
$$
\|\lambda f\|_\infty
= \max_{t \in [0,1]} |\lambda f(t)|
\underbrace{=}_\text{by hom of abs value}  |\lambda| \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f(t)|
= |\lambda| \|f\|_\infty.
$$

3.
Triangle inequality.
Let $f,g \in C([0,1])$.
For each $t \in [0,1]$,
$$
|(f+g)(t)| \underbrace{=}_\text{def of sum of functions} |f(t) + g(t)| \le |f(t)| + |g(t)|.
$$
Hence:
$\|f+g\|_\infty\ = \sup_t |f(t)+g(t)|\le \sup_t(|f(t)|+|g(t)|)\le \sup_t |f(t)|+\sup_t |g(t)|=\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$

nodes.title: Norm for continuous functions using absolute val + ppt 1 special
nodes.content:
Trick: write it explicitely and then use ppt of abs val!
7.1.5 Norm $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm

Let$$
X=C([0,1],\mathbb{R}), \qquad \|f\|_1=\int_0^1 |f(t)|\,dt.
$$We verify the three norm axioms.
1.
**Positivity and definiteness**

Since $|f(t)| \ge 0$ for all $t \in [0,1]$, we immediately have

$$
\|f\|_1=\int_0^1 |f(t)|\,dt \ge 0.
$$

- If $f=0$, then $|f(t)|=0$ for all $t$, hence
$$
\|f\|_1=0.
$$

- Conversely, assume
$$
\|f\|_1=\int_0^1 |f(t)|\,dt=0.
$$
Define the auxiliary functions
$$
h(t)=|f(t)| \ge 0,
\qquad
F(s)=\int_0^s h(t)\,dt,
$$
for $s \in [0,1]$.
Then: 
$$
0 \le F(s)=\int_0^s h(t)\,dt \le \int_0^1 h(t)\,dt=\|f\|_1=0
$$

for all $s \in [0,1]$, hence $F(s)=0$ for all $s$.
Since f is continuous, h is continuous, and by Fundamental theorem of calculus F is continuous differentiable  $$F'(s)=h(s)$$Therefore, $$
h(s)=F'(s)=0 \quad \forall s \in [0,1],
$$ which implies $|f(s)|=0$ for all $s$, and thus $f=0$.
2.
Homogeneity

Let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then
$$
\|\lambda f\|_1=\int_0^1 |\lambda f(t)|\,dt
=|\lambda|\int_0^1 |f(t)|\,dt
=|\lambda|\,\|f\|_1.
$$

note we used the homogeneity of the norm!
3.
Triangle inequality.
For every $t \in [0,1]$, the triangle inequality in $\mathbb{R}$ gives
$$
|f(t)+g(t)| \le |f(t)|+|g(t)|.
$$
Integrating both sides,
$$
\|f+g\|_1
=\int_0^1 |f(t)+g(t)|\,dt
\le \int_0^1 |f(t)|\,dt + \int_0^1 |g(t)|\,dt
=\|f\|_1+\|g\|_1.
$$
Conclusion

The function $\|\cdot\|_1$ satisfies positivity, definiteness, homogeneity, and the triangle inequality.
Therefore, $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm on $C([0,1])$.

nodes.title: Norm for continuous functions using absolute val + ppt 1 special + CS for triangular inequality
nodes.content:
Norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ on $C([0,1])$

Let$$
X=C([0,1],\mathbb{R}), \qquad \|f\|_2=\left(\int_0^1 |f(t)|^2\,dt\right)^{1/2}.
$$We verify the three norm axioms.

1. Positivity and definiteness

Since $|f(t)|^2 \ge 0$ for all $t \in [0,1]$, we have

$$
\|f\|_2^2=\int_0^1 |f(t)|^2\,dt \ge 0,
$$
hence $\|f\|_2 \ge 0$.

- If $f=0$, then $|f(t)|^2=0$ for all $t$, so
$$
\|f\|_2=0.
$$
Conversely, assume $\|f\|_2=0$. Then
$$
\int_0^1 |f(t)|^2\,dt=0.
$$
Define
$$
h(t)=|f(t)|^2 \ge 0,
\qquad
F(s)=\int_0^s h(t)\,dt,
$$
for $s \in [0,1]$. Then
$$
0 \le F(s)=\int_0^s h(t)\,dt \le \int_0^1 h(t)\,dt=\|f\|_2^2=0
$$

for all $s \in [0,1]$, hence $F(s)=0$ for all $s$. Since $f \in C([0,1])$, the function $h$ is continuous. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $F$ is continuously differentiable and
$$
F'(s)=h(s).
$$
Therefore,
$$
h(s)=F'(s)=0 \quad \forall s \in [0,1],
$$
which implies $|f(s)|^2=0$ and hence $f(s)=0$ for all $s$. Thus $f=0$.

2. Homogeneity

Let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$. Then$$
\|\lambda f\|_2^2
=\int_0^1 |\lambda f(t)|^2\,dt
=\int_0^1 |\lambda|^2 |f(t)|^2\,dt
=|\lambda|^2 \|f\|_2^2.
$$Note: Since $\lambda x|=|\lambda|\,|x|.$ Squaring both sides gives $|\lambda x|^2=|\lambda|^2\,|x|^2.$

3. Triangle inequality

We compute
$$
\|f+g\|_2^2
=\int_0^1 |f(t)+g(t)|^2\,dt
=\int_0^1 \left(|f(t)|^2+2f(t)g(t)+|g(t)|^2\right)dt.
$$
Thus,
$$
\|f+g\|_2^2
=\|f\|_2^2 + 2\int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,dt + \|g\|_2^2.
$$
By the (integral) Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$
\left|\int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,dt\right| \le \|f\|_2\,\|g\|_2.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\|f+g\|_2^2 \le \|f\|_2^2 + 2\|f\|_2\|g\|_2 + \|g\|_2^2
=(\|f\|_2+\|g\|_2)^2.
$$
Since both sides are nonnegative, taking square roots gives
$$
\|f+g\|_2 \le \|f\|_2+\|g\|_2.
$$

Conclusion

The function $\|\cdot\|_2$ satisfies positivity, definiteness, homogeneity, and the triangle inequality. Therefore, $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on $C([0,1])$.

nodes.title: Norms can always induce distances with particular properties
nodes.content:
### A. Translation Invariance

For all $v,w,x \in V$,
$$
d(v+x,w+x)=\lVert v+x-(w+x)\rVert=\lVert v-w\rVert=d(v,w).
$$
Intuition: shifting both points by the same vector leaves distance unchanged.

### B. Homogeneity
For all $v,w \in V$ and all scalars $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
d(\lambda v,\lambda w)=\lVert \lambda v-\lambda w\rVert=\lVert \lambda (v-w)\rVert=\lvert \lambda \rvert \lVert v-w\rVert=\lvert \lambda \rvert d(v,w).
$$
Intuition: scaling both vectors by $\lambda$ scales their distance by $\lvert \lambda \rvert$.


**BUT not all distances can be induced by norms!

nodes.title: Example how Euclidean norm induces the Euclidean Distance
nodes.content:
## Euclidean Norm

The Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is defined by

$$
\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}\quad \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
$$

Obviously it satisfies the properties of the norm.  For each $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
$$
\lVert x\rVert_2=d_2(x,0).
$$
We can therefore see the euclidean norm as the primitive notion in whose terms it is posisle to define the euclidean distance!  Indeed, more generally, for each $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
$$
d_2(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert_2.
$$
That is: 
$$
d_2(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-y_i)^2}.
$$

nodes.title: Example how Maximum norm induces the Maximum Distance
nodes.content:
## Infinity Norm

The $\infty$-norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is defined by

$$
\lVert x\rVert_\infty=\max_{1\le i\le n}\lvert x_i\rvert.
$$
## Induced Distance

The distance induced by the $\infty$-norm is

$$
d_\infty(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty=\max_i\lvert x_i-y_i\rvert.
$$

nodes.title: Example how a strange norm induces a strange Distance
nodes.content:
## Weighted ℓ¹ Norm

Pick any positive weights $w_i > 0$.

Define the norm:

$$
\lVert x \rVert_{w,1} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \lvert x_i \rvert
$$

This is a valid norm for any choice of positive weights.

**Induced distance:**

$$
d_{w,1}(x,y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \lvert x_i - y_i \rvert
$$

**Intuition:** movements along different coordinates have different “costs”.

nodes.title: But not all distances can be induced by norms
nodes.content: You can just show the distance does not satisfy **translation invariance / homogeneity!**

nodes.title: Discrete distance not induced by a norm
nodes.content:
### The Discrete Metric Is Not Induced by Any Norm


**Claim.**  
There is no norm $\lVert \cdot \rVert$ on $V$ such that

$$
d_{\text{disc}}(v,w) = \lVert v - w \rVert \qquad \forall\, v,w \in V.
$$
### Proof 
Recall a norm has to satisfy: $\|\alpha v\| = |\alpha|\,\|v\| \qquad \text{for each } \alpha \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and each } v \in V.$

Pick any two distinct vectors $v,w \in V$ (so $v \ne w$). Then, by definition of $d_{\text{disc}}$,
$$
d_{\text{disc}}(v,w) = 1.
$$
Let λ = 1/2. Then λv ≠ λw, so again by discreteness,
$$
d_{\text{disc}}\!\left(\tfrac12 v,\tfrac12 w\right) = 1.
$$

But if $d_{\text{disc}}$ were induced by a norm, we would also have the homogeneity property_ 
$$
d_{\text{disc}}\!\left(\tfrac12 v,\tfrac12 w\right)
= \left|\tfrac12\right|\,d_{\text{disc}}(v,w)
= \tfrac12 \cdot 1
= \tfrac12.
$$
a contradiction. Therefore, no norm on V can induce the discrete metric.

nodes.title: Strange distance not induced by a norm
nodes.content:
Let $V$ be a vector space of real functions on $[0,1]$ (e.g. continuous functions), and define

$$
d(f,g) = \int_{0}^{1} \min(\lvert f(t) - g(t) \rvert, 1)\, dt
$$

We show: **this metric is not induced by any norm on $V$.**

### Compute $d$ on a simple example
If it comes from a norm: 
$$d(\tfrac12 f,0) = \lvert \tfrac12 \rvert\, d(f,0)$$
Take the constant function $f(t) \equiv 2$ on $[0,1]$ and the zero function. First,
$$
d(f,0) = \int_{0}^{1} \min(\lvert 2 - 0 \rvert, 1)\, dt
= \int_{0}^{1} \min(2,1)\, dt
= \int_{0}^{1} 1\, dt
= 1
$$
Now scale $f$ by $\tfrac12$. Then $(\tfrac12 f)(t) \equiv 1$, and $$
d(\tfrac12 f,0) = \int_{0}^{1} \min(\lvert 1 \rvert,1)\, dt
= \int_{0}^{1} 1\, dt
= 1
$$Thus $$
d(f,0) = 1, \qquad d(\tfrac12 f,0) = 1
$$If $d$ came from a norm, then positive homogeneity would give
$$
d(\tfrac12 f,0) = \lvert \tfrac12 \rvert\, d(f,0) = \tfrac12
$$
But we computed
$$
d(\tfrac12 f,0) = 1
$$
Contradiction.

nodes.title: Convergence of operations in NVS
nodes.content:
All you do is rearranging everything so that you can exploit your assumption!
Below you have convergence in $|| \cdot ||$
(i) Continuity of addition.
Assume
$$
x_n \underbrace{\to}_{ \text{in }  || \cdot ||} x
\quad\text{and}\quad
y_n \underbrace{\to}_{ \text{in }  || \cdot ||}  y.
$$
Consider
$$
d(x_n+y_n,x+y)
=
\|x_n+y_n-(x+y)\|
=
\|(x_n-x)+(y_n-y)\|\le
\|x_n-x\|+\|y_n-y\|.
$$

Both terms go to $0$ by assumption, hence
$$
d(x_n+y_n,x+y)\to 0.
$$
Therefore,
$$
x_n+y_n \underbrace{\to}_{ \text{in }  || \cdot ||}  x+y.
$$


(ii) Continuity of scalar multiplication.
Assume
$$
\lambda_n \underbrace{\to}_{ \text{in }  || \cdot ||}  \lambda
\quad\text{and}\quad
x_n \underbrace{\to}_{ \text{in }  || \cdot ||}  x.
$$Consider
$$
d(\lambda_n x_n,\lambda x)
=
\|\lambda_n x_n-\lambda x\| = \|\lambda_n x_n-\lambda_n x+\lambda_n x-\lambda x\| 
\underbrace{=}_\text{want to use assmpts above} 
\|\lambda_n(x_n-x)+(\lambda_n-\lambda)x\|
\le
\|\lambda_n(x_n-x)\|+\|(\lambda_n-\lambda)x\|
=
|\lambda_n|\|x_n-x\|+|\lambda_n-\lambda|\|x\|.
$$
The issue with the last expression on the right is that || x || is fixes the other two things are going to 0 but $\lambda_n$ could be going to infinite!
But Since $\lambda_n\to\lambda$, the sequence $(\lambda_n)$ is bounded, so there exists $M>0$ such that $|\lambda_n|\le M$.
Hence,
$$
\|\lambda_n x_n-\lambda x\|
\le
M\|x_n-x\|+\|x\||\lambda_n-\lambda|.
$$
Both terms go to $0$, so$$
\lambda_n x_n \underbrace{\to}_{ \text{in }  || \cdot ||}  \lambda x.
$$
