nodes.title: Continuity in NVS
nodes.content:
## 7.0 Continuous Operators

Let $(V_{1},\lVert \cdot \rVert_{1})$ and $(V_{2},\lVert \cdot \rVert_{2})$ be two normed vector spaces.
An operator $T : V_{1} \to V_{2}$ is continuous at $v \in V_{1}$ if, for each $\varepsilon > 0$ (the house king), there exists $\delta_{\varepsilon} > 0$ such that: $$
\lVert w - v \rVert_{1} < \delta_{\varepsilon}
\implies
\lVert T(w) - T(v) \rVert_{2} < \varepsilon,
\qquad \forall w \in V_{1}
$$ Equivalently, by [[6.6.1 Corollary 230 Sequential characterization of continuity]], $T$ is continuous at $v$ if and only if: $$v_{n} \to v \implies T(v_{n}) \to T(v)
$$ 
Note that this charcaterization is a propoerty linked to metric spaces: basically because from the sequential condition above we can recover (ie we can say that the sequential condition is equivalent to) the e d conditions, which is the pure definition of continuity.
To disprove continuity we often prove we can build a sequence of vectors that witnesses noncontinuity at v
[[Note that linearity implies continuity only in finite dimensional spaces]]

nodes.title: The norm induces a valid distance in NVS
nodes.content:
## Normed Vector Spaces are naturally endowed with a distance
**Lemma 248**  
Let $(V,\lVert \cdot \rVert)$ be a normed vector space, The function $d : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by
$$
d(v,w) = \lVert v - w \rVert \qquad \forall v,w \in V
$$is a distance.
### **1.Definiteness**
**Claim**  $$
d(x,y) = 0 \iff x = y
$$
**Proof**
$$
d(x,y) = \lVert x - y \rVert = 0
$$
By norm definiteness:
$$
\lVert v \rVert = 0 \iff v = 0
$$
Hence
$$
x - y = 0 \iff x = y
$$
---
### **2.Symmetry**
**Claim**  
$$
d(x,y) = d(y,x)
$$
**Proof**
$$
d(x,y) = \lVert x - y \rVert = \lVert -(y - x) \rVert \underbrace{=}_\text{hom. of the norm} \lvert -1 \rvert \lVert y - x \rVert = 1 \lVert y - x \rVert = \lVert y - x \rVert = d(y,x)
$$
---
### **3.Triangle Inequality**
**Claim**  $$
d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)
$$Apply the norm triangle inequality:
$$
d(x,z) = \lVert x - z \rVert \le \lVert x - y \rVert + \lVert y - z \rVert = d(x,y) + d(y,z)
$$\

nodes.title: In every normed vector space The norm itself is a continuous operator
nodes.content:
### 7.0.1 The norm is a continuous Operator

In every normed space $(V,\lVert \cdot \rVert)$, the norm itself   $\lVert \cdot \rVert : V \to \mathbb{R}$   is a continuous (nonlinear) functional.
Proof If $\{v_{n}\}$ is a sequence in $V$ such that $v_{n} \to v$, then by the reverse tringualr inequality:
$$
\big\lvert \lVert v_{n} \rVert - \lVert v \rVert \big\rvert \le \lVert v_{n} - v \rVert \to 0,
$$
Hence:$$
v_{n} \underbrace{\to}_{\text{in} ||\cdot||} v \implies \lVert v_{n} \rVert \underbrace{\to}_{\text{in} ||\cdot||} \lVert v \rVert
$$that is$$||v_{n} \to v ||\implies \lVert ||  v_{n} \rVert \to\lVert v \rVert ||$$

nodes.title: The norm has the Reverse triangular inequality property
nodes.content:
## Lemma 257  
We have
$$
\big\lvert \lVert v \rVert - \lVert w \rVert \big\rvert \le \lVert v - w \rVert
$$
**Proof.**  
For each $v \in V$ it holds
$$
\lVert v \rVert = \lVert v - w + w \rVert \le \lVert v - w \rVert + \lVert w \rVert,
$$
i.e.
$$
\lVert v \rVert - \lVert w \rVert \le \lVert v - w \rVert.
$$
Similarly, for each $w \in V$ it holds
$$
\lVert w \rVert - \lVert v \rVert \le \lVert v - w \rVert.
$$
Hence,
$$
\big\lvert \lVert v \rVert - \lVert w \rVert \big\rvert \le \lVert v - w \rVert.
$$

This is also called the **reverse triangle inequality** (look similitudes $\lVert v + w \rVert \le \lVert v \rVert + \lVert w \rVert$)

nodes.title: Bounded operators
nodes.content:
**Definition 260**  
An operator $T : V_{1} \to V_{2}$ between normed vector spaces is said to be **bounded** if there exists a scalar $K > 0$ such that
$$
\lVert T(v) \rVert_{2} \le K \lVert v \rVert_{1},
\qquad \forall v \in V_{1}.
$$
Note the for every v!
Intuition: “Is there a _single number_ K that controls TT on **every** vector?”


To prove unboundedness you need “No matter how large a stretch limit K you allow,  I can always find a vector that exceeds it.”

$$
\frac{\lVert T(v) \rVert_{2}}{\lVert v \rVert_{1}} \ge K,
\qquad \forall k \in R.
$$

But you see a single k will never work!
A sequence is the best way to do so: because 
$$
\forall K > 0 \;\; \text{ you show that  }\exists n \;\text{such that}\;
\frac{\|T(v_n)\|_2}{\|v_n\|_1} > K.
$$
A sequence is just a **systematic way to win all those challenges at once**.
**Remark.**  
This definition of boundedness **differs** from the usual one for functions.
Recall from Calculus that a function $f : A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded when there exists $M > 0$ such that   $\lvert f(x) \rvert \le M$ for each $x \in A$, i.e., its image is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
A characterization: [[7.2.1 Theorem 261 Bounded unit sphere characterization]]

nodes.title: Bounded unit sphere characterization
nodes.content:
**Lemma 261**  
A linear operator $T : V_{1} \to V_{2}$ between normed vector spaces is bounded **iff** the image   $T(B_{V_{1}})$ of the closed unit ball of $V_{1}$ is a bounded set in $V_{2}$.
Recall: [[unit Ball of V vs sphere]]

**Proof (“Only if”)**  
Let $T : V_{1} \to V_{2}$ be bounded.
Then by [[7.2.1 Definition 260 Bounded Operator in NVS]],
$$
\lVert T(v) \rVert_{2} \le K \lVert v \rVert_{1} \qquad \text{hence} \quad \forall v \in B_{V_{1}} \underbrace{\rightarrow}_{\lVert v \rVert_{1} \le 1.}  \lVert T(v) \rVert_{2} \le K
$$
So every $T(v)$ lies in the closed ball of radius $K$ : $\bar{B}_{K}(0) = \{ w \in V_{2} : \lVert w \rVert_{2} \le K \}$, hence: $T(B_{V_{1}}) \subseteq \bar{B}_{K}(0)$ This is precisely what the line states.
Hence $T(B_{V_{1}})$  is a bounded set in $V_{2}$!
**IF.**  
Suppose $T(B_{V_{1}})$ is bounded in $V_{2}$.
Then there $\exists$ $K' > 0$ such that
$$
T(B_{V_{1}}) \subseteq \bar{B}_{K'}(0).
$$
If $v \in V_{1}$ and $v \ne 0$, consider
$$
\frac{v}{\lVert v \rVert_{1}},
\qquad
\left\lVert \frac{v}{\lVert v \rVert_{1}} \right\rVert_{1} = 1.
$$
Since this vector lies in the unit ball $B_{V_{1}}$, we have
$$
\left\lVert 
T\!\left( \frac{v}{\lVert v \rVert_{1}} \right)
\right\rVert_{2}
\le K'.
$$
Hence:
$$
\left\lVert T\!\left( \frac{v}{\lVert v \rVert_{1}} \right)\right\rVert_{2}
\underbrace{=}_\text{linearity} 
\left\lVert 
\frac{1}{\lVert v \rVert_{1}}\, T(v).
\right\rVert_{2}
\underbrace{=}_\text{norm homogeneity (no need to put abs val)} 
\frac{1}{\lVert v \rVert_{1}}\, \lVert T(v) \rVert_{2}
\le K'
$$

HERE HAPPENS THE MAGIC: Linearity allows you to put the denominator out of the operator!
(as in [[7.3.7 Proposition 259 L Op continuous at a point iff continuous everywhere]]).
Multiplying both sides by $\lVert v \rVert_{1}$ yields

$$
\lVert T(v) \rVert_{2}
\le K' \lVert v \rVert_{1},
\qquad \forall v \ne 0.
$$

The inequality also holds trivially for $v = 0$: $$
\lVert T(0) \rVert_{2} \underbrace{=}_\text{linearity!} 0 \le K' \lVert 0 \rVert_{1} = K' \cdot 0 
$$
Thus $T$ is bounded, completing the proof.
Example!
Example 262

When $V_1 = V_2 = \mathbb{R}$, the only linear operators $T:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ have the form

$$
T(x)=\alpha x
$$

with $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$.
The function $T$ is obviously unbounded on the entire real line.
However, its restriction to the closed unit ball

$$
B_{\mathbb{R}}=[-1,1]
$$

is bounded, since

$$
|T(x)| \le |\alpha|
\quad
\forall x \in [-1,1].
$$

In particular,

$$
T([-1,1]) \subseteq [-\alpha,\alpha].
$$

Therefore, by Lemma 261, $T$ is bounded as a linear operator in the sense of Definition 260.
Indeed,

$$
|T(x)| \le |\alpha|\,|x|
\quad
\forall x \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

The next result shows why we devoted all this attention to boundedness.
Comment: 
A linear operator is therefore bounded **iff** it is bounded in the familiar Calculus sense when restricted to the closed unit ball
Moreover, one can check that for bounded linear operators the image of **any** bounded subset of $V_{1}$, not only $B_{V_{1}}$, is bounded in $V_{2}$.
Hence, restricted to bounded subsets of $V_{1}$, bounded linear operators behave as in the traditional sense.
Basically the calculus defintion looks at the entire domain.
Our definition looks at the unit ball.

nodes.title: Unit sphere
nodes.content:
Unit ball.
The geometry of a normed vector space is encoded by its unit ball.
Let $V$ be a normed vector space.
The unit ball of $V$ is the set
$$
B=\{x\in V:\|x\|\le 1\}.
$$

The unit sphere is the set
$$
S=\{x\in V:\|x\|=1\}.
$$

Geometrically, $\|x\|$ represents the distance of $x$ from the origin.

nodes.title: Example continuous but non linear unbounded operator
nodes.content:
Use $F(f)=\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt$ for each $f \in C([0,1])$.
**Example 264**  
The operator $T : C([0,1]) \to C([0,1])$ of Example 255 is continuous and is not linear.
We prove that $T$ is not bounded.
If $T$ were bounded, then there must exist a constant $K > 0$ such that:
$$
\lVert T(f) \rVert_{\infty} \le K \lVert f \rVert_{\infty}, 
\qquad \forall f \in C([0,1]).
$$
The SAME number K must work for ALL functions in the entire infinite-dimensional space.
Since $T(f) = f^{2}$, this becomes:
$$
\lVert f^{2} \rVert_{\infty} \le K \lVert f \rVert_{\infty} \qquad \forall f \in C([0,1]).
$$
This is what we are going to disprove.
But you cannot do this with one function.
The SAME number K must work for ALL functions in the entire infinite-dimensional space.
To prove that no constant $K$ works, you must show there exist some function such that (recall [[0.0.8 Supremum theorem]])
$$
\sup_{f \ne 0} \frac{\lVert f_n^{2} \rVert_{\infty}}{\lVert f_n \rVert_{\infty}} = +\infty.
$$

Let $f_{n}(t) = e^{nt}$ for each $t \in [0,1]$,  t is chosen to b 1.
We have $\lVert f_{n}^{2} \rVert_{\infty} = e^{2n}$ and $\lVert f_{n} \rVert_{\infty} = e^{n}$, so that:
$$
\frac{\lVert f_{n}^{2} \rVert_{\infty}}{\lVert f_{n} \rVert_{\infty}}
=
\frac{e^{2n}}{e^{n}}
=
e^{n}
\to +\infty,
$$

which proves that such a $K$ cannot exist.
It follows that $T$ is not bounded.
■

nodes.title: 1. Bounded implies Lipshitz continuous
nodes.content:
Assum3 that $T$ is bounded, that is, there exists $k>0$ such that
$$
\|T(z)\|_2 \le k\|z\|_1
\quad
\forall z\in V_1.
$$

Then
$$
\|T(x)-T(y)\|_2
\underbrace{=}_\text{linearity}
\|T(x-y)\|_2
\underbrace{\le}_\text{bounded}
k\|x-y\|_1.
$$

This proves that $T$ is Lipschitz continuous.

nodes.title: Lipschitz continuous
nodes.content:
$T$ is Lipschitz continuous**, that is, there exists $k>0$ such that
$$
\|T(x)-T(y)\|_2 \le k\|x-y\|_1
\quad
\forall x,y\in V_1.
$$

nodes.title: If linear, TFAE
nodes.content:
Let $(V_1,\|\cdot\|_1)$ and $(V_2,\|\cdot\|_2)$ be NVSs and let $T:V_1\to V_2$ be a **linear** operator.
Then the following are **equivalent (TFAE)**:
Continuity: (local property)

- Continuity means that any demanded precision in the output (at a given output point) can be ensured by demanding a sufficiently small precision in the input; engineering intuition: you decide how much output error you accept, this translates in a maximum acceptable input error
- from sequential characterization, NO Surprise: If a sequence of inputs converges to a point, then the sequence of outputs converges to the image of that point; engineering: If the input noise tends to zero (even in a messy, irregular way), then the output noise must also tend to zero.
- Sequential idea: All roads leading to a point must give the same output limi
- Zoom-in principle: Take any graph and zoom in around a point x0, recall that continuity is a local property of points If, after enough zooming, the graph looks like a smooth curve, you can’t see any jumps no matter how much you zoom.
- engineering intuition: Continuity means stability under noise

Boundedness:
“Output grows at most linearly with input size” → global property


**Linearity allows us to generalize local behaviour**

**Differentiability means you must be able to approximate the function locally by a straight line.**

nodes.title: 2. Lipschitz continuous implies continuous everywhere
nodes.content:
Assume (2): $T$ is Lipschitz continuous.
Thus, there exists $k>0$ such that
$$
\|T(x)-T(y)\|_2 \le k\|x-y\|_1
\quad
\forall x,y\in V_1.
$$
We prove that $T$ is continuous.
Let $x\in V_1$ and let $(x_n)$ be any sequence in $V_1$ such that
$$
x_n \to x.
$$
By definition of convergence in a normed vector space,
$$
\|x_n-x\|_1 \to 0.
$$
Applying the Lipschitz inequality with $y=x_n$, we obtain
$$
\|T(x_n)-T(x)\|_2 \le k\|x_n-x\|_1
\quad
\forall n.
$$
Since $\|x_n-x\|_1 \to 0$, it follows that
$$
\|T(x_n)-T(x)\|_2 \to 0.
$$
Therefore,
$$
T(x_n) \to T(x).
$$
By the sequential characterization of continuity, $T$ is continuous at $x$.
Since $x$ was arbitrary, $T$ is continuous on $V_1$.

nodes.title: 3. Continuous everywhere is clearly continuous at a point
4. Continuous at some point implies continuous at 0
nodes.content:
Assume $T:V_1 \to V_2$ is linear and continuous at some point $\bar x \in V_1$. By the sequential characterization of continuity,

$$
x_n \to \bar x \Rightarrow T(x_n) \to T(\bar x).
$$

We prove that $T$ is continuous at $0$, that is if  $$
y_n \to 0  \Rightarrow T(y_n)\to T(0)
$$


Let $(y_n)$ be any sequence in $V_1$ such that
$$
y_n \to 0.
$$
Define
$$
x_n=\bar x+y_n.
$$
y linearity
$$
T(x_n)=T(\bar x+y_n)=T(\bar x)+T(y_n).
$$

We know $$
x_n \to \bar x \Rightarrow T(x_n) \to T(\bar x).
$$ hence $$
T(\bar x)+T(y_n)\to T(\bar x).
$$
Subtracting $T(\bar x)$ from both sides yields

$$
T(y_n)\to 0=T(0).
$$

Therefore, $T$ is continuous at $0$.

nodes.title: 5. Continuous at 0 then bounded
nodes.content:
Let $T:V_1 \to V_2$ be linear.
Assume $T$ is continuous at $0$.
By the sequential characterization of continuity,
$$
x_n \to 0 \Rightarrow T(x_n) \to 0.
$$We prove that $T$ is bounded
Suppose by contradiction that $T$ is not bounded, then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$  there exists $x_n \in V_1$ such that
$$\|T(x_n)\|_2 > n \|x_n\|_1.
$$Define the normalized sequence
$$
y_n=\frac{x_n}{\|T(x_n)\|_2}.
$$ **On the one hand**:  $$
\|y_n\|_1
=\frac{\|x_n\|_1}{\|T(x_n)\|_2}
<\frac{1}{n}.
$$Thus,$$
y_n \to 0.
$$ By continuity of $T$ at $0$, this implies $$
T(y_n) \to 0.
$$


**On the other hand** (simpler than generic continuous case proof wise):

$$
\|T(y_n)\|_2
=\left\| \frac{1}{\|T(x_n)\|_2} T(x_n) \right\|_2
\underbrace{=}_\text{ by homogeneity of the norm! }1.
$$

A contraddiction.
This contradiction shows that $T$ must be bounded.

nodes.title: A linear operator is Continuous everywhere iff bounded
nodes.content:
**Theorem 263**  
A **linear** operator between normed vector spaces is **continuous if and only if it is bounded.**

**Proof**  
Let $T : V_{1} \to V_{2}$ be a linear operator among the normed vector spaces $(V_{1}, \lVert \cdot \rVert_{1})$ and $(V_{2}, \lVert \cdot \rVert_{2})$.
**“If.”**   Suppose that $T$ is bounded.
We prove that $T$ is continuous.
Let $v_{n} \to v$, that is, $\lVert v_{n} - v \rVert_{1} \to 0$.  
$$
\lVert T(v_{n}) - T(v) \rVert_{2}
\underbrace{=}_\text{linearity} \lVert T(v_{n} - v) \rVert_{2}
\underbrace{\le}_\text{boundedness} K \lVert v_{n} - v \rVert_{1} \to 0,
$$
and therefore $T(v_{n}) \to T(v)$.
By [[6.6.1 Corollary 230 Sequential characterization of continuity]], $T$ is continuous at $v$.
**“Only if.”**   Suppose $T$ is continuous.
We show that $T$ is bdd ( $\lVert T(v) \rVert_{2} \le K \lVert v \rVert_{1},\quad \forall v \in V_{1}.$)
Suppose, per contra, that there exists a sequence $\{v_{n}\}$ in $V_{1}$ such that:
$$
\frac{\lVert T(v_{n}) \rVert_{2}}{\lVert v_{n} \rVert_{1}} \to +\infty.
$$
Set $\alpha_{n} = \frac{\lVert T(v_{n}) \rVert_{2}}{\lVert v_{n} \rVert_{1}}$ and $w_{n} = \frac{v_{n}}{\alpha_{n} \lVert v_{n} \rVert_{1}}, \qquad \forall n \ge 1$

A.
Since $\lVert w_{n} \rVert_{1} = 1 / \alpha_{n} \to 0$, we have $w_{n} \to 0$.
Being $T$ continuous, it follows that $T(w_{n}) \to T(0) = 0$, hence $\lVert T(w_{n}) \rVert_{2} \to \lVert 0 \rVert_{2} = 0$ by [[8.1.0 The norm is a continuous operator]].
B, But,
$$
\begin{align}
\lVert T(w_{n}) \rVert_{2}
&= \left\lVert T\!\left( \frac{v_{n}}{\alpha_{n} \lVert v_{n} \rVert_{1}} \right) \right\rVert_{2} \\
&\underbrace{=}_{\text{lin.}} \left\lVert \frac{1}{\alpha_{n} \lVert v_{n} \rVert_{1}}\, T(v_{n}) \right\rVert_{2} \\
&\underbrace{=}_{\text{hom.}} \frac{1}{\alpha_{n} \lVert v_{n} \rVert_{1}}\, \lVert T(v_{n}) \rVert_{2} \\
&= \frac{\lVert T(v_{n}) \rVert_{2}}{\alpha_{n} \lVert v_{n} \rVert_{1}} \\
&= 1.
\end{align}
$$

which contradicts $\lVert T(w_{n}) \rVert_{2} \to 0$.
This contradiction proves that $T$ is bounded.

nodes.title: Continous at a point implies continuous everywhere
nodes.content:
### Proposition 259  
A linear operator $T : V_{1} \to V_{2}$ between normed vector spaces is continuous at a point $v \in V_{1}$  $\iff$ it is continuous on $V_{1}$.

wow: for linear operators, continuity at a single point guarantees continuity on the entire space. AND, to verify whether a linear operator is continuous it is enough to check that it is continuous at one point of $V_{1}$ (for example the neutral element $0$).

### **Proof**
**ONLY if**
Assume $T$ is continuous at a vector $v_{0} \in V$.   We prove that $T$ is continuous at any other vector $v \in V$.

Let $\{v_{n}\}$ be a sequence in $V$ such that 
$$
v_{n} - v \to 0,
$$
and so
$$
v_{n} - v + v_{0} \to v_{0}.
$$
Being $T$ continuous at $v_{0}$ (THIS IS THE MAGIC OF THE PROOF), we have
$$
T(v_{n} - v + v_{0}) \to T(v_{0}).
$$
By the linearity of $T$, this implies
$$
T(v_{n}) - T(v) + T(v_{0}) \to T(v_{0}),
$$
and hence
$$
T(v_{n}) - T(v) \to 0.
$$
By Corollary 230, $T$ is continuous at $v$.

**IF.**
If $T$ is continuous on $V_{1}$, then in particular it is continuous at every point $v \in V_{1}$.  


## Intuition: 

1) linear maps have no location dependence. Proof: The change in output is, using linearity: 
$$
T(x+h)-T(x)=T(h).
$$
Key insight: The output change depends only on $h$, not on $x$.

2) Continuity means: small input changes produce small output changes. For a general function, the size of the output change may depend on where you are. For a linear map, this never happens. So the same small input change always produces the same output change, behavior is identical at every point, there is no local distortion. A linear operator behaves the same everywhere.   This is why continuity at one point implies continuity everywhere.

nodes.title: Always Lipschniz continuous implies continous everhwhere
nodes.content:
## Proposition: Lipschitz implies continuity

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces.
Let $f:X\to Y$ be **Lipschitz continuous**, that is, there exists $L>0$ such that
$$
d_Y(f(x),f(y)) \le L\, d_X(x,y)
\quad
\forall x,y\in X.
$$

Then $f$ is continuous at every point of $X$.
even without linearity 


## Key intuition

Lipschitz continuity gives a **uniform linear bound** on how much the output can change.
Continuity only requires that small input changes give small output changes, without a linear bound.
Thus Lipschitz continuity is strictly stronger than continuity.
## Counterexample: a continuous function that is not Lipschitz (use $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb R$)

Let $X=Y=\mathbb R$ with the usual distance $d(x,y)=|x-y|$.
Define $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ by $f(x)=x^2$.
---

## 1) $f$ is continuous

For any $x_0\in\mathbb R$ and any $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$
|f(x)-f(x_0)|
=
|x^2-x_0^2|
=
|x-x_0||x+x_0|.
$$
As $x\to x_0$, we have $|x-x_0|\to 0$ and $|x+x_0|\to 2|x_0|$, hence the product goes to $0$.
So $f$ is continuous at every $x_0$.
---

## 2) $f$ is NOT Lipschitz on $\mathbb R$

Assume by contradiction that $f$ is Lipschitz on $\mathbb R$.
Then $\exists L>0$ such that for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$,
$$
|x^2-y^2|\le L|x-y|.
$$
Set $y=0$.
Then for all $x\in\mathbb R$, FOR ALL R!!!!!!!!
$$
|x^2|\le L|x|.
$$
If $x\neq 0$, divide by $|x|$:
$$
|x|\le L.
$$
This would mean every real number satisfies $|x|\le L$, which is impossible.
Contradiction.
Therefore $f(x)=x^2$ is continuous but not Lipschitz on $\mathbb R$.

nodes.title: continuous functional is linear iff the kernel is closed set
nodes.content:
# 8.1.5 Linear functional is continuous iff the kernel is closed

## Theorem
Let $$V$$ be a normed vector space and let $$L:V \to \mathbb{R}$$ be a linear functional. Then
$$
L \text{ is continuous } \Longleftrightarrow \ker L \text{ is closed}.
$$

---

## Proof

### (⇒) Continuity implies closed kernel

Assume $$L$$ is continuous.

Let $$\{v_n\} \subset \ker L$$ be a sequence such that
$$
v_n \to v \in V.
$$
To show that $$\ker L$$ is closed, it suffices to prove $$v \in \ker L$$.

Since $$L$$ is continuous,
$$
L(v_n) \to L(v).
$$
But $$v_n \in \ker L$$ implies
$$
L(v_n)=0 \quad \forall n.
$$
Hence,
$$
L(v)=0,
$$
so $$v \in \ker L$$. Therefore $$\ker L$$ is closed.

---

### (⇐) Closed kernel implies continuity

Assume now that $$\ker L$$ is closed and $$L \neq 0$$. Then there exists $$a \in V$$ such that
$$
L(a)=1.
$$

---

### Step 1: Translation of the kernel

Let
$$
H := \ker L.
$$
Define the translate
$$
H+a := \{h+a : h \in H\}.
$$

Since $$H$$ is closed and translations preserve closedness, $$H+a$$ is closed.

We claim that
$$
0 \notin H+a.
$$

Indeed, if $$0 \in H+a$$, then $$a \in H$$ and hence
$$
L(a)=0,
$$
contradicting $$L(a)=1$$.

Thus $$H+a$$ is a closed set not containing the origin.

---

### Step 2: Separation from the origin

Since $$H+a$$ is closed and $$0 \notin H+a$$, there exists $$r>0$$ such that
$$
rB_V \cap (H+a)=\varnothing,
$$
where
$$
B_V := \{x \in V : \|x\| \le 1\}.
$$

---

### Step 3: Control of $$L$$ on a ball

We claim
$$
|L(x)| \le 1 \quad \forall x \in rB_V.
$$

Suppose not. Then there exists $$\bar{x} \in rB_V$$ such that
$$
L(\bar{x})=\gamma \quad \text{with } |\gamma|>1.
$$

Define
$$
y := \frac{\bar{x}}{\gamma}.
$$
Then
$$
\|y\|=\frac{\|\bar{x}\|}{|\gamma|}<r,
$$
so $$y \in rB_V$$.

By linearity,
$$
L(y)=\frac{1}{\gamma}L(\bar{x})=1.
$$

Hence
$$
L(y-a)=L(y)-L(a)=1-1=0,
$$
so $$y-a \in H$$ and therefore $$y \in H+a$$.

This contradicts
$$
rB_V \cap (H+a)=\varnothing.
$$

Thus
$$
|L(x)| \le 1 \quad \forall x \in rB_V.
$$

---

### Step 4: Boundedness and continuity

From the previous step,
$$
L(rB_V) \subset [-1,1],
$$
which implies
$$
L(B_V) \subset [-r^{-1},r^{-1}].
$$

Therefore,
$$
|L(x)| \le \frac{1}{r}\|x\| \quad \forall x \in V.
$$

Hence $$L$$ is bounded, and therefore continuous.

---

## Intuition: one-dimensional picture

Let
$$
H=[1,2] \subset \mathbb{R}, \quad a=2.
$$
Then
$$
H+a=[3,4].
$$

This illustrates that translating a closed set preserves closedness and can move it away from the origin.

---

## Key identities

If $$x \in H$$, then
$$
L(x)=0.
$$

For any $$h \in H$$,
$$
L(h+a)=L(h)+L(a)=1 \neq 0,
$$
so $$h+a \notin H$$.

If
$$
L(x)=1,
$$
then
$$
L(x-a)=0,
$$
so
$$
x \in H+a.
$$

---

## Why linearity is essential

This theorem fails without linearity.

Define $$f:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$$ by
$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
x & x \ge 0\\
x-1 & x<0
\end{cases}
$$

Then $$\ker f=\{0\}$$ is closed, but $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$0$$.

Thus closed kernel does not imply continuity without linearity.

---

## Final takeaway
For linear functionals, continuity is completely characterized by the closedness of the kernel. This relies essentially on linearity.

nodes.title: Topological dual
nodes.content:
Call the set of all continuous linear functionals $L : V \to \mathbb{R}$  the **topological dual** of $V$, denoted by $V^{*}$.
Denote by $B(V1,V2)$ the vector subspace of $L( V1, V2)$ formed by all linear operators $T : V1 \to V2$ that are continuous.
By Proposition 242-(i), it is a vector subspace of the algebraic dual $V'$ (lc of continuous functions are continuous).
By [[7.3.6 Theorem 263 linear and continuous iff Bounded]], every continuous operator $T : V_{1} \to V_{2}$ satisfies:
$$
\lVert T(v) \rVert_{2} \le K \lVert v \rVert_{1} \qquad \forall v \in V_{1},
$$
for some scalar $K > 0$.
Many such $K$ exist; if $K$ works, then any $K' \ge K$ also works.
The relevant quantity is the **smallest** constant $K$ for which the inequality holds for all $v \in V_{1}$.
We know show such K exists.

nodes.title: A minimum scalar exists
nodes.content:
**Lemma 267.** Let $T \in B(V_1, V_2)$.
The set
$$
\{ K \ge 0 : \|T(v)\|_2 \le K \|v\|_1,\ \forall v \in V_1 \}
$$
has a minimum.
**Proof.** Set  $$
A = \{ K \ge 0 : \|T(v)\|_2 \le K \|v\|_1,\ \forall v \in V_1 \}.
$$
- Since $A$ consists of positive numbers, it is obviously lower bounded (logic); 
- By the completeness of $\mathbb R$, it has infimum $\inf A$ (then we don't know if it is a min, that is, if any sequence reaches it).
- It is easy to see that [[A is a closed subset of R]] (instructive proof).
Since $\inf A \in \overline{A}$ [[Theorem the infimum belongs to the closure]], in turn this implies $\inf A \in A$.
Hence $\inf A$ is the minimum of $A$ 
■

nodes.title: Operator norm
nodes.content:
**Definition 268** :  Operator Norm 
Given a $T \in B(V_{1}, V_{2})$, define the quantity $\lVert T \rVert$ by:$$
\lVert T \rVert = \min \{ K \ge 0 : \lVert T(v) \rVert_{2} \le K \lVert v \rVert_{1} \;\; \forall v \in V_{1} \}.
$$

Think of T as a machine:

input: a vector  v

output: the vector T (v).
The operator norm answers:
“In the worst case, how much can this machine stretch vectors?”

nodes.title: Operator norm is a norm
nodes.content:
Norm measures how big is a vector, operator norm measures how big is the stretch generated by an operator on a vector, and, it has the properties of a norm.
We must check the three norm axioms:

1. $\|T\| \ge 0$ and $\|T\| = 0 \iff T = 0$.
2. $\|T_1 + T_2\| \le \|T_1\| + \|T_2\|$.
3. $\|\alpha T\| = |\alpha|\,\|T\|$.
Proof  
**Condition (i)**
- Obviously, $\|T\| \ge 0$ for each $T \in B(V_1,V_2)$: By def $\|T\|$ is the minimum of numbers $K$ with $K \ge 0$.
A minimum of nonnegative numbers is automatically $\ge 0$.
- The neutral element of the vector space $B(V_1,V_2)$ is the zero operator $0 : V_1 \to V_2$: 
$$\|T\| = 0 \underbrace{\iff}_{\|T(v)\|_2 \le \|T\|\,\|v\|_1 \quad \forall v \in V_1}   \|T(v)\|_2 \underbrace{=}_\text{bc is multiplied by 0} 0 \quad \forall v \in V_1 \underbrace{\iff}_\text{norm ppt i. } T(v) = 0 \quad \forall v \in V_1 \iff T = 0 $$
You are applying norm ppt to T(v) why directly not to T first step?
because that property applies to vectors in V1!
T is an operator in B(V1, V2)!
**As to Condition (ii),** given any two operators $T_1$ and $T_2$ in $B(V_1,V_2)$, for each $v \in V_1$ we have:

$$
\|(T_1 + T_2)(v)\|_2
\underbrace{=}_\text{by linearity} \|T_1(v) + T_2(v)\|_2
\le \|T_1(v)\|_2 + \|T_2(v)\|_2
\underbrace{\le}_{\|T(v)\|_2 \le \|T\|\,\|v\|_1} \|T_1\|\,\|v\|_1 + \|T_2\|\,\|v\|_1
= (\|T_1\| + \|T_2\|)\|v\|_1,
$$

which implies $\|T_1 + T_2\| \le \|T_1\| + \|T_2\|$.
**Finally, Condition (iii)** trivially holds if $\alpha = 0$.
**If $\alpha = 0$**, then for every $v \in V_1$, by linearity:
$$
(0T)(v) = 0 \cdot T(v) = 0,
$$Hence
$$
\|(0T)(v)\|_2 = \|0\|_2 = 0,
$$ so the smallest $K \ge 0$ such that
$$
\|(0T)(v)\|_2 \le K\|v\|_1 \quad \forall v
$$ is $K = 0$.
Assume $\alpha \ne 0$.
Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\alpha T\|
&= \min\{K \ge 0 : \|(\alpha T)(v)\|_2 \le K\|v\|_1 \;\forall v\} 
&& \text{(definition of operator norm)} \\[6pt]
&= \min\{K \ge 0 : \|\alpha\,T(v)\|_2 \le K\|v\|_1 \;\forall v\}
&& \text{(by definition of product, $(\alpha T)(v)=\alpha T(v)$)} \\[6pt]
&= \min\{K \ge 0 : |\alpha|\,\|T(v)\|_2 \le K\|v\|_1 \;\forall v\}
&& \text{(use homogeneity ppt $\|\alpha x\|=|\alpha|\|x\|$)} \\[6pt]
&= \min\{K \ge 0 : \|T(v)\|_2 \le \tfrac{K}{|\alpha|}\|v\|_1 \;\forall v\}
&& \text{(divide inequality by positive $|\alpha|$)} \\[6pt]
&= |\alpha|\min\{\tfrac{K}{|\alpha|} \ge 0 : \|T(v)\|_2 \le \tfrac{K}{|\alpha|}\|v\|_1 \;\forall v\}
&& \text{(divide and multiply)} \\[6pt]
&= |\alpha|\min\{\kappa \ge 0 : \|T(v)\|_2 \le \kappa\|v\|_1 \;\forall v\}
&& \text{(rename variable $\kappa = K/|\alpha|$)} \\[6pt]
&= |\alpha|\,\|T\|
&& \text{(last line is exactly the definition of $\|T\|$).}
\end{aligned}
$$


In conclusion, $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm.

nodes.title: Other characterizations for the operator norm
nodes.content:
# 8.2.3 Proposition 270 — Other characterizations of the operator norm.
Let $(V_1,\|\cdot\|_1)$ and $(V_2,\|\cdot\|_2)$ be normed vector spaces, and let $T:V_1 \to V_2$ be a **continuous linear operator**.
All the following expressions define the **same quantity**:  $$
\|T\| = \sup_{v \neq 0} \frac{\|T(v)\|_2}{\|v\|_1}
=
\sup_{\|v\|_1 \le 1} \|T(v)\|_2
=
\sup_{\|v\|_1 = 1} \|T(v)\|_2.
$$
The intuition is just linearity: the stretch on the unit ball is generalizable to any other vector, indeed the only salient counterintuitive point of the proof below uses linearity.
## Proof 
=> By definition of the operator norm, for every $$v \neq 0$$,
$$
\frac{\|T(v)\|_2}{\|v\|_1} \le \|T\|.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\|T\|
\ge
\sup \left\{ \frac{\|T(v)\|_2}{\|v\|_1} : 0 \neq v \in V_1 \right\}
\ge
\sup \left\{ \|T(v)\|_2 : v \in B_{V_1} \right\}
\ge
\sup \left\{ \|T(v)\|_2 : v \in S_{V_1} \right\}.
$$

<= To prove the reverse inequality, set
$$
\alpha := \sup \left\{ \|T(v)\|_2 : v \in S_{V_1} \right\}.
$$

Let $v \in V_1$ with $v \neq 0$, Then, $$
\|\frac{v}{\|v\|_1}\|_1 = 1,
$$
so $$\frac{v}{\|v\|_1} \in S_{V_1}$$.
Hence,
$$
\| T\left( \frac{v}{\|v\|_1} \right)\|_2 \le \alpha.
$$

By linearity of $T$,$$
\|T(v)\|_2
\underbrace{=}_\text{divide and multiply}
\|v\|_1 \| T ( \frac{v}{\|v\|_1} ) \|_2
\le
\alpha \|v\|_1.
$$

For $v = 0$ since $T(0)=0$, the inequality holds for all $v \in V_1$.
Therefore,
$$
\alpha \in \left\{ K \ge 0 : \|T(v)\|_2 \le K\|v\|_1 \ \forall v \in V_1 \right\},
$$
which implies
$$
\|T\| \le \alpha.
$$

Combining with the previous inequalities, we conclude
$$
\|T\|
=
\sup \left\{ \|T(v)\|_2 : v \in S_{V_1} \right\}.
$$

nodes.title: Examples
nodes.content:
# Example 271

Consider the map $F:C([0,1]) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $F(f)=\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt$ for each $f \in C([0,1])$.
The functional $F$ ("take the integral from 0 to 1") is linear on the normed vector space $(C([0,1]),\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ and is continuous.
We compute its operator norm $\|F\|$
## Upper bound
By Proposition 270, $$
\|F\|=\sup \left\{ |F(f)| : \|f\|_\infty=1 \right\}$$
Note we can use the absolute vale of |F(f)| because it is already giving a unidimensional output in $R$!
Write:
$$
|F(f)|
=
\left|\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt\right|
\le
\int_0^1 |f(t)|\,dt
\le
\|f\|_\infty.
$$ Therefore,
$$
\|F\|
=
\sup \left\{ |F(f)| : \|f\|_\infty=1 \right\}
\le 1.
$$
## Lower bound
Consider the constant function
$$
\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}:[0,1] \to \mathbb{R},
\qquad
\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}(t)=1 \ \forall t \in [0,1].
$$ Then
$$
\|\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}\|_\infty=1
$$ and
$$
|F(\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]})|
=
\left|\int_0^1 1\,dt\right|
=
1.
$$ Hence, $$
1
=
|F(\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]})|
\le
\|F\|.
$$
# Example 272
Let $(V_1,\|\cdot\|_1)=(V_2,\|\cdot\|_2)=(C([0,1]),\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ and define the operator $T:C([0,1]) \to C([0,1])$ by $$
T(f)(s)=\int_0^1 (h_1(t)+h_2(s))f(t)\,dt
\quad \forall s \in [0,1],
$$
for each $f \in C([0,1])$, where $h_1,h_2 \in C([0,1])$ are positive functions.
## Upper bound for the operator norm
Recall:
$$
\|T\|
=
\sup \left\{ \|T(f)\|_\infty : \|f\|_\infty=1 \right\}
$$

We compute
$$
\|T(f)\|_\infty
=
\max_{s \in [0,1]}
\left|
\int_0^1 (h_1(t)+h_2(s))f(t)\,dt
\right|
\underbrace{\le}_\text{By triangular Inequality}
\max_{s \in [0,1]}
\int_0^1 |(h_1(t)+h_2(s))f(t)|\,dt$$
$$\underbrace{=}_\text{Since $h_2(s)$ does not depend on $t$,}
\int_0^1 h_1(t)|f(t)|\,dt
+
\max_{s \in [0,1]}
\int_0^1 h_2(s)|f(t)|\,dt.
$$ Using
$$
|f(t)| \le \|f\|_\infty \quad \forall t \in [0,1],
$$
we obtain (after grouping)
$$
\|T(f)\|_\infty
\le
\|f\|_\infty
\left(
\int_0^1 h_1(t)\,dt
+
\max_{s \in [0,1]} h_2(s)
\right).
$$

Hence:
$$
\|T\|
=
\sup \left\{ \|T(f)\|_\infty : \|f\|_\infty=1 \right\}
\le
\int_0^1 h_1(t)\,dt
+
\max_{s \in [0,1]} h_2(s).
$$.
## Lower bound
Consider the constant function
$$
\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}(t)=1 \quad \forall t \in [0,1].
$$ Then
$$
\|\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}\|_\infty=1
$$
and
$$
\|T(\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]})\|_\infty
=
\max_{s \in [0,1]}
\int_0^1 (h_1(t)+h_2(s))\,dt.
$$ Since $h_2(s)$ is independent of $t$,
$$
\|T(\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]})\|_\infty
=
\int_0^1 h_1(t)\,dt
+
\max_{s \in [0,1]} h_2(s).
$$

## Conclusion
Combining both inequalities,
$$
\|T\|
=
\int_0^1 h_1(t)\,dt
+
\max_{s \in [0,1]} h_2(s).
$$
## Comments
The first use of the maximum is a version of the triangle inequality.
The maximum exits the integral because $$h_2(s)$$ does not depend on the integration variable $$t$$.
The restriction $$\|f\|_\infty=1$$ is exactly what the definition of the operator norm requires.

nodes.title: A is a closed subset of R
nodes.content:
Direct “limits of sequences” proof

Take any sequence $(K_n)$ in $A$ such that $K_n \to K$ in $\mathbb R$.
We must prove $K \in A$.
That means two things:
- $K \ge 0$,
- $\|T(v)\|_2 \le K \|v\|_1$ for all $v \in V_1$.
Step 1: $K \ge 0$.
Each $K_n \in A$, so $K_n \ge 0$ for all $n$.
The limit of a sequence of nonnegative reals is also nonnegative, so $K \ge 0$ (Theorem: Order Preservation of Limits).
Step 2: pass to the limit in the inequality.
Fix any $v \in V_1$.
If $v = 0$, then $$\|T(v)\|_2 = \|T(0)\|_2 = 0,
$$ and the inequality $$
\|T(v)\|_2 \le K \|v\|_1
$$ is $0 \le K \cdot 0$, which holds.
If $v \ne 0$, then for every $n$ we have **(because $K_n \in A$):**
$$
\|T(v)\|_2 \le K_n \|v\|_1.
$$ Divide by $\|v\|_1 > 0$:
$$
\frac{\|T(v)\|_2}{\|v\|_1} \le K_n \quad \text{for all } n.
$$ By the same arhiment of the orde rpreservation of limits this implies $$
\frac{\|T(v)\|_2}{\|v\|_1} \le K.
$$Since this holds for every $v \in V_1$, we conclude $K \in A$.

nodes.title: the infimum belongs to the closure

Step 1 — Why $\inf A \in \overline{A}$?
Definition of closure:  
A point $x$ belongs to $\overline{A}$ iff there exists a sequence $a_n \in A$ with $$
a_n \to x.
$$Construction:  
Let $\alpha = \inf A$.
Using the definition of infimum, for each $n$, choose $a_n \in A$ such that $$
\alpha \le a_n < \alpha + \frac{1}{n}.
$$Then:$$
a_n \to \alpha.
$$Hence: $$
\alpha \in \overline{A}.
$$ This is a classical property of infimum:  every infimum is the limit of a decreasing sequence in the set.

nodes.title: Linearity does not imply boundedness in infinite dimensions
nodes.content:
Why linearity does not imply boundedness in infinite dimensions
(and why it does in finite dimensions)



INTUITION: IN FINITE DIMENSIONS ONCE YOU KNOW THE STRATCH ON ONE VECTOR YOU KNOW THE STRATCH ON THE ELEMENTS OF THE BASIS THAT WILL COMPSOE EVERY VECTOR, WHILE WHEN YOU HAVEINFINITE IDMENSION THE STRATCH ON A VECTORS JUST TELLS YOU ABOUT THE STRATCH ON THE ELEMENTS COMPOSING ITS BASIS, OTHER VECTORS WILL HAVE OTHER DIMENSIONS NOT YET EXPLORED, AND THIS GOES TO INFINITY.
= NEW MAS IS CONSTANTLY HIDING IN NEW DIRECTIONS (MASS ESCAPES IN NEW DIRECTIONS)


1.
What linearity actually gives (and what it does not)
Let $T:X\to Y$ be a linear operator between normed spaces.
Linearity means
$$
T(\lambda v)=\lambda T(v)\quad\forall v\in X,\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

This gives perfect control along each fixed direction: once $v$ is fixed, scaling $v$ scales $T(v)$ proportionally.
Equivalently, for each fixed $v\neq 0$,
$$
\|T(v)\|=K_v\|v\|\quad\text{with}\quad K_v:=\frac{\|T(v)\|}{\|v\|}.
$$ Thus linearity always implies
$$
\forall v\in X,\ \exists K_v>0\ \text{such that}\ \|T(v)\|\le K_v\|v\|.
$$Crucial point: boundedness requires one single constant working for all vectors,
$$
\exists K>0\ \text{such that}\ \|T(v)\|\le K\|v\|\quad\forall v\in X.
$$ The difference is purely logical:
$$
\forall v\,\exists K_v\neq\exists K\,\forall v.
$$ The min of a finite set exists yes but the mean of an infinite set?
2 Why finite dimension forces boundedness
Let $X$ be finite dimensional with $\dim X=n$, and let $\{e_1,\dots,e_n\}$ be a basis.
The reason is the presence of only finitely many independent directions.
3 Why infinite dimension breaks boundedness
In infinite dimensions:
there are infinitely many independent directions
linearity imposes no uniform restriction across all of them
the constants $K_v$ may grow without bound as $v$ varies

Each vector is individually controlled, but uniform control may fail.
4.
First counterexample (linear functional)

Define
$$
V=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}:x\ \text{is eventually }0\},\qquad\|x\|_\infty=\sup_n|x_n|.
$$

This is an infinite-dimensional normed space.
Define
$$
f:V\to\mathbb{R},\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n x_n.
$$

The sum is well defined since each $x\in V$ has finitely many nonzero entries.
Let $e_k$ be the standard basis vector.
Then
$$
\|e_k\|_\infty=1,\qquad f(e_k)=k.
$$

Thus
$$
\frac{|f(e_k)|}{\|e_k\|_\infty}=k\to\infty.
$$

No global constant $K$ exists.
Each new direction requires a larger bound.
5.
Second counterexample (derivative operator)

Let
$$
X=C^1([0,1]),\qquad\|f\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|f(x)|.
$$

Define
$$
T(f)=f'.
$$

Linearity is immediate:
$$
T(\alpha f+g)=\alpha f'+g'.
$$

Define
$$
f_n(x)=\sin(nx).
$$

Then
$$
\|f_n\|_\infty=1,\qquad\|T(f_n)\|_\infty=\|f_n'\|_\infty=n.
$$

Hence
$$
\frac{\|T(f_n)\|_\infty}{\|f_n\|_\infty}=n\to\infty.
$$

Again, no uniform bound exists.
The insight is that the norm controls function size, not oscillation, while the derivative detects oscillation.
6.
Final synthesis

Linearity controls scaling along each individual vector, but boundedness requires one uniform constant to control infinitely many independent directions.
Finite dimension forces such uniformity.
Infinite dimension does not.
Therefore:
in finite dimensions, linearity implies boundedness
in infinite dimensions, linearity alone is insufficient

nodes.title: Solving Operator equations with fp
nodes.content:
Operator equations defined by operators $T : V \to V$ that have the same vector space $V$ as both domain and range are especially important.
The solution of such equations can be reduced to the search of fixed points of suitable operators.
For, given any $w_{0} \in V$, consider the operator equation
$$T(v) = w_{0} \tag{8.19}
$$


Then if the rhs is a constant, +- v:  $$T(v) +v = +v + w_{0} \rightarrow v = +v + (w_{0} - T(v))$$

$v + (w_{0} - T(v))$ is just some function of v: $T_w0(v)$

Define $T_{w_{0}} : V \to V$ by
$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{w_{0}}(v) &= w_{0} - T(v) + v \\
             &= w_{0} + (I - T)(v)
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.20}
$$
Then, $\bar{v} \in V$ solves the operator equation (8.19) if and only if
$$
T_{w_{0}}(\bar{v}) = \bar{v}
$$
that is, if and only if $\bar{v}$ is a fixed point of $T_{w_{0}}$$
$$
$$$$Hence note the equivalence:  $$T_{w_{0}}(\bar{v}) = \bar{v} \iff T(v) = w_0
$$
$$$$

$$

$$To solve the operator equation (8.19) thus amounts to finding the fixed points of the operator $T_{w_{0}}$.
In particular, if a fixed point exists for any given $w_{0} \in V$, equation (8.19) can be solved globally.
Otherwise, it is solved locally at the $w_{0} \in V$ for which the fixed point exists.
Note: what if the rhs is not a constant but is depending on x?

nodes.title: Def Contractions
nodes.content:
**Definition 318**  
A selfmap $T : X \to X$ defined on a metric space $X$ is a contraction if there exists a scalar $0 < \alpha < 1$ such that
$$
d\bigl(T(x), T(y)\bigr) \le \alpha\, d(x,y) \qquad \forall x, y \in X.
\tag{9.1}
$$
That is, contractions are Lipschitz functions with constant $\alpha \in (0,1)$.
**Continuity of contractive self-maps**
In turn this easily implies their continuity Using sequential characterization: given any $\{x_n\} \subseteq X$ such that $x_n \to x \in X$, by (9.1) it holds
$$
0 \le d\bigl(T(x_n), T(x)\bigr) \le \alpha\, d(x_n, x) \to 0,
$$

and so $d\bigl(T(x_n), T(x)\bigr) \to 0$.

nodes.title: If exists, the fp of a a-contraction is unique and globally attracting
nodes.content:
**Lemma 319**  
**If it exists,** the fixed point $\bar{x}$ of an $\alpha$-contraction $T : X \to X$ is 
- **Unique** and 
- **Globally attracting**: 
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} d\bigl(T^{n}(x_{0}), \bar{x}\bigr) = 0
\qquad \forall x_{0} \in X .
\tag{9.2}
$$
**Proof**  
We first prove uniqueness.

Suppose $\bar{x}_{1}$ and $\bar{x}_{2}$ are fixed points. Then, for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$,
$$
0 \le d(\bar{x}_{1}, \bar{x}_{2})
\underbrace{=}_\text{def fp} d\bigl(T(\bar{x}_{1}), T(\bar{x}_{2})\bigr)
\le \alpha\, d(\bar{x}_{1}, \bar{x}_{2}),
$$and so $d(\bar{x}_{1}, \bar{x}_{2}) = 0$. As that inequality is possible only if the distance is $0$, because otherwise $\alpha$ would have to be $\ge$. This implies $\bar{x}_{1} = \bar{x}_{2}$, as desired.


As to attractivity, let $x_{0} \in X$. THINK ABOUT THE ORBITS GETTING CLOSER. We have

-  $d\bigl(T(x_{0}), \bar{x}\bigr) = d\bigl(T(x_{0}), T(\bar{x})\bigr) \le \alpha\, d(x_{0}, \bar{x}),$

- $d\bigl(T^{2}(x_{0}), \bar{x}\bigr) = d\bigl(T(T(x_{0})), T(\bar{x})\bigr) \le \alpha\, d\bigl(T(x_{0}), \bar{x}\bigr) \le \alpha^{2} d(x_{0}, \bar{x}).$

- ...

-  $d\bigl(T^{n}(x_{0}), \bar{x}\bigr) \le \alpha^{n} d(x_{0}, \bar{x})  \qquad \forall n \ge1$

and so $\lim_{n \to \infty} d\bigl(T^{n}(x_{0}), \bar{x}\bigr) = 0$. ■


Any sequence $\{T^{n}(x_{0})\}$ of iterates, regardless of the initial point $x_{0}$, thus converges to the fixed point (if it exists). Therefore, the iterates can be regarded as successive, better and better, approximations of the fixed point, which can thus be actually computed, when it exists.  
Uniqueness and the method of successive approximations, ensured by 9.2, will be used for the computation of the fixed point.

nodes.title: Characterization of contractivity with derivatives + example
nodes.content:
Take a function 1) that is a selfmap 2) on a complete metric space.
Conceptual point: If $f$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ then by the Mean Value Theorem, for any $x,y\in[a,b]$ there exists $c$ between them such that

$$
\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y}=f'(c).
$$
Taking absolute values gives
$$
|f(x)-f(y)|\le \alpha|x-y|.
$$

If $$
|f'(x)|\le\alpha<1\quad\forall x\in[a,b],
$$
Then the funciton is contractive.
This allows us to check contractivity using derivatives instead of checking the inequality directly.
Exmaple.
Take:
$$
f(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{4}\quad\text{on }[0,1] \longrightarrow f'(x)=\frac{x}{2}.
$$
On $[0,1]$:
$$
|f'(x)|=\frac{x}{2}\le\frac{1}{2}.
$$
Thus $f$ is a contraction with $\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}<1$.
Then with successive approximations, iterating from $x_{0}=1$, we know this will be converging to the fixed point:
$$
x_{1}=\frac{1}{4},\quad
x_{2}=\frac{1}{16},\quad
x_{3}=\frac{1}{256},\ \ldots
$$

and $x_{n}\to 0$.

nodes.title: Being a contraction on a complete metric space is a sufficient, but not necessary, condition for the existence of a unique and globally attracting fixed point!
nodes.content:
Example 324  The function $f:[0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ given by $$f(x)=2 + \sqrt{x}$$ is not a contraction (Example 445).
In fact,

$$\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x-0}
=\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}}{x}
=\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}
=+\infty
$$

and so, setting $y=0$, it cannot exist $\alpha \in (0,1)$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le\alpha|x-y|$ for each $x,y\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$.
Note you coulld have just heve copmuputed the derivative.
Nevertheless, it has a unique fixed point, which is globally attractive: look at the graph of the mapping $f:[0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ (graph is the intersection with the 45 degree line.

| $n$ | $x_n$ | comment |
|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $2 + \sqrt{0} = 2$ | jumps up |
| $2$ | $2 + \sqrt{2} \approx 3.414$ | increasing |
| $3$ | $2 + \sqrt{3.414} \approx 3.848$ | still increasing |
| $4$ | $2 + \sqrt{3.848} \approx 3.962$ | closer to $4$ |
| $5$ | $2 + \sqrt{3.962} \approx 3.990$ | very close |
| $6$ | $2 + \sqrt{3.990} \approx 3.998$ | $\to 4$ |




It has clearly the unique fixed point $\bar{x}=4$.
Moreover, the sequence of iterates $\{f^{n}(x_{0})\}$ converges increasingly to $\bar{x}$ for every $x_{0}\in[0,\bar{x}]$, while it does decreasingly for $x_{0}\in[\bar{x},\infty)$.

nodes.title: Contractions may not have fp if the space is incomplete!
nodes.content:
# Example 325

The space
$$
X=(0,1)
$$
endowed with the standard metric is **not complete**.
Define the function $f:X \to \mathbb{R}$
by $f(x)=\frac{x}{2}$

Then $f$ is a **contraction** on $X$, but it has **no fixed points** in $X$.
---

## Remark

The unique fixed point would be $x=0,$ but $0 \notin (0,1)$

nodes.title: Banach contraction theorem
nodes.content:
It can be stated in any complete metric space (X, d); Banach space: A normed vector space that is complete!
**Theorem 320 (Banach Contraction Theorem)**  
Let $T : X \to X$ be a **$\alpha$-contraction** defined on a **complete** metric space $X$ $\longrightarrow$ $T$.
Then T has a unique and globally attracting fixed point $\bar{x}$.
Moreover, the following error estimate holds:
$$
d\bigl(\bar{x}, T^{n}(x_{0})\bigr)
\le
\frac{\alpha^{n}}{1 - \alpha}\,
d\bigl(T(x_{0}), x_{0}\bigr)
\qquad \forall x_{0} \in X.
\tag{9.3}
$$
**Proof**  
0.
Let $\{x_{n}\}$ be the seq.
of iterates defined by $x_{n} = T^{n}(x_{0})$, given any $x_{0} \in X$.
WTP: the sequence is Cauchy.
1.
Fix $n$ and take any $m \ge n$.
Since $T$ is a $\alpha$-contraction, by iterating we get
$$
d(x_{m}, x_{n})
\le \alpha\, d(x_{m-1}, x_{n-1})
\le \alpha^{2} d(x_{m-2}, x_{n-2})
\le \cdots
\le \alpha^{n} d(x_{m-n}, x_{0}),
$$
2.
By iterating the triangular inequality on the $x_0$ term:
$$
d(x_{m-n}, x_{0})
\le d(x_{m-n}, x_{m-n-1}) + d(x_{m-n-1}, x_{0})
\le \underbrace{d(x_{m-n}, x_{m-n-1}) + d(x_{m-n-1}, x_{m-n-2}) + \cdots + d(x_{1}, x_{0})}_\text{these are m-n terms}
$$
3.
By iterating the $\alpha$-contraction $T$ ([[9.1.1 Definition 318 Contraction]]) we get:
$$
d(x_{m-n}, x_{m-n-1}) + d(x_{m-n-1}, x_{m-n-2}) + \cdots + d(x_{1}, x_{0})
\le (\alpha^{m-n-1} + \alpha^{m-n-2} + \cdots + 1)\, d(x_{1}, x_{0}).
$$
4.
Hence,$$\begin{aligned}
d(x_{m}, x_{n})
&\le \alpha^{n} d(x_{m-n}, x_{0})
\le \alpha^{n} \bigl(\alpha^{m-n-1} + \alpha^{m-n-2} + \cdots + 1\bigr)\, d(x_{1}, x_{0}) \le \frac{\alpha^{n}}{1 - \alpha}\, d(x_{1}, x_{0}),
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.5}
$$The rhs converges to $0$ as $n \to \infty$.
5.
This is still not exactly [[6.3.0 Definition 192 Cauchy criterion]] in its usual form.
Consider $m, p \ge n$, we have 
$$
d(x_{m}, x_{p})
\le d(x_{m}, x_{n}) + d(x_{n}, x_{p})
\le 2 \frac{\alpha^{n}}{1 - \alpha}\, d(x_{1}, x_{0}),
$$
6.
Since the space is complete, Cauchy sequences converge: there is some point $\bar{x} \in X$ such that $x_{n} \to \bar{x}$ [+].
Since contractions are continuous, we have $T(x_{n}) \to T(\bar{x})$:
$$
T(\bar{x}) \underbrace{=}_\text{Continuity} \lim_{n \to \infty} T(x_{n}) \underbrace{=}_\text{just apply T} \lim_{n \to \infty} x_{n+1} \underbrace{=}_\text{same limit!} \lim_{n \to \infty} x_{n} \underbrace{=}_\text{Completeness} \bar{x}
$$
	The point $\bar{x}$ is thus a fixed point for $T$.
7.
By the previous lemma, it is unique and globally attracting.
8.
Since $x_{m}\to\bar{x}$ as $m\to\infty$ (completeness, written above [+] ), the term $d(x_{m},x_{n})$ converges to $d(\bar{x},x_{n})$.
Substituting this limit into (9.5) gives the estimate (9.3):$$
d(\bar{x},T^{n}(x_{0}))\le\frac{\alpha^{n}}{1-\alpha}d(T(x_{0}),x_{0}).
$$


Under the mild assumption that $X$ is complete, this theorem ensures the existence of fixed points of contractions, which, by Lemma 319, have the remarkable properties of being unique and globally attracting.
The latter property, through the successive approximations $T^{n}(x_{0})$ from any initial point $x_{0} \in X$, gives a procedure — the method of successive approximations — to actually compute the unique fixed point, with an error upper bound given by (9.3).
Such bound depends, at each $n$, only on $x_{0}$ and $\alpha$, and can be thus easily computed.
Note that a careful choice of the norm used determines if T is a contraction or not!
(example done in class)

nodes.title: Operator norm characterization of contraction
nodes.content:
**Proposition 327.**  
A **continuous linear** operator $T : V \to V$ defined on a normed vector space is a contraction $\iff$ $\lVert T \rVert < 1$.
In this case, it is a $\lVert T \rVert$-contraction.
In other words, norms of continuous linear operators are contraction coefficients.
To check whether a linear operator is a contraction thus amounts to checking whether its norm is smaller than $1$.
**Proof.**  
**Only if.** Suppose $T$ is an $\alpha$-contraction.
Then,$$
\lVert T(v) \rVert = \lVert T(v) - T(0) \rVert \le \alpha \, \lVert v - 0 \rVert = \alpha \lVert v \rVert = \alpha
\qquad \forall v \in S_V
$$

By [[8.2.3 Proposition 270 Other characterizations to compute the operator Norm]]: 
By definition:
$$
\lVert T \rVert = \sup_{\lVert v \rVert = 1} \lVert T(v) \rVert .
$$For all unit vectors $v$:
$$
\lVert T(v) \rVert \le \alpha .
$$
Thus:
$$
\lVert T \rVert \le \alpha < 1 .
$$

This proves the “only if’’ direction.
**If** Suppose $\lVert T \rVert < 1$.
By the inequality of proposition 269:    $\lVert T(v) \rVert_{2} \le \lVert T \rVert \,\lVert v \rVert_{1} \qquad \forall v \in V_{1}$

$$
\lVert T(v_1) - T(v_2) \rVert 
= \lVert T(v_1 - v_2) \rVert
\le \lVert T \rVert \, \lVert v_1 - v_2 \rVert
\qquad \forall v_1, v_2 \in V
$$

and so $T$ is a $\lVert T \rVert$-contraction.

nodes.title: Applying banach to the auxiliary operator: the auxiliar operator invertibility
nodes.content:
$T_{w_0}$ is a contraction if and only if the operator $I-T$ is.
For,
 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\|T_{w_0}(v_1)-T_{w_0}(v_2)\|
&=\|w_0-(I-T)(v_1)-(w_0-(I-T)(v_2))\|\\
&=\|(I-T)(v_1)-(I-T)(v_2)\|.
\end{aligned}
$$

By [[8.8 Corollary 326 Banach contraction in Banach Spaces]], we can invoke the Banach Contraction Theorem provided $T_{w_0}$ is a contraction, that is, provided the operator $I-T$ is a contraction (obvious).
This remark becomes especially interesting when $T$ is a continuous linear operator.
Indeed, in this case also the operator $I-T$ is a continuous linear operator.
By the last proposition, $T_{w_0}$ is a contraction if and only if $\|I-T\|<1$.
In this case, $T_{w_0}$ is a $\|I-T\|$-contraction, that is,
$$
\|T_{w_0}(v_1)-T_{w_0}(v_2)\|\le \|I-T\|\,\|v_1-v_2\|
$$
$\forall v_1,v_2\in V.$ (9.7)

nodes.title: Example: contractivity of the Fredholm operator
nodes.content:
# 9.2.4 Contractivity of the Fredholm Operator

## Fredholm equation of the second kind

We consider the Fredholm (operator) equation of the second kind$$
(I-G)(\varphi)=g
$$where$$
G:C([a,b]) \to C([a,b])
$$is defined by$$
G(\varphi)(s)=\int_a^b k(s,t)\varphi(t)\,dt
\quad \forall s \in [a,b].
$$

---

## Fixed point formulation

Set$$
T:=I-G.
$$Define the auxiliary operator$$
T_g:C([a,b]) \to C([a,b])
$$by$$
T_g(\varphi)=g+(I-T)(\varphi)=G(\varphi)+g.
$$ A function $\bar{\varphi} \in C([a,b])$ solves the Fredholm equation if and only if it is a fixed point of $T_g$, that is,
$$
T_g(\bar{\varphi})=\bar{\varphi}.
$$ Thus solving the Fredholm equation is equivalent to finding a fixed point of $T_g$.
## Linear Fredholm operator

For simplicity, we assume $G$ is linear, i.e. $$
G(\varphi)(s)=\int_a^b k(s,t)\varphi(t)\,dt.
$$ Define
$$
M:=\max_{s,t \in [a,b]} |k(s,t)|.
$$ The maximum exists since $k$ is continuous on the compact set $[a,b]^2$.
## Background

Since $T=I-G$, the operator $T_g$ is a contraction if and only if $G$ is a contraction; Indeed,
$$
\|T_g(\varphi_1)-T_g(\varphi_2)\|_\infty
=
\|G(\varphi_1)-G(\varphi_2)\|_\infty.
$$

We present two equivalent proofs.
## Proposition 328
The operator $T_g$ is a contraction with respect to the supremum norm if $$
M<\frac{1}{b-a}.
$$
## Alternative 1: operator norm argument

By Proposition 270, $$
\|G\|
=
\sup \left\{ \|G(\varphi)\|_\infty : \|\varphi\|_\infty=1 \right\}.
$$ For any $\varphi \in C([a,b])$,$$
\|G(\varphi)\|_\infty
=
\max_{s \in [a,b]}
\left|
\int_a^b k(s,t)\varphi(t)\,dt
\right|
\le
\max_{s \in [a,b]}
\int_a^b |k(s,t)|\,|\varphi(t)|\,dt.
$$ Using the definition of $M$,
$$
\|G(\varphi)\|_\infty
\le
M\int_a^b |\varphi(t)|\,dt
\le
M\int_a^b \|\varphi\|_\infty\,dt
=
M(b-a).
$$ Hence,$$
\|G\| \le M(b-a).
$$ If $$
M(b-a)<1,
$$then $$\|G\|<1$$, and therefore $G$ (and thus $T_g$) is a contraction.
## Alternative 2: direct contraction estimate

For any $\varphi_1,\varphi_2 \in C([a,b])$,$$
\|G(\varphi_1)-G(\varphi_2)\|_\infty
=
\max_{s \in [a,b]}
\left|
\int_a^b k(s,t)(\varphi_1(t)-\varphi_2(t))\,dt
\right|.
$$ By monotonicity of the Riemann integral,
$$
\|G(\varphi_1)-G(\varphi_2)\|_\infty
\le
M\int_a^b |\varphi_1(t)-\varphi_2(t)|\,dt
\le
M(b-a)\|\varphi_1-\varphi_2\|_\infty.
$$ Thus $G$ is a contraction whenever
$$
M(b-a)<1.
$$

# Consequences of Contractivity for Fredholm Equations: Existence, uniqueness, and convergence

Assume condition
$$
M(b-a)<1.
$$

Then, by the Banach Contraction Theorem, the Fredholm linear equation
$$
(I-G)(\varphi)=g
$$
has a **unique solution**
$$
\bar{\varphi} \in C([a,b])
$$
for every
$$
g \in C([a,b]).
$$

Moreover, the solution is **globally attracting**.

nodes.title: Example: Contractivity of the Bellman Operator
nodes.content:
# 9.5.2 Bellman Equation

## Setting

Let $$X$$ be a set and let
$$
\Gamma:X \to 2^X
$$
be a correspondence.

Let
$$
\phi:\operatorname{Gr}\Gamma \to \mathbb{R}
$$
be a bounded function, where
$$
\operatorname{Gr}\Gamma=\{(x,y)\in X\times X : y\in \Gamma(x)\}.
$$

In applications:
- $$\phi$$ represents utility,
- $$\beta \in [0,1]$$ is a discount factor,
- $$\Gamma$$ encodes feasibility or technological constraints.

---

## Bellman equation

The Bellman equation is the operator equation
$$
f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x)}\{\phi(x,y)+\beta f(y)\}
\quad \forall x \in X.
$$

Define the **Bellman operator**
$$
T:B(X)\to B(X)
$$
by
$$
T(f)(x)=\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x)}\{\phi(x,y)+\beta f(y)\}.
$$

---

## Lemma 338 — Contractivity of the Bellman operator

If
$$
\beta \in (0,1)
$$
and $$\phi$$ is bounded, then the Bellman operator $$T$$ is a **$$\beta$$-contraction** with respect to the supremum norm.

---

## Proof

### Step 1: Well-definedness

Since $$\phi$$ is bounded, $$T$$ maps bounded functions to bounded functions. Hence
$$
T:B(X)\to B(X).
$$

---

### Step 2: Monotonicity

Let $$f_1,f_2 \in B(X)$$ with
$$
f_1 \le f_2.
$$

Then for all $$x \in X$$ and all $$y \in \Gamma(x)$$,
$$
\phi(x,y)+\beta f_1(y) \le \phi(x,y)+\beta f_2(y).
$$

Taking suprema,
$$
T(f_1)(x)
=
\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x)}\{\phi(x,y)+\beta f_1(y)\}
\le
\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x)}\{\phi(x,y)+\beta f_2(y)\}
=
T(f_2)(x).
$$

Thus $$T$$ is monotone.

---

### Step 3: Discounting property

Let $$c \in \mathbb{R}$$. Then for all $$x \in X$$,
$$
T(f+c)(x)
=
\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x)}\{\phi(x,y)+\beta f(y)+\beta c\}
=
\beta c + T(f)(x).
$$

Thus $$T$$ satisfies the **discounting property**.

---

### Step 4: Contractivity

By the Blackwell Theorem, monotonicity and discounting imply that $$T$$ is a $$\beta$$-contraction:
$$
\|T(f_1)-T(f_2)\|_\infty \le \beta \|f_1-f_2\|_\infty.
$$

---

## Consequences

By the Banach Contraction Theorem, the Bellman equation has a **unique solution**
$$
\bar{f} \in B(X).
$$

Moreover, the solution is **globally attracting**.

---

## Method of successive approximations

For any initial condition
$$
f_0 \in B(X),
$$
define the sequence
$$
f_{n+1}=T(f_n),
$$
that is,
$$
f_{n+1}(x)=\sup_{y\in\Gamma(x)}\{\phi(x,y)+\beta f_n(y)\}.
$$

Then
$$
\|f_n-\bar{f}\|_\infty \to 0.
$$

Thus the solution can be computed by **value iteration**.

---

## Proposition 339 — Existence and uniqueness

If
$$
\beta \in (0,1)
$$
and $$\phi$$ is bounded, then the Bellman equation has a **unique and globally attracting solution** in $$B(X)$$.

---

## Key intuition

- The Bellman operator averages the future via discounting.
- Discounting prevents amplification of differences.
- The contraction property guarantees convergence from any starting point.
- This is the abstract reason value iteration always works.

This is the complete picture.

nodes.title: Characterization of contractivity: Blackwell
nodes.content:
- **Theorem 337 (Blackwell)**  
The self-map $T : B(X) \to B(X)$ is a $\beta$-contraction with respect to the sup-norm if it satisfies the following two conditions:

(i) $T$ is monotone, i.e., $f \le g \Rightarrow T(f) \le T(g)$;
(ii) $T$ has the discounting property, i.e., there  $\exists \beta \in (0,1)$ such that
$$
T(f + c) \le T(f) + \beta c \qquad \forall c \ge 0
$$

**Proof** Let $f, g \in B(X)$. Clearly, $f - g \le \|f - g\|_\infty$. Hence, $f \le g + \|f - g\|_\infty$ and so, by conditions (i) and (ii),
$$
T(f) \le T(g + \|f - g\|_\infty) \le T(g) + \beta \|f - g\|_\infty
$$
which implies $T(f) - T(g) \le \beta \|f - g\|_\infty$, that is,
$$
T(f)(x) - T(g)(x) \le \beta \|f - g\|_\infty \qquad \forall x \in X
$$

Exchanging the role between $f$ and $g$, we also have $T(g) - T(f) \le \beta \|f - g\|_\infty$, that is,
$$
T(g)(x) - T(f)(x) \le \beta \|f - g\|_\infty \qquad \forall x \in X
$$
Hence,
$$
|T(f)(x) - T(g)(x)| \le \beta \|f - g\|_\infty \qquad \forall x \in X
$$
which implies
$$
\|T(f) - T(g)\|_\infty
=
\sup_{x \in X} |T(f)(x) - T(g)(x)|
\le
\beta \|f - g\|_\infty
$$

We conclude that $T$ is a $\beta$-contraction.

nodes.title: Multiplicity of solutions under unboundedness of phi
nodes.content:
# Multiplicity of solutions

When the function $$\phi$$ is not bounded (and hence the previous contraction result does not apply), the Bellman equation may admit **multiple solutions**.  
The following quadratic example provides a simple illustration of this phenomenon.

---

## Example 340

Consider the Bellman equation
$$
f(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}
\left\{
-\frac12 (y-mx)^2+\beta f(y)
\right\}
$$
with
$$
|m|>1.
$$

---

## A quadratic solution

Define the quadratic function
$$
w(x)=-\frac12 \frac{\beta m^2-1}{\beta}\,x^2.
$$

This function is easily seen to be a solution of the Bellman equation provided
$$
\beta>\frac{1}{m^2}.
$$

---

## Attractivity of the quadratic solution

The solution is **attractive** in the following sense.  
Starting from a quadratic function and iterating the Bellman operator, one obtains the recursion
$$
A_n=\frac{\beta m^2 A_{n-1}}{1+\beta A_{n-1}},
$$
where $$A_n$$ are the coefficients of the quadratic functions
$$
w_n(x)=-\frac12 A_n x^2.
$$

For every
$$
A_0>0,
$$
it holds that
$$
A_n \to A=\frac{\beta m^2-1}{\beta}.
$$

---

## Repelling fixed point and multiplicity

The fixed point
$$
A=0
$$
is **repelling**.

The value
$$
A=0
$$
corresponds to the function
$$
w(x)=0\cdot x^2=0,
$$
which is therefore **another solution** of the Bellman equation.

Hence the equation admits **at least two distinct solutions**.

---

## Additional family of solutions

The reader can verify that the family of linear functions
$$
y=ax+\frac12\frac{\beta^2 A^2}{1-\beta},
\quad
\forall a\in\mathbb{R},
$$
also solves the Bellman equation, provided
$$
\beta=\frac{1}{m}.
$$

---

## Key takeaway

When the reward function $$\phi$$ is unbounded, the Bellman operator need not be a contraction.  
As a consequence, **existence of a solution does not imply uniqueness**, and multiple equilibria may arise.

nodes.content:
# 9.9.1 Equivalent Metrics

## Motivation

Checking whether a self-map
$$
T:X \to X
$$
is a contraction can be difficult. Even verifying that some iterate $$T^n$$ is a contraction may be nontrivial.

Two key facts motivate this section:
1. Contractivity may depend on the chosen metric.
2. A map may fail to be a contraction for one metric but become a contraction for an equivalent one.

We formalize this idea via **Lipschitz equivalence of metrics**.

---

## Definition 350 — Lipschitz equivalent metrics

Let $$d_1,d_2$$ be metrics on a set $$X$$.

They are **Lipschitz equivalent** if there exist constants
$$
c_1,c_2>0
$$
such that
$$
c_1 d_1(x,y) \le d_2(x,y) \le c_2 d_1(x,y)
\quad
\forall x,y \in X.
$$

If $$d_1$$ and $$d_2$$ are Lipschitz equivalent, then
$$
(X,d_1) \text{ is complete } \Longleftrightarrow (X,d_2) \text{ is complete}.
$$

---

## Proposition 351 — Equivalent characterizations of eventual contractivity

Let $$T:X\to X$$ be a self-map on a metric space $$(X,d)$$.  
The following conditions are equivalent.

---

### (i) Contracting iterate

$$
T \text{ is Lipschitz and } T^n \text{ is a contraction for some } n \ge 1.
$$

---

### (ii) Uniform exponential bound

There exist $$k>0$$ and $$\alpha \in (0,1)$$ such that
$$
d(T^n x,T^n y)\le k\alpha^n d(x,y)
\quad
\forall n\ge 0,\ \forall x,y\in X.
$$

---

### (iii) Contractive under an equivalent metric

There exists a metric $$\rho$$ Lipschitz equivalent to $$d$$ such that
$$
\rho(Tx,Ty)\le \alpha \rho(x,y)
\quad
\forall x,y\in X
$$
for some $$\alpha\in(0,1)$$.

---

### (iv) Subexponential growth of Lipschitz constants

Let $$k_n$$ be Lipschitz constants of $$T^n$$. Then
$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{k_n} < 1.
$$

---

### (v) Exponential decay of Lipschitz constants

There exists a sequence $$k_n$$ such that
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{k_n} < 1.
$$

---

## Proof structure (idea only)

- (ii) ⇒ (i): exponential decay implies some iterate contracts  
- (i) ⇒ (iii): construct an equivalent metric under which $$T$$ contracts  
- (iii) ⇒ (ii): compare metrics via equivalence constants  
- (v) ⇒ (iv): trivial  
- (iv) ⇒ (i): decay ensures contraction of some iterate  
- (ii) ⇒ (v): explicit construction $$k_n = k\alpha^n$$

---

## Important remarks

### 1. Near-optimal contraction constants

If
$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{k_n}=\alpha,
$$
then for every $$\varepsilon>0$$ there exists an equivalent metric $$\rho$$ such that
$$
\rho(Tx,Ty)\le(\alpha+\varepsilon)\rho(x,y).
$$

---

### 2. Norm-induced metrics

Even if $$X$$ is a Banach space and $$d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$$, the metric $$\rho$$ constructed above need not be induced by a norm.

However, if $$T$$ is linear, then
$$
\|x\|_\rho
=
\|x\|+\frac{1}{\beta}\|Tx\|+\cdots+\frac{1}{\beta^{n-1}}\|T^{n-1}x\|
$$
defines a norm generating $$\rho$$.

---

### 3. Lipschitz regularity is essential

The assumption that $$T$$ is Lipschitz in (i) is crucial.

In general,
$$
T^n \text{ contractive } \nRightarrow T \text{ continuous}.
$$

---

## Weak contraction vs true contraction

The inequality
$$
d(Tx,Ty)\le \alpha d(x,y)
$$
is **strictly stronger** than
$$
d(Tx,Ty)<d(x,y)
\quad
\forall x\ne y.
$$

The latter does **not** guarantee existence of fixed points.

---

## Counterexample

Define
$$
f(x)=x+\frac{1}{1+x}
$$
on $$\mathbb{R}_+$$.

Then
$$
d(f(x),f(y))<d(x,y)
$$
but $$f$$ has **no fixed points**.

---

## Proposition 352 — Edelstein fixed point theorem

Let $$X$$ be a **compact metric space** and let
$$
T:X\to X
$$
satisfy
$$
d(Tx,Ty)<d(x,y)
\quad
\forall x\ne y.
$$

Then $$T$$ has a **unique and globally attracting fixed point**.

---

## Proof idea

- The function $$x\mapsto d(x,T(x))$$ attains its minimum by compactness
- The minimizer must be a fixed point
- Monotonicity of distances along trajectories yields global attraction

---

## Equivalence vs Lipschitz equivalence

Two metrics are **topologically equivalent** if they induce the same open sets.  
This is strictly weaker than Lipschitz equivalence.

---

## Example 353 — Equivalent but not Lipschitz equivalent metrics

On $$\mathbb{R}$$ define
$$
d_1(x,y)=|x-y|,
\quad
d_2(x,y)=|\arctan x-\arctan y|.
$$

Then:
1. $$d_2$$ is a metric  
2. $$d_1$$ and $$d_2$$ are topologically equivalent  
3. $$d_2$$ is incomplete, hence not Lipschitz equivalent to $$d_1$$  

---

## Incompleteness of $$d_2$$

Let $$x_n\to+\infty$$. Then
$$
\arctan x_n \to \frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Hence $$\{x_n\}$$ is Cauchy in $$d_2$$ but does not converge in $$\mathbb{R}$$.

Thus $$d_2$$ is incomplete.

---

## Final takeaway

- Contractivity depends on the metric  
- Equivalent metrics can restore contractivity  
- Lipschitz equivalence preserves completeness  
- Weak contractions need compactness, not completeness  
- Fixed point theory is deeply metric-dependent

nodes.title: Def Iterates
nodes.content:
To see the basic properties of contractions, we need some notation.

Given any self-map
$$
T : X \to X,
$$
its second iterate
$$
T \circ T : X \to X
$$
is denoted by
$$
T^2.
$$

More generally, $T^n$ denotes the $n$-th iterate
$$
T^n = T^{n-1} \circ T,
$$
that is,
$$
T^n(x) = T(T^{n-1}(x))
\quad
\forall x \in X.
$$

We adopt the convention
$$
T^0 = I,
$$
that is, $T^0$ is the identity map.

---

Using the iterates $T^n$ of a self-map $T : X \to X$, we can construct a sequence
$$
\{T^n(x_0)\}
$$
of points in $X$ by starting from any initial point $x_0 \in X$.

NOTE HOW ALL THESE POINTS ARE IN X

These sequences of iterates, called the **orbits** of $x_0$ under $T$, will play a key role.

nodes.title: Exampel auxiliary operator
nodes.content:
## Fixed-point iteration example

### Definition of the operator
Define
$$
T(x) = \frac{1}{2}x.
$$

Choose
$$
w_0 = 10.
$$


Actually this is easy and we can solve it!


It will give us a nice benchmark:
$$
T(x) = 10.
$$

This gives
$$
\frac{1}{2}x = 10
\quad \Rightarrow \quad
x = 20.
$$

Thus, the true solution is
$$
x^* = 20.
$$

---

## Step 2: Define the fixed-point operator

Step by step: 
$$
T(x) = w_0 => T(x) + x = w_0 + x => x = w_0 + x - T(x) => x = 10 + x - \frac{1}{2}x 
$$

Hence:
$$
T_{10}(x) = 10 - \frac{1}{2}x + x = 10 + \frac{1}{2}x
$$

See the error correction spirit: 
$$
T_{w_0}(x) = x  + (10 - T(x))
$$


Now FP theorems will tell us the conditions under which the fp exists!


in this case I tell you these conditions are respected; Methods of successive iterations will alllow you to get the fp.

## Step 3: Start with a bad guess and iterate
Let
$$
x_0 = 0.
$$

The iteration rule is
$$
x_{n+1} = T_{10}(x_n).
$$

### Iteration 1
$$
x_1 = 10 + \frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 = 10.
$$

### Iteration 2
$$
x_2 = 10 + \frac{1}{2}\cdot 10 = 15.
$$

### Iteration 3
$$
x_3 = 10 + \frac{1}{2}\cdot 15 = 17.5.
$$

### Iteration 4
$$
x_4 = 10 + \frac{1}{2}\cdot 17.5 = 18.75.
$$

### Iteration 5
$$
x_5 = 10 + \frac{1}{2}\cdot 18.75 = 19.375.
$$

nodes.title: Example homogenous abstract equation
nodes.content:
## Method of successive approximations

If we have a contraction on a complete metric space the solution $\bar{\varphi}$ can be computed by **successive approximations**.
## Example 330 — Homogeneous Fredholm equation

Consider the homogeneous Fredholm equation
$$
\varphi(s)=\int_a^b k(s,t)\varphi(t)\,dt
\quad \forall s \in [a,b].
$$

If condition
$$
M(b-a)<1
$$
holds, then the **only solution** is
$$
\varphi \equiv 0.
$$
that is, if we have a contraction!
## Why the zero solution is unique
The zero function $$
0 \in C([a,b])
$$ always satisfies the $homogeneous equation$, since $$
(G(0))(s)
=
\int_a^b k(s,t)\cdot 0\,dt
=
0.
$$

Since the solution of the Fredholm equation is unique under condition $M(b-a)<1$, the zero function must be the only solution.

nodes.title: Another Example
nodes.content:
## Aim of the example

We want to solve the homogeneous integral equation
$$
\varphi(s)=\lambda\int_0^1 e^{\,s-t}\,\varphi(t)\,dt
\quad s\in[0,1],
$$
by rewriting it as a fixed-point problem and applying the Banach contraction theorem.

---

## Step 1. Fixed-point formulation

Define the operator $T:C([0,1])\to C([0,1])$ by
$$
(T\varphi)(s):=\lambda\int_0^1 e^{\,s-t}\,\varphi(t)\,dt.
$$

The equation is equivalent to
$$
\varphi=T(\varphi),
$$
so solutions are fixed points of $T$.

---

## Step 2. Why Banach applies

The kernel is
$$
k(s,t)=\lambda e^{s-t}.
$$

On $[0,1]^2$,
$$
|k(s,t)|\le\lambda e.
$$

Hence
$$
\|T\|\le\lambda e(b-a)=\lambda e.
$$

If
$$
0<\lambda<e^{-1},
$$
then
$$
\|T\|<1,
$$
so $T$ is a contraction on $C([0,1])$.

Therefore:
- a solution exists,
- it is unique,
- Picard iterates converge to it.

---

## Step 3. Choice of the initial function

We choose
$$
\varphi_0(t)=e^t.
$$

Reason: the kernel separates as
$$
e^{s-t}=e^s e^{-t},
$$
so functions proportional to $e^t$ are preserved in shape by $T$.

---

## Step 4. Explicit iterates

First iterate:
$$
\varphi_1(s)
=\lambda\int_0^1 e^{s-t}e^t\,dt
=\lambda e^s.
$$

Induction: if
$$
\varphi_{n-1}(t)=\lambda^{n-1}e^t,
$$
then
$$
\varphi_n(s)
=\lambda^n e^s.
$$

Thus
$$
\varphi_n(s)=\lambda^n e^s
\quad\forall s\in[0,1].
$$

---

## Step 5. Limit and conclusion

Since
$$
0<\lambda<1,
$$
we have
$$
\lambda^n\to 0,
$$
and therefore
$$
\varphi_n\to 0
$$
uniformly on $[0,1]$.

The unique fixed point (and unique solution of the equation) is
$$
\varphi^\*\equiv 0.
$$

nodes.title: Correspondence
nodes.content:
Given two sets $X$ and $Y$, a **correspondence** is a multivalued function $\varphi : D \subseteq X \to 2^Y$ with $\varphi(x) \neq \varnothing$ for all $x \in D$ (for each input in the set D the correspondence must return at least one possible value, to each element $x \in D$ we associate a nonempty subset $\varphi(x)$ of $Y$). 

When $\varphi(x)$ is a singleton for all $x \in D$, the correspondence reduces to a function. In particular, all functions $f : D \to X \to Y$ such that $f(x) \in \varphi(x)$ for all $x \in D$ are called **selections** of $\varphi$. A correspondence is a function iff it has a unique selection.

**Example** **A**, we have the correspondence $\varphi(x)$: 
$$
\varphi(1) = \{10, 11, 12\}, \qquad
\varphi(2) = \{20, 21\}, \qquad
\varphi(3) = \{30\}.
$$

nodes.title: Example: the budhet set
nodes.content:
**Example 402.** The budget correspondence $B : \mathbb R_+^{n+1} \to 2^{\mathbb R_+^n}$ is given by the budget set

$$
B(p,w) = \{\, x \in \mathbb R_+^n : p \cdot x \le w \,\}
$$

Note that $B(p,w) \neq \varnothing$ for all $(p,w) \in \mathbb R_+^{n+1}$ since $0 \in B(p,w)$ for all $(p,w) \in \mathbb R_+^{n+1}$.

**The budget set is a correspondence because a single input $(p,w)$ generally corresponds to many feasible choices $x$.

nodes.title: Graph
nodes.content:
**Definition:** The **graph** $\mathrm{Gr}\,\varphi$ of a correspondence $\varphi : D \subseteq X \to 2^Y$ is the set

$$
\mathrm{Gr}\,\varphi = \{\, (x,y) \in D \times Y : y \in \varphi(x) \,\} \subseteq X \times Y
$$

**Example 404.** The graph of the budget correspondence $B : \mathbb R_+^{n+1} \to 2^{\mathbb R_+^n}$ is

$$
\mathrm{Gr}\,B = \{\, (p,w,x) \in \mathbb R_+^n \times \mathbb R_+ \times \mathbb R_+^n : x \in B(p,w) \,\}
$$

**Example B**
 Let $X = Y = \mathbb R$ and consider the correspondence $\varphi : \mathbb R \to 2^{\mathbb R}$ given by

$$
\varphi(x) = [-|x|,\, |x|] \qquad \forall x \in \mathbb R.
$$

For instance, $\varphi(1) = \varphi(-1) = [-1,1]$ and $\varphi(0) = \{0\}$.
As to the graph, it holds

$$
\mathrm{Gr}\,\varphi = \{ (x,y) \in \mathbb R^2 : -|x| \le y \le |x| \}.
$$

nodes.title: Intro: optimization
nodes.content:
# Decision problem of an agent

The problem of decision of an agent consists of a set of possible actions, among which the agent has to choose according to an objective function.
Formally, given any space $$X$$, consider an agent whose objective function
$$
f:A \subseteq X \to \mathbb{R}
$$
is defined on some set of alternative actions $$A \subseteq X$$.
Suppose that a subset
$$
C \subseteq A
$$
represents the actions actually available to the agent in a given decision problem.
The following definition describes the optimal actions in such a problem.

nodes.title: Point of maximum
nodes.content:
# Definition 362 — Point of maximum

Let
$$
f:A \subseteq X \to \mathbb{R}
$$
be a real-valued function and let
$$
C \subseteq A.
$$

An element
$$
\hat{x} \in C
$$
is called a **(global) point of maximum** of $$f$$ on $$C$$ if
$$
f(\hat{x}) \ge f(x)
\quad
\forall x \in C.
$$

The value
$$
f(\hat{x})
$$
is called the **maximum value** of $$f$$ on $$C$$.
---

## Choice (feasible) set

The set $$C$$ is called the **choice set** (or **feasible set**).
In the particular case
$$
C=A,
$$
that is, when the choice set coincides with the entire domain, the element $$\hat{x}$$ is simply called a **point of maximum**.
---

## Maximum value and arg max

The maximum value is unique and is denoted by
$$
\max_{x\in C} f(x).
$$

The points of maximum need not be unique.
Their set is denoted by
$$
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in C} f(x),
$$
that is,
$$
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in C} f(x)
=
\left\{
x \in C : f(x)=\max_{x\in C} f(x)
\right\}.
$$

nodes.title: Example of point of maximum
nodes.content:
## Example

Consider the function
$$
f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}
$$
defined by
$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
x & \text{if } x<1,\\
1 & \text{if } 1\le x\le 2,\\
-x+3 & \text{if } x>2.
\end{cases}
$$

nodes.title: Strict point of maximum is unique
nodes.content:
# Proposition 364 — Strong maximum and uniqueness

A point of maximum is **strong** if and only if it is **unique**, that is, if and only if
$$
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in C} f
$$
is a singleton.

---

## Proof

### Only if

Suppose, by contradiction, that there exist two distinct points of strong maximum
$$
\hat{x}_1 \ne \hat{x}_2.
$$

By definition of strong maximum,
$$
f(\hat{x}_1) > f(\hat{x}_2)
\quad \text{and} \quad
f(\hat{x}_2) > f(\hat{x}_1),
$$
which is impossible.

Hence, a strong maximum must be unique.

---

### If

Assume
$$
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in C} f = \{\hat{x}\}.
$$

Then
$$
f(\hat{x}) \ge f(x)
\quad
\forall x \in C.
$$

Suppose, by contradiction, that $$\hat{x}$$ is **not** a strong maximum.  
Then there exists
$$
y \in C,\ y \ne \hat{x},
$$
such that
$$
f(y)=f(\hat{x}).
$$

But then
$$
f(y)=f(\hat{x})=\max_{x\in C} f(x),
$$
which implies
$$
y \in \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in C} f,
$$
contradicting the fact that $$\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in C} f$$ is a singleton.

Therefore, $$\hat{x}$$ is a strong maximum.

---

## Conclusion

A point of maximum is strong **if and only if** it is unique.
